Hypothesis:
Replacing the “TPHG” framing with a *buried piezoelectric interfacial dipole layer* (PIL) will measurably and falsifiably improve charge extraction and slow degradation in p–i–n perovskite solar cells, provided the electromechanical polarization is (a) sufficiently large at the perovskite/ETL interface, (b) only weakly screened on the relevant time scales, and (c) implemented without transport penalties.

Mechanistic rationale (quantitative and testable): A poled Zn-Car_MOF–polymer composite PIL generates an areal polarization charge density σ at the perovskite/C60 interface under operational strain ε(t) (thermal expansion mismatch + controlled vibration). For a piezoelectric composite with effective d33, σ(t) ≈ d33·Yeff·ε(t), producing a displacement field discontinuity that changes interfacial band bending. Even if the *field inside the perovskite bulk* is largely governed by the built-in potential, a localized Δφ at the extraction interface can reduce interfacial recombination (lower J0) and contact barrier losses, increasing Voc and FF and improving EQE near the band edge where interfacial recombination is most influential.

Screening-limited operating window: Mobile ions screen electric fields over a characteristic Debye length λD and time τscr ~ λD^2/Dion. Therefore the measurable effect will be frequency- and temperature-dependent: at sufficiently high mechanical excitation frequency (f ≫ 1/τscr) and/or reduced Dion (by interface stabilization), the polarization modulation persists during a significant fraction of the carrier extraction time, producing a detectable ΔVoc and ΔJsc under 1-sun. This yields falsifiable signatures: (i) ΔVoc(f,T) should roll off as f decreases or T increases (faster ion motion), and (ii) the sign of ΔVoc and ΔJsc must invert upon reversing PIL poling direction.

Degradation suppression pathway: The primary stabilization claim is *ion-migration/accumulation suppression at the extraction interface* (not “tribo” harvesting): σ(t) periodically counter-biases ionic accumulation at the perovskite/C60 contact, reducing interfacial halide/vacancy pile-up and thus slowing interfacial decomposition and contact barrier growth during MPP operation. A secondary, de-risked catalytic concept is optional: an ultrathin Cu-HHTP “redox-buffer” sub-monolayer is only retained if its electrochemical window is shown (by energy-level alignment and operando analysis) to selectively quench interfacial radicals/iodine-related residues without parasitic carrier loss; otherwise the baseline PIL is pursued without Cu-HHTP.
Plan:
Step 0 — Device baseline and fixed architecture (no tribo claims)
• Baseline PSC: ITO/MeO-2PACz/perovskite/C60/BCP/Ag in p–i–n.
• Perovskite: Cs0.05(FA0.83MA0.17)Pb(I0.83Br0.17)3 (as in outdoor-stability literature) with a thin 2D surface treatment (e.g., PEA-based) reserved as a *constant* across all variants to avoid conflating bulk stability with PIL effects.
• Encapsulation: identical glass–glass + edge seal for all samples used in vibration/thermal tests.

Step 1 — De-risked piezoelectric interfacial layer (PIL) materials and thickness
1.1 PIL composition (transport-safe)
• Replace 50–100 nm PDMS with a *semiconducting or ultrathin insulating, pinhole-free binder* to avoid series resistance:
  – Primary binder: crosslinkable fluorinated polymer or siloxane-acrylate (thin, dense) compatible with C60 deposition.
  – Zn-Car_MOF loading: 5–20 wt% (screened). Target: continuous film with isolated nanocrystals (<50–100 nm lateral) to avoid percolation voids.
• Target thickness: 5–20 nm (hard constraint). A 50–100 nm layer is only tested as a stress-test control after transport is proven.

1.2 Deposition route (coverage + solvent compatibility)
• Deposit perovskite fully; then apply PIL by:
  – Initiated chemical vapor deposition (iCVD) of an ultrathin polymer matrix followed by MOF nanoparticle deposition (dry aerosol/low-solvent), or
  – Orthogonal-solvent spin of MOF dispersion in perfluorinated/weakly interacting solvent plus in-situ crosslink (UV or thermal).
• Confirm pinhole-free coverage before C60:
  – AFM (RMS roughness, pinhole statistics),
  – Cross-sectional TEM (continuous interface, no voiding),
  – XRR/ellipsometry thickness mapping.

1.3 Dipole orientation (key variable)
• Create three PIL states:
  A) Poled “+” orientation (dipoles normal to interface toward ETL),
  B) Poled “−” orientation (reversed),
  C) Unpoled/randomized (mechanically matched control).
• Poling method (buried-layer compatible): apply an external field across ITO/temporary top electrode during PIL curing (Epol ~ 50–150 V/µm depending on breakdown; thickness 5–20 nm reduces required voltage). Validate remanent polarization via PFM/KPFM on reference stacks.

Step 2 — Coupled electromechanical + drift–diffusion modeling (quantitative predictions)
2.1 Electromechanical estimate of σ(t)
• Measure effective composite d33, Yeff on standalone PIL films (on rigid substrate) using piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) and Berlincourt-type d33 meter where applicable.
• Strain mapping in-device:
  – Attach strain gauges to encapsulation and calibrate substrate strain vs shaker amplitude.
  – Finite-element model (FEM): compute interfacial ε(t) for vibration (1–500 Hz) and thermal cycling (25–85 °C).
• Compute σ(t) = d33·Yeff·ε(t) and its sign reversal for inverted poling.

2.2 Screening model (ions)
• Extract ionic diffusivity/conductivity from temperature-dependent EIS (see Step 5): estimate λD and τscr ~ λD^2/Dion.
• Define testable regime: select mechanical frequencies f spanning below and above 1/τscr at multiple T (e.g., 25/45/65 °C) to intentionally cross screening thresholds.

2.3 Drift–diffusion (DD) device simulation with interfacial polarization sheet charge
• Implement a Poisson–DD model (SCAPS/Sentaurus or equivalent) with:
  – A sheet charge ±σ at perovskite/C60 interface,
  – Realistic interfacial recombination velocity Sn/Sp and defect density Dit (from experiments),
  – Ionic species with measured mobility to include dynamic screening.
• Outputs (pre-registered): predicted ΔVoc, ΔFF, ΔJsc and their sign with σ; predicted frequency response ΔVoc(f) under modulated σ(t).
• Falsifiability criterion: if measured ΔVoc/ΔJsc does not match predicted sign inversion and frequency/temperature roll-off, the piezoelectric-field mechanism is rejected.

Step 3 — Transport-risk mitigation and metrics (must pass gates before stability claims)
3.1 Contact/transport resistance
• Measure contact resistivity (ρc) of perovskite/PIL/C60 using TLM-like test structures or conductive-AFM mapping.
• SCLC mobility measurements in electron-only stacks (ITO/SnO2 or ITO/C60 analog)/PIL/C60/Ag as appropriate.
• EIS under illumination: extract transport resistance (Rtr) and recombination resistance (Rrec). Gate: PIL must not increase Rtr by >10% relative to baseline at matched thickness.

3.2 Energy level/energetics preservation
• UPS/KPFM on perovskite vs perovskite+PIL to ensure PIL does not introduce a blocking barrier at C60 contact.
• If barrier detected, adjust binder/MOF loading or introduce ultrathin (<1 nm) dipole/anchoring SAM compatible with C60 (kept constant across controls).

Step 4 — Decisive controls and mechanical protocol (artifact rejection)
4.1 Control matrix (mandatory)
• C0: Baseline (no PIL).
• C1: Mechanically matched non-piezo layer (same polymer thickness, same roughness; MOF replaced with inert nanoparticles).
• C2: Zn-Car_MOF PIL unpoled/random.
• C3: Zn-Car_MOF PIL poled “+”.
• C4: Zn-Car_MOF PIL poled “−”.

4.2 Mechanical stimulation with full metrology
• Use calibrated electrodynamic shaker:
  – Frequency sweep 1–500 Hz; acceleration 0.01–1 g.
  – In-situ strain measurement (strain gauge) and device temperature (IR camera/thermocouple) to decouple heating.
• Run “light-only”, “mechanical-only (dark)”, and “light+mechanical” sequences.
• Lock-in style measurement: modulate mechanical excitation and detect synchronous ΔVoc/ΔJsc to reject drift/light fluctuations.

4.3 Artifact checks
• Measure series resistance Rs vs vibration amplitude (from J–V and impedance) to ensure ΔPCE is not from contact intermittency.
• Post-test microscopy (cross-sectional SEM/TEM) to rule out microcracking delamination.

Step 5 — Quantifying ion-migration suppression (beyond activation energy slogans)
5.1 Temperature-dependent EIS + distribution of relaxation times (DRT)
• Perform EIS (dark and 1-sun bias, near Voc and at MPP) from 1 MHz to 0.1 Hz across 25–85 °C.
• Apply DRT to separate ionic (low-frequency) vs electronic processes.
• Extract ionic conductivity σion(T), characteristic ionic time constants, and compare across C0–C4. Expect: reduced low-frequency ionic signature and slower drift for poled PIL vs controls.

5.2 Bias-stress mapping of ion accumulation
• Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) on cross-sections or EBIC under bias-stress (forward bias at elevated T) to visualize field screening/charge accumulation near perovskite/C60.
• ToF-SIMS depth profiling (I−/Br−/organic cations, metal diffusion) pre/post stress to quantify reduced interfacial ionic pile-up.

Step 6 — AQY/EQE, recombination, and performance under 1-sun steady state
• EQE spectra and integrated Jsc under static and mechanically modulated conditions; analyze where changes occur (band-edge vs blue) to attribute to interfacial recombination vs optics.
• TRPL on perovskite/C60 with and without PIL to quantify interfacial quenching changes; transient photovoltage/photocurrent to separate recombination vs extraction.
• Voc(T, light intensity) analysis to extract ideality factor changes consistent with reduced interface recombination.

Step 7 — Optional Cu-HHTP module (only if non-parasitic is proven)
7.1 Clear chemistry target and energetics
• Target: remove/neutralize iodine-rich interfacial residues (I2/I3−-related) or organic decomposition fragments that create deep traps at perovskite/C60.
• Before integration, determine Cu-HHTP redox window and alignment (UPS/CV). Gate: Cu-HHTP must not introduce an efficient parallel recombination pathway (no reduced Jsc at 1-sun).

7.2 Thickness and placement
• If passed: introduce Cu-HHTP as discontinuous islands or <2 nm equivalent thickness at the PIL surface (not a continuous carrier-consuming layer).

7.3 Operando proof (non-parasitic)
• Operando/near-operando XPS or ambient-pressure XPS (where available) and/or ToF-SIMS: quantify iodine/organic residue evolution under illumination with/without Cu-HHTP.
• EPR spin-trap assays on reference stacks to detect radical suppression.
• Dark/light controls: ensure any chemical change is light-driven but does not reduce photocurrent.

Step 8 — Outdoor-relevant stability with MPP tracking (aligned with established protocols)
• Perform MPP tracking under controlled irradiance/temperature (lab solar simulator with NOCT-like temperatures) and limited outdoor trials.
• Introduce controlled mechanical perturbation blocks (on/off) while keeping irradiance constant; compare energy yield (modeled vs measured) to separate intrinsic degradation from reversible piezo-modulation.
• Endpoint analyses: EIS/DRT, ToF-SIMS, XPS, cross-sectional imaging to connect stability gains to reduced ionic accumulation/contact degradation.

Pre-registered success metrics (falsifiable)
• Sign inversion: poled “+” and poled “−” must produce opposite-signed ΔVoc and/or ΔFF under identical mechanical modulation.
• Frequency dependence: ΔVoc(f) must decrease when f drops below predicted 1/τscr and must vary systematically with temperature.
• No transport penalty: Rs and Rtr must not increase beyond gate thresholds; otherwise abandon thickness/composition and iterate.
• Ion suppression: reduced low-frequency ionic features in DRT and reduced interfacial ion accumulation in ToF-SIMS/KPFM relative to C0–C2.
Feasibility:
1) Addressing the “field too small / screened” critique with a quantitative, falsifiable model
• The proposal no longer asserts a generic 10–50 mV µm−1 bulk field improvement; instead it targets a *sheet-charge-driven interfacial potential modulation* Δφ that primarily reduces interfacial recombination/contact losses. This is the regime where modest interfacial electrostatics can yield measurable ΔVoc via J0 reduction.
• Screening is treated explicitly through τscr extracted from temperature-dependent ionic impedance; the hypothesis predicts a frequency/temperature window and sign inversion upon poling reversal. These are decisive falsification tests.

2) Removing the non-implementable “tribo” claim in a buried interface
• The device is explicitly defined as a piezoelectric interfacial dipole layer (PIL) with no reliance on contact electrification or sliding. No electrode configuration is claimed for triboelectric charge collection.

3) De-risking the interlayer against series resistance, voiding, and solvent incompatibility
• Thickness is reduced to 5–20 nm with pinhole-free validation (AFM/TEM/XRR) and transport gates (ρc, SCLC, EIS-derived Rtr). The original 50–100 nm PDMS concept is treated as high-risk and not the primary path.
• Deposition uses orthogonal/dry or crosslinking routes to protect the perovskite and preserve C60 energetics, verified by UPS/KPFM and contact-resistance metrics.

4) Cu-HHTP ambiguity resolved by gating and operando proof
• Cu-HHTP is demoted to an optional module with explicit pass/fail gates: energetics must not enable parasitic carrier loss; thickness is constrained to sub-nm–2 nm and non-continuous coverage; operando spectroscopy (XPS/ToF-SIMS/EPR) plus dark/light controls must show selective removal of targeted residues without Jsc penalty.

5) Controls and protocol eliminate mechanical artifacts
• Mechanically matched non-piezo controls, unpoled controls, and inverted-poling controls are mandatory.
• Strain is measured directly and correlated to device response; lock-in detection rejects drift and light fluctuations; Rs monitoring and post-mortem microscopy reject contact intermittency and microcracking explanations.

6) Ion migration suppression quantified with state-of-the-art diagnostics
• Temperature-dependent EIS with DRT separates ionic and electronic processes and yields σion(T).
• KPFM/EBIC mapping and ToF-SIMS depth profiling provide spatially resolved evidence for reduced ion accumulation and contact degradation under bias-stress.

Collectively, these changes convert the concept into a model-driven, experimentally falsifiable interface-electrostatics study with explicit transport-risk gates and control experiments that can decisively attribute (or refute) performance/stability changes to piezoelectric polarization rather than morphology or measurement artifacts.
Critique: Methodology is unusually well-specified for an interface-electrostatics hypothesis: tight thickness constraints, pinhole/void metrology, polarity-reversal controls, lock-in detection, and explicit falsifiers (sign inversion + f,T roll-off) are strong. The main scientific risk is magnitude and persistence: the proposed σ(t) derived from d33·Yeff·ε(t) under realistic encapsulated-device strain may be too small once (i) viscoelastic mechanical damping of the binder, (ii) imperfect/relaxing poling in a nanocomposite, and (iii) fast interfacial ionic/electronic screening (including in C60 and at the perovskite surface) are included. The proposal gestures at τscr but does not rigorously bound expected Δφ and resulting ΔVoc (e.g., via J0 sensitivity to interfacial band bending) with realistic parameter ranges; without that, feasibility hinges on detecting very small synchronous signals that could be confounded by piezoresistive/contact micro-motion even with Rs checks. Additionally, the “ion suppression by periodic counter-bias” stabilization pathway is plausible but not uniquely attributable without an explicit comparison to a purely electrostatic (non-piezo) driven-bias waveform control that matches the inferred interfacial Δφ. Finally, relative to the rubric’s required chain, photocatalysis/AQY are not concretely defined (no photocatalytic reaction, no AQY protocol distinct from PV EQE), so grounding against the target chain is incomplete.

Hypothesis: Embedding rigorously verified, halide-stable Co–N4 single-atom sites *within* a thin (5–15 nm) Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) 2D perovskite surface cap—followed by an electronically decoupled Zn-carnosine MOF/thymol molecular reservoir at the outer interface—will measurably reduce hydroxyl-radical (OH•) flux and interfacial Shockley–Read–Hall recombination *without introducing new redox-driven degradation pathways*. The central mechanistic claim is quantitatively falsifiable: (i) Co remains predominantly N-coordinated and single-atom under halide-rich, illuminated, biased conditions; (ii) Co–N4 shifts interfacial oxygen reduction toward benign 2e− pathways with *lower steady-state H2O2 and suppressed H2O2→OH• conversion* relative to halide-labile or redox-inert controls; and (iii) this chemical suppression of ROS, combined with canonical 2D defect passivation, yields a statistically significant increase in implied Voc, reduced interfacial recombination velocity, and higher stabilized maximum-power-point power density under heat/RH/UV stress. The Zn-Car_MOF/thymol layer functions strictly as a chemically protective, antioxidant reservoir whose influence on charge extraction is explicitly deconvoluted and bounded through contact-physics controls.
Plan:
A. De-risking and verification of Co–N4 chemical identity (precondition to device claims).
1) Design of halide-stable vs halide-labile Co controls:
   a) Primary Co–N4 precursor: ZIF-67-derived Co–N fragments pre-chelated with rigid bidentate N-ligands (e.g., bipyridine-dicarboxylate) to kinetically suppress Co–I re-ligation.
   b) Hard negative control: a deliberately halide-labile Co–amine complex (e.g., Co(en)2^2+) introduced identically into the 2D cap to demonstrate failure modes (Co–I/CoOx formation, increased ROS/recombination).
2) Near-operando speciation under realistic conditions:
   a) Co K-edge XANES/EXAFS on biased (Voc and MPP), illuminated 2D/3D stacks in controlled O2/H2O atmospheres to quantify coordination number, bond distances (Co–N vs Co–I/O), and oxidation state drift.
   b) Depth-resolved XPS/ToF-SIMS before and after 100–300 h stress to confirm confinement to top 10–20 nm and absence of metallic Co or cobalt oxide signatures.
   *Decision gate:* progression to full device statistics only if >80–90% of Co signal remains single-atom N-coordinated after stress.

B. Quantitative ORR/ROS selectivity testing (device-relevant translation).
3) Model electrochemical analogs:
   a) Fabricate planar ITO/2D-perovskite/Co–N films (no 3D bulk) as working electrodes for rotating-disk electrode (RDE) measurements in aprotic/low-water electrolytes mimicking perovskite environments.
   b) Extract electron-transfer number (n), H2O2 yield, and kinetic current densities; compare Co–N4 vs halide-labile Co vs Zn–N (redox-inert) controls.
4) Optical/chemical H2O2 assays on simplified stacks:
   a) Apply Amplex Red/HRP on optically isolated, encapsulation-free test stacks under controlled illumination and bias to quantify steady-state H2O2.
   b) Correlate H2O2 levels with OH• adduct intensity (EPR) to explicitly test whether Co–N suppresses or accelerates H2O2→OH• conversion.

C. Validated operando EPR methodology (artifact mitigation).
5) Spin-trap access and stability checks:
   a) Diffusion/penetration tests using fluorescently labeled analogs to verify access to the 2D-cap interface.
   b) Optical controls quantifying spin-trap photolysis under identical UV/visible spectra.
   c) Calibration stacks with known OH• generators to establish detection limits and linearity.
6) Full-device EPR only after validation on simplified stacks; report absolute signal normalization to absorbed photon flux and device area.

D. Proof of electronic benignity of Co–N seeding.
7) Absolute PLQY and implied Voc at matched 2D thickness for: 2D-only, 2D+Co–N, 2D+halide-labile Co.
8) Temperature-dependent PL/TRPL and transient absorption spectroscopy to extract SRH activation energies and rule out new mid-gap states.
9) Confocal PL/EL mapping to confirm spatial homogeneity and exclude Co clustering-induced recombination hotspots.

E. Zn-Car_MOF/thymol: separation of chemical protection from contact physics.
10) MOF synthesis and SSA–thymol metrics on powders and flat witness films (BET, TGA, adsorption isotherms) to establish intrinsic capacity.
11) Thin-film relevance:
    a) Ellipsometric porosimetry/QCM on nm-scale MOF films to estimate accessible porosity and thymol uptake.
    b) Thymol photostability and release kinetics under illumination/heat (GC–MS).
12) Contact deconvolution controls:
    a) HTL (PTAA) or ETL (C60) deposition on MOF-free vs MOF-bearing surfaces with identical perovskite quality.
    b) Kelvin probe/UPS to quantify surface dipole shifts; TLM or impedance-derived contact resistance to bound Voc/FF effects unrelated to ROS.

F. Device endpoints.
13) MPP tracking (300–1000 h, 65 °C, 30–50% RH, UV-enriched) reporting stabilized power density, T80/T90, hysteresis, and Rs/Rsh evolution.
14) Full control matrix to isolate each mechanism (no cap, 2D-only, Co–N-only, MOF-only, thymol-only, Zn–N control, halide-labile Co failure case).
Feasibility: The revised plan directly addresses the principal scientific risks by imposing explicit decision gates and negative controls. In situ/near-operando Co K-edge XAS and depth-resolved XPS provide unambiguous speciation under halide-rich, illuminated conditions, preventing over-interpretation of nominal Co–N chemistry. ORR pathway selectivity is translated from electrocatalysis to perovskite-relevant energetics via RDE analogs and optical H2O2 assays, enabling quantitative correlation between H2O2, OH•, and device degradation. Operando EPR is de-risked through staged validation, penetration tests, and photochemical controls. Electronic benignity is enforced by absolute PLQY/implied-Voc improvements and temperature-dependent recombination analysis, while spatial imaging rules out clustering artifacts. Finally, the Zn-Car_MOF/thymol layer is rigorously decoupled from charge extraction through surface dipole, contact resistance, and nucleation controls, ensuring that any gains in stabilized power density can be causally attributed to reduced ROS flux and suppressed interfacial recombination rather than contact artifacts. Together, these measures convert the catalytic-chemistry claim into a falsifiable, quantitatively constrained hypothesis aligned with state-of-the-art perovskite photovoltaic physics.
Critique: The proposal is unusually strong in experimental rigor: it anticipates the key failure mode (Co speciation drift to Co–I/CoOx or clustering) and installs appropriate negative controls and a quantitative decision gate using near-operando XAS/XPS/ToF-SIMS. The ORR/ROS package is also thoughtfully staged (RDE analogs → optical H2O2 assay → EPR) with explicit artifact controls, and the contact-deconvolution plan for the Zn-Car_MOF/thymol cap is a needed safeguard against falsely attributing Voc/FF changes to chemistry. Main score deductions arise from (1) environmental mismatch risk in the RDE translation: aprotic/low-water electrolytes and planar electrodes may not reproduce the perovskite interfacial microenvironment (halide activity, local fields, ionic migration, heterogeneous water activity), so inferred n and H2O2 yield may not map uniquely to device operation; (2) an under-specified mechanistic partition between thymol vs carnosine vs Zn-Car_MOF: the proposal asserts an ‘antioxidant reservoir’ but does not provide a quantitative, falsifiable mass-balance/flux framework linking MOF specific surface area and thymol loading/release to an expected reduction in OH• flux at the buried interface; (3) insufficiently bounded redox and coordination chemistry of Co–N4 under illumination: even if Co remains atomically dispersed, changes in Co valence and potential Fenton-like activity (or H2O2 activation) are acknowledged but not constrained by a clear kinetic model with measurable rate constants under device-relevant potentials; and (4) the 5–15 nm RP cap plus embedded single atoms introduces a nontrivial possibility of altered band alignment, dielectric environment, and ion-transport bottlenecks that could masquerade as ‘recombination suppression’—the deconvolution plan is good, but not yet fully closed with a quantitative drift-diffusion/impedance model that predicts the magnitude of contact vs recombination changes.

Hypothesis: A hierarchically porous, electrically percolating MOF-on-fiber interfacial scaffold can be made *functionally dual* (ionic buffering + electronic extraction) if—and only if—two quantitative conditions are simultaneously met: (H1) a depth-limited, self-terminating conversion of only the outer 1–3 nm of nm-scale ZIF-8 crystallites into a continuous N-rich conjugated “skin” that lowers interlayer sheet resistance by ≥10× while preserving ≥80% of the original ZIF-8 micropore capacity and micropore uptake kinetics; and (H2) the preserved ZIF-8 micropores are loaded with *device-relevant, size-compatible mobile species* that ZIF-8 can actually admit and bind under operational fields/chemical potentials, yielding measurable field-driven uptake/release hysteresis suppression. Mechanistically, the scaffold is engineered to decouple transport: (i) electronic percolation is provided by a conductive nanofiber backbone plus an ultrathin, partially graphitized N-rich surface skin that forms low-barrier contacts to adjacent transport layers and avoids an insulating barrier; (ii) ionic polarization is reduced not by assuming free halide passage through hydrophobic 3.4 Å apertures, but by targeting and immobilizing the most mobile *small* ionic species at the interface (notably Li+ from spiro-OMeTAD doping, and small halide-related complexes that can access/adsorb at ZIF-8 pore mouths and defect sites), and by hosting tethered/immobilized cationic passivators within accessible micropores to pin halide vacancies electrostatically at the perovskite-facing boundary. The preserved internal ZIF-8 microporosity thus acts as a high-SSA ‘interfacial ionic capacitance buffer’ (adsorption + slowed release) that reduces low-frequency ionic capacitance and bias-stress drift, while the gradient-conductive skin + fiber network prevents interfacial electronic charge pileup (higher QFLS/Voc) and limits recombination. If these constraints are met, the PSC will show simultaneously improved Voc (reduced non-radiative loss), FF (reduced ionic polarization/series resistance penalties), and operational stability. The stabilized DC output will translate into demonstrably steadier direct-coupled PV-to-electrolyzer hydrogen generation without masking by power electronics.
Plan:
Step 0 — Pre-define quantitative design constraints (go/no-go gating)
0.1 Target interlayer geometry: total thickness 10–25 nm; fiber areal coverage 10–30% (revised upward from 5–20% to meet percolation and contact constraints while still limiting optical/shunt risks); ZIF-8 shell thickness 5–12 nm; ZIF-8 crystallite size ≤15–20 nm.
0.2 Electrical constraints (must not add Rs): interlayer sheet resistance Rsh reduction ≥10× after skin formation; contact resistivity to adjacent TLs < 10−3 Ω·cm2 (TLM); CAFM maps show continuous conduction paths (no isolated conductive islands over >90% scanned area).
0.3 Porosity constraints: ≥80% retained micropore capacity (ellipsometric porosimetry on sister thin films) and ≤20% change in micropore uptake time constant (kinetics) after skin formation.
0.4 Ionic-buffering constraints: demonstrate bias-dependent uptake/release of targeted species in symmetric test stacks with a measurable reduction of low-frequency capacitance (DRT-EIS) by ≥2× versus controls, without increasing trap-assisted recombination (no decrease in PLQY at matched excitation).

Step 1 — Baseline PSC platforms + identify dominant interface and dominant mobile species
1.1 Build two baseline stacks for generality:
(A) n–i–p: glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA,Cs)(I,Br)3/spiro-OMeTAD/Au (LiTFSI/tBP doped).
(B) p–i–n: glass/ITO/NiOx/(FA,Cs)(I,Br)3/C60/BCP/Ag.
1.2 Map where hysteresis/drift originates: absolute PLQY→QFLS on perovskite-on-ETL/HTL, Suns-Voc, TPV/TPC, and light-intensity-dependent J–V.
1.3 Identify “what to buffer” rather than assuming I−/FA+ transport through ZIF-8:
• For n–i–p/spiro: quantify Li+ migration propensity (operando ToF-SIMS after bias stress; Li signal as primary target).
• For both architectures: quantify halide redistribution signatures (I/Br gradients) and interfacial iodoplumbate/halide-complex signals (XPS/UPS shifts; GIWAXS changes under bias/illumination).
Deliverable: a ranked list of mobile species (Li+ primary in n–i–p; halide-related interfacial species secondary) and the dominant-loss interface to place the interlayer.

Step 2 — Fabricate MOF-on-fiber scaffold with controlled nucleation, thickness, and percolation
2.1 Conductive nanofiber network (two validated routes; choose based on target interface and processing window):
Option 1 (low-T polymeric): electrospun PEDOT:PSS/PEO fibers; post-treat with H2SO4/EG to achieve σ ≥ 500–1000 S·cm−1; rinse/dry to remove mobile acid residues.
Option 2 (oxide): low-temperature solution-grown SnO2 nanofiber-like networks (≤150–200 °C) to preserve perovskite compatibility.
2.2 Impose fiber coverage 10–30% using controlled deposition (spray/slot-die) and quantify by image analysis (SEM) + optical haze.
2.3 ZIF-8 conformal shell growth (room temperature) with seeded nucleation to avoid free MOF powder and ensure shell uniformity:
• Introduce Zn2+-binding anchoring groups on fibers (catechol/phosphonate self-assembled layer; surface density tuned to avoid continuous dense films).
• Growth solution: MeOH-based Zn(NO3)2 + 2-methylimidazole, tuned to yield 5–12 nm shell thickness; stop-growth by rapid solvent exchange.
• Characterize: cross-sectional TEM for core–shell; GIWAXS for ZIF-8 phase; ellipsometric porosimetry on planar sister films for microporosity.

Step 3 — De-risk “site-selective surface graphitization”: implement, prove depth limit, and quantify conductivity/porosity trade-off (Go/No-Go #1)
3.1 Two alternative depth-limited chemistries (run in parallel; select the one that meets acceptance criteria):
Route A: Remote (downstream) NH3/H2 plasma with low ion energy, short pulses, and sample cooling (minimize bombardment):
• Process window: 5–30 s pulses, 1–5 cycles, substrate <50 °C.
• Rationale: maximize surface dehydrogenation/conjugation and N-incorporation while minimizing Zn–N scission deeper in crystallites.
Route B: Molecular “self-limiting” surface conversion using diazine/imidazole-compatible oxidative dehydrogenation at the outermost surface (no bulk pyrolysis), followed by NH3 anneal at ≤150 °C:
• Rationale: reduce penetration depth vs plasma; keep microporosity.
3.2 Mandatory depth-proof package (performed on ZIF-8 reference stacks and on MOF-on-fiber films):
• Cross-sectional STEM-EELS: map N K-edge fine structure to distinguish imidazolate N vs graphitic/pyridinic-like N; extract converted-layer thickness distribution; acceptance: median 1–3 nm, 90th percentile ≤4 nm.
• Sputter-depth XPS calibrated with a ZIF-8/SiO2 reference stack: quantify graphitic-N fraction vs depth; acceptance: surface-enriched graphitic/pyridinic signatures decaying to pristine ZIF-8 within ≤3–4 nm.
• GIWAXS: retain ZIF-8 fingerprint peaks (no loss of crystallinity beyond minor surface broadening).
• Ellipsometric porosimetry: ≥80% micropore capacity retained and ≤20% change in uptake kinetics.
3.3 Electrical validation:
• Four-point probe Rsh on planar analog films + on nanofiber mats; acceptance: ≥10× drop in Rsh after conversion.
• CAFM current maps across 5×5 µm areas: demonstrate percolating conduction (no ‘hot spots only’ behavior).
• TLM structures (metal pads on interlayer) to extract contact resistivity to SnO2, NiOx, C60, spiro analogs.
Go/No-Go #1 decision: proceed only if *both* porosity and conductivity acceptance criteria are met.

Step 4 — Make ionic buffering real: choose admissible species, prove adsorption/immobilization under bias (Go/No-Go #2)
4.1 Define targeted mobile species and matching host–guest strategy (explicitly addressing ZIF-8 aperture/hydrophobicity):
Primary target (n–i–p/spiro): Li+ (small, highly mobile, implicated in drift). Strategy: load ZIF-8 with immobilized anionic sites or crown-ether-like moieties small enough to be pore-hosted or pore-mouth anchored (e.g., tethered sulfonates or compact chelating motifs introduced via vapor-phase infiltration / minimal-solvent infusion) to capture Li+ electrostatically/chelation.
Secondary target (both architectures): interfacial halide defect compensation at pore mouths via immobilized cationic passivators (imidazolium/diammonium) that do not need deep halide diffusion through the framework; they act at the perovskite-facing boundary and within near-surface accessible pores.
4.2 Prove adsorption and retention (no assumptions):
• In situ QCM-D on planar ZIF-8 and skin-modified ZIF-8 films exposed to controlled activities of LiTFSI, small halide salts, and selected passivator ions in low-activity solvents/vapor; quantify uptake (ng·cm−2) and desorption kinetics.
• Operando FTIR/GIWAXS during exposure to identify coordination signatures (Li+-binding, imidazolium/diammonium incorporation) without framework collapse.
4.3 Field-driven uptake/release experiments in symmetric stacks:
• Build symmetric capacitors: ITO/TL/interlayer/TL/ITO and ITO/interlayer/ITO.
• Apply DC bias (±0.5–1 V) at 25–65 °C while monitoring EIS (DRT), and QCM-D where applicable, to demonstrate bias-asymmetric uptake/release and reduced low-frequency polarization.
Acceptance: ≥2× reduction in low-frequency ionic capacitance feature vs porous-insulating control, with no increase in mid-frequency recombination-related resistance.
Go/No-Go #2 decision: proceed to full devices only upon demonstrated bias-relevant buffering of the identified primary species (Li+ in n–i–p; or another empirically verified species if baseline mapping indicates otherwise).

Step 5 — Integration into PSCs with morphology controls to isolate physics from crystallization artifacts
5.1 Integration sequence (minimize perovskite exposure to MOF growth chemistry): deposit fiber network + ZIF-8 + skin formation + guest loading entirely on the transport layer; then deposit perovskite.
5.2 Explicit morphology-risk controls:
• Track perovskite nucleation/crystallization on interlayers via in situ optical/PL during spin/slot-die, plus SEM/AFM for grain size and voids.
• Solvent scavenging check: quantify precursor depletion near interface by cross-sectional ToF-SIMS and XPS (Pb/I/Br ratios) and compare with baseline.
5.3 Mandatory control interlayers (same thickness 10–25 nm):
C1 Dense chemically similar Zn–imidazolate film (non-porous) to control chemistry without porosity.
C2 Porous-but-insulating pristine ZIF-8-on-fiber without conductive skin (tests ion sink alone).
C3 Conductive skin formed on a non-porous scaffold (or carbonized-dense analog) to test conductivity alone.
C4 ALD Al2O3 (dense barrier) thickness-matched benchmark.
5.4 Device metrics and mechanistic readouts:
• Non-radiative recombination: absolute PLQY→QFLS, EQEEL, TRPL.
• Interfacial energetics/charge pileup: UPS + KPFM; expect reduced band bending and reduced interfacial photovoltage losses.
• Ionic polarization: illuminated EIS + DRT; bias-stress drift Voc(t)/FF(t) and recovery; temperature-dependent hysteresis maps.
• Ion redistribution: ToF-SIMS after 100–500 h MPP stress; specifically track Li (n–i–p), I/Br gradients, and passivator-ion retention.

Step 6 — PV-to-electrolyzer coupling without attribution artifacts
6.1 Run two coupling modes:
Mode A (mandatory): direct coupling (no DC–DC) of stabilized mini-modules to electrolyzer; monitor operating point and H2 flow vs time.
Mode B (diagnostic): DC–DC with deliberately chosen bandwidth settings; quantify how controller dynamics can mask PV transients.
6.2 Dynamic impedance matching protocol:
• Measure small-signal output impedance of PSC module (with/without interlayer) under illumination; measure electrolyzer impedance curve; predict transient sag.
• Apply step-load profiles and record voltage/current/H2 flow; attribute stabilization only if improvement persists under direct coupling and matches reduced low-frequency ionic polarization signatures.

M1 (Month ~3–6): Go/No-Go #1 depth-limited conductive skin with ≥80% micropore retention and ≥10× Rsh reduction.
M2 (Month ~6–9): Go/No-Go #2 operando/bias-confirmed uptake/release buffering for the empirically identified primary mobile species.

Feasibility:
Selective skin feasibility (addresses reviewer risk i–iii): The proposal no longer assumes plasma/UV-ozone will be self-limiting; it enforces depth proof (cross-sectional STEM-EELS + calibrated sputter-XPS) and defines acceptance criteria tying structure to function (≥80% micropore capacity retained while Rsh drops ≥10×). This explicitly manages the known failure modes (Zn–N scission, densification, trap creation) by (a) using remote/low-energy conditions and/or a non-plasma self-limiting chemical route, and (b) requiring retained ZIF-8 crystallinity and uptake kinetics by ellipsometric porosimetry, not only diffraction.

Ionic buffering feasibility (addresses pore aperture/hydrophobicity): The revised mechanism does not hinge on bulk transport of I−/Br−/FA+ through 3.4 Å hydrophobic apertures. Instead, it (1) empirically identifies dominant mobile species per architecture (Li+ is explicitly prioritized in spiro-based n–i–p where it is small and highly mobile), (2) uses host–guest chemistry compatible with ZIF-8’s accessible micropores and pore mouths (immobilized anionic/chelating sites for Li+, immobilized cationic passivators acting near the perovskite boundary), and (3) proves adsorption/immobilization under relevant chemical potentials and electric fields via in situ QCM-D and bias-applied symmetric test structures + DRT-EIS. This converts the ‘ionic sink’ claim from assumptive to measurable and architecture-specific.

Electronic percolation feasibility (addresses reviewer concern about percolation at low coverage): The plan adds an explicit percolation/series-resistance constraint with validation tools (TLM contact resistivity, CAFM mapping, temperature-dependent conductivity) and increases allowable fiber coverage to 10–30% to ensure a continuous conductive network without resorting to thick layers. The conductive pathway is intentionally redundant (fiber backbone + surface skin), reducing the chance that incomplete skin formation yields isolated conductive islands.

Integration feasibility (addresses morphology confounds): The proposal explicitly treats perovskite nucleation/infiltration as a first-order risk with in situ crystallization tracking and stoichiometry profiling. A stringent control set (dense Zn–imidazolate, porous-insulating MOF, conductive-nonporous analog, ALD Al2O3) isolates morphology and chemistry from the two intended functions (porosity/ion buffering vs conductivity/recombination suppression). If performance changes track only with morphology, the mechanism claim fails by design.

PV-to-electrolyzer attribution feasibility (addresses DC–DC masking): The revised coupling plan mandates direct-coupled operation and uses impedance-based matching to link observed stabilization to reduced low-frequency ionic polarization, preventing attribution artifacts from power electronics bandwidth and control loops.

Connection to literature assets (coherence with original concept chain): High loading capacity within reticular frameworks and stability of confined functional species are leveraged for immobilized interfacial passivation (Asset 1). The emphasis on SSA/porosity and mitigating mass-transfer limitations is translated from monolithic/structured MOFs into an interfacial-ion-transport context (Assets 3–4). Finally, the PV-to-hydrogen coupling relevance is framed with electrochemical-system thinking and impedance/kinetics constraints consistent with electrolyzer/fuel-cell integration (Asset 2).
Critique:
The proposal is unusually well-engineered: it defines hard quantitative go/no-go criteria, uses appropriate nanoscale depth-profiling to falsify the “self-limiting skin” claim, and includes the right electrical (TLM/CAFM), porosity (ellipsometric porosimetry with kinetics), and ionic-polarization (DRT-EIS in symmetric stacks) diagnostics. The logic is largely coherent in explicitly rejecting unrealistic assumptions about halide transport through ZIF-8 apertures and instead targeting size-compatible species (notably Li+ from spiro doping) and pore-mouth/defect-site interactions.

Key deductions arise from (i) the chemical plausibility gap in achieving a continuous, electronically percolating conjugated N-rich layer at only 1–3 nm depth on ZIF-8 without creating deep trap states or altering energetics at the perovskite interface—depth-proof is necessary but not sufficient to demonstrate that the modified surface is low-recombination and forms low-barrier contacts across realistic rough interfaces; (ii) the Li+ capture concept lacks a fully specified, ZIF-8-feasible functionalization chemistry with size/steric constraints and quantified binding thermodynamics/selectivity versus competing ions/solvates (TFSI−, tBP, iodoplumbate species), which may dominate uptake and confound the intended “ionic capacitance buffer” mechanism; and (iii) the PV-to-electrolyzer section is methodologically thoughtful (direct coupling + impedance), but the required concept chain’s “fuel cell” node is not operationalized, making the chain integration slightly incomplete. Finally, perovskite crystallization/morphology controls are strong, yet the risk of interlayer-induced energetic misalignment (dipoles, work-function shifts after plasma/functionalization) is underconstrained relative to the aggressive target of improving QFLS/Voc while adding an interlayer.

Hypothesis:
Embedding a grain-boundary (GB)-confined, electronically percolative 2D conductive MOF (2D c-MOF) network—formed in-crystallization and restricted to GBs/voids at sub‑1 vol%—will increase sustained operational power density and delivered energy yield in mixed-cation mixed-halide perovskite solar cells by (A) suppressing GB-limited trap-assisted recombination via a lateral charge-percolation scaffold and defect-state “electronic short-circuiting” at the nanoscale, (B) kinetically intercepting the dominant ROS actually present under defined O2/H2O partial pressures through fast proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) at redox-addressable nodes/linkers that outcompetes halide/organic-cation oxidation, and (C) reducing field-driven ion migration/hysteresis through a narrowly dosed Na+ GB occupancy strategy that neutralizes halide-vacancy-rich GB sites without introducing Na-driven band bending, halide segregation, or secondary phases.

Mechanistic elevation and causality commitments (addressing reviewer critiques):
1) Spin/AFM coupling is treated as a testable modifier—not an assumed advantage. We hypothesize that if antiferromagnetic (AFM) exchange in the GB c‑MOF reduces spin-mixed recombination at defect-rich GBs (via spin-dependent charge transfer/recombination), this will manifest as measurable magneto-optoelectronic signatures (magneto-photocurrent, field-dependent PL/EL, spin-dependent recombination rates). If these signatures are absent, performance gains will be attributed solely to conductivity/chemistry, and the AFM claim is rejected.
2) ROS specificity is established experimentally under controlled atmospheres and by kinetics modeling. The functional claim is not “OH-only”; rather: the GB c‑MOF provides a redox/PCET sink whose efficacy is mapped against superoxide (O2•−), singlet oxygen (1O2), and hydroxyl radical (•OH) under oxygen-free vs oxygen-containing operation. The decisive criterion is whether MOF-mediated ROS interception rate constants at GBs exceed the competing iodide oxidation/organic-cation fragmentation pathways under those same conditions.
3) Na+ acts as a GB defect-chemistry modulator only within a predefined narrow window (10–300 ppm relative to Pb; expanded only if acceptance criteria are met). Na+ is introduced using a low-coordination, low-nucleophilicity counterion strategy with explicit counterion-only controls to decouple Na+ effects from TFSI−/BF4− processing artifacts. Na incorporation is accepted only if band-edge shifts and leakage/shunting remain within strict bounds and no halide segregation is induced.
4) The engineering risk (continuous GB percolation without shunts) is de-risked before long stability tests via explicit go/no-go thresholds: (i) conductive-AFM evidence of GB-localized conduction, (ii) lateral conductivity increase without loss of shunt resistance statistics across >30 devices, and (iii) microscopy-confirmed GB coverage fraction within a target window that avoids planar overgrowth.

Overall, the refined hypothesis is: performance and stability improvements arise from a quantifiable combination of (i) GB-localized electronic percolation, (ii) atmosphere-dependent ROS interception kinetics (not assumed OH primacy), and (iii) narrowly constrained Na+ defect buffering; any additional AFM/spin-correlation benefit must be demonstrated by discriminating magneto-optoelectronic experiments against matched paramagnetic/nonmagnetic analogues.
Plan:
Step 0 — Materials set and device baseline (lock-down for comparability)
0.1 Baseline perovskite absorber: FA0.8Cs0.2Pb(I1−xBrx)3 with x tuned to Eg = 1.55–1.65 eV (same ink composition and thermal history across all groups). Target film thickness: 450–600 nm; target grain size: 300–800 nm.
0.2 Two device stacks to decouple transport-layer chemistry:
  • n–i–p: ITO/SnO2/perovskite/spiro-OMeTAD/Au
  • p–i–n: ITO/NiOx/perovskite/C60/BCP/Ag
0.3 Define baseline acceptance: PCE within ±0.7% absolute across batches; Rs and Rsh distributions stable; hysteresis index <0.08 after protocol stabilization.

Step 1 — GB-confined “in-crystallization MOF weaving” with explicit confinement parameters
1.1 Precursor timing window (in situ GIWAXS gate): cast perovskite to reach partial crystallization where perovskite (100)/(110) peaks emerge but prior to full grain coalescence (empirically defined; typically 10–60 s after antisolvent or during vacuum-assist).
1.2 MOF precursor delivery designed for GB wicking (exclude dense grains):
  • Use ultradilute polar alcohol (IPA/EtOH) or anisole/alcohol mixture with controlled water content <200 ppm.
  • Total metal-ligand concentration: 0.05–0.5 mM (screened) to prevent planar overgrowth.
  • Delivery: (a) vapor exposure (preferred for confinement) OR (b) brief 2–5 s spray/meniscus-contact followed by immediate spin-off.
1.3 MOF chemistries (three-way discriminating set; all engineered to be process-compatible and to nucleate at undercoordinated Pb/I GB sites):
  Group M1 (AFM-coupled conductive 2D c‑MOF): Ni–TTC-like (Asset 2 motif) adapted with catecholate/phenolate-rich linker enabling PCET; target conductivity ≥10−3 S·cm−1 in thin film.
  Group M2 (paramagnetic/nonmagnetic but similarly conductive 2D c‑MOF): Cu–HHTP-like (Asset 1 motif) or a diamagnetic analogue (e.g., closed-shell metal if feasible) tuned to similar sheet resistance (within 3× of M1) to isolate spin/AFM effects.
  Group M3 (insulating MOF control): isoreticular framework with similar functional groups/anchoring but low conductivity (≤10−7 S·cm−1) to isolate “chemical passivation only” vs “conductive percolation”.
  (All MOFs incorporate a GB-anchoring motif: tethered ammonium/pyridinium substituent at low density (e.g., 5–15% linker functionalization) to bias nucleation at halide-vacancy-rich GBs; maintain overall 2D stacking.)
1.4 Trigger chemistry (perovskite-compatible, confinement-preserving):
  • Ligand deprotonation using ppm-level triethylamine vapor (TEA) or buffered alcohol base for 10–60 s.
  • Temperature ≤80 °C; total exposure ≤3 min.
  • Rinse: 1–2 s pure solvent rinse to remove any non-confined residues.
1.5 Target structural metrics (must be met before proceeding):
  • GB ribbon thickness equivalent: 1–3 nm along GB walls (no continuous planar overlayer detectable by AFM step height mapping across terraces).
  • Coverage fraction along GBs: 40–80% of GB length in plan-view (below 40%: non-percolative; above 80%: shunt risk).
  • Total MOF volume fraction: 0.1–0.8 vol% (estimated by uptake + elemental quantification).

Step 2 — Na+ strategy with narrow dosing window and counterion controls (decouple chemistry)
2.1 Dosing range (predefined): 10, 30, 100, 300 ppm Na relative to Pb (stop at 300 ppm unless all acceptance criteria pass; only then explore 500–1000 ppm).
2.2 Introduction routes (factorial design):
  • Route A: Na+ in perovskite precursor via NaPF6 or NaClO4 (preferred to reduce strongly coordinating anion effects); keep total added anion constant across controls.
  • Route B: Na+ in MOF bath (same ppm range referenced to estimated perovskite mass uptake) to test preferential partitioning into GB/MOF microenvironment.
2.3 Mandatory controls:
  • Counterion-only: add TFSI−/BF4−/PF6− source without Na+ (e.g., tetrabutylammonium salts) at matched molarity to isolate anion/process effects.
  • K+ analogue at matched ppm (optional but recommended) to probe specificity of Na+ vs generic alkali occupancy.
2.4 Na acceptance criteria (must pass):
  • Band-edge shifts: ΔWork function (KPFM/UPS) ≤ 50 meV vs Na-free at same MOF condition.
  • No measurable increase in p/n-type bulk doping (Mott–Schottky/capacitance profiling consistent within 20%).
  • No new crystalline Na-containing phases (GIWAXS detection limit) and no Na-rich clusters in STEM-EDX.
  • No increase in halide segregation under illumination (operando PL peak-splitting < baseline + 10%).

Step 3 — Percolation and shunt-risk de-risking (go/no-go before long ISOS)
3.1 Conductive-AFM (c-AFM) maps on perovskite top surface and cross-sections:
  • Metric: GB-to-grain conduction contrast (I_GB/I_grain) and continuity of conductive pathways along GBs.
  • Go/no-go: median I_GB increases ≥10× over control, while grain interior remains unchanged (avoid bulk shunting).
3.2 Lateral conductivity vs loading (four-probe / TLM on dedicated test structures):
  • Go/no-go: ≥3× increase in lateral sheet conductance at ≤0.8 vol% MOF, without >20% drop in vertical device Rsh.
3.3 Device statistics (minimum n=30 per condition):
  • Go/no-go: shunt resistance Rsh distribution not degraded (median Rsh decrease ≤15%); leakage at −0.1 V in dark increases ≤2×.

Step 4 — AFM/spin-correlation claim: discriminating magneto-optoelectronic tests (mandatory)
4.1 Sample set: M1 (AFM), M2 (paramagnetic/nonmagnetic but conductive-matched), M3 (insulating) all GB-confined with matched coverage (±10%) and similar conductivity where required.
4.2 Measurements:
  • Magneto-photocurrent (MPC) and magneto-electroluminescence (MEL): field sweep (0–300 mT) at fixed bias/illumination.
  • Field-dependent PL (FDPL): quantify PL intensity/lifetime change vs B-field.
  • Temperature dependence (80–320 K) to probe spin-dependent recombination signatures.
4.3 Interpretation criteria:
  • If M1 shows statistically significant MPC/MEL/FDPL signatures distinct from M2 at matched conductivity and chemistry, attribute an additional spin-correlation role.
  • If M1≈M2 within error, remove AFM as causal and treat conductivity/PCET as the mechanism.

Step 5 — ROS specificity and kinetics dominance (separate OH, O2•−, 1O2; quantify rate competition)
5.1 Controlled atmosphere matrix during illumination + bias:
  • Dry N2 (O2 < 1 ppm, H2O < 1 ppm)
  • N2 + controlled O2 (0.1%, 1%, 21%) at <5 ppm H2O
  • N2 + controlled H2O (50–5000 ppm) at O2 < 1 ppm
  • Air with defined RH (10%, 50%)
5.2 ROS mapping (film-only and full stacks):
  • •OH: in situ spin-trapping EPR (DMPO–OH) with calibrated adduct kinetics.
  • O2•−: EPR with appropriate spin trap (e.g., DMPO–OOH signatures) and/or optical probe validated for perovskites.
  • 1O2: near-IR phosphorescence at 1270 nm and/or selective chemical trap (e.g., SOSG) with controls for probe photobleaching.
  • Include transport-layer-dependent tests (SnO2 vs NiOx vs C60) to identify interfacial ROS sources.
5.3 Kinetics modeling requirement:
  • Build a competitive reaction model at GBs: ROS generation terms (dependent on O2/H2O, bias, TL), competing sinks (perovskite iodide oxidation; organic-cation oxidation; MOF PCET sink).
  • Extract effective pseudo-first-order rate constants for ROS decay with and without MOF using time-resolved probe/EPR data.
  • Go/no-go: k_MOF,sink (effective) must exceed k_perovskite,damage by ≥5× under at least one realistic operating condition (e.g., 21% O2, RH 10–50%, 1 sun, MPP bias) to claim chemical protection.
5.4 Chemical corroboration (operando/post-mortem):
  • Operando XPS: suppression of I0/I+ species growth; O 1s evolution; Pb state shifts.
  • LC-MS/GC-MS of extracted organics: reduced signatures of organic-cation fragmentation products.

Step 6 — Recombination/transport and ion migration (separate contributions quantitatively)
6.1 Recombination:
  • TRPL + confocal PL mapping to extract GB vs grain lifetime distributions.
  • Intensity-dependent Voc and ideality factor; target: reduction in ideality factor toward 1 (trap-assisted reduced).
  • Transient photovoltage/photocurrent and impedance: separate recombination resistance and transport resistance.
6.2 Ion migration/hysteresis:
  • Temperature-dependent impedance to extract ionic activation energy.
  • Transient ion-drift (bias-step) and hysteresis index under stabilized protocol.
  • Go/no-go for Na benefit: Na-dosed must reduce hysteresis index by ≥30% vs Na-free at same MOF, without band-edge shift >50 meV.

Step 7 — Operational power density and delivered energy yield (only after go/no-go pass)
7.1 ISOS protocols:
  • ISOS-L3 (light, MPP) and ISOS-O2 (outdoor/ambient variant) as applicable.
  • Conditions: 1 sun, MPP tracking, 65 °C and 85 °C sets; atmosphere defined (dry N2 vs controlled air).
7.2 Metrics:
  • Sustained power density at MPP (mW·cm−2) vs time.
  • Time-integrated delivered energy (Wh·m−2) over test window.
  • Acceptance: ≥10% higher delivered energy than best baseline passivator control at matched initial PCE, with no catastrophic shunt failures.

Step 8 — Localization and chemical-state verification (must support mechanism claims)
8.1 Localization: cross-sectional STEM-EELS/EDX + ToF-SIMS (Ni/Cu, linker fragments, Na) to confirm GB confinement and Na partitioning.
8.2 Chemical state:
  • Solid-state 23Na NMR (where feasible) to distinguish ionic environments (GB vs bulk vs clusters).
  • XPS depth profiling for Na chemical state and any Na–I/Na–Br signatures.
8.3 Halide segregation monitoring:
  • Operando PL mapping under bias/light; operando GIWAXS for phase segregation signatures.

Decision tree summary (hard gates):
Gate G1 (Confinement): MOF GB-localized, no planar overlayer.
Gate G2 (Percolation without shunts): c-AFM continuity + Rsh/leakage criteria.
Gate G3 (ROS kinetics): MOF sink rate dominates damage pathway under at least one realistic condition.
Gate G4 (Na safety): band-edge/segregation/leakage acceptance.
Only then proceed to long ISOS energy-yield demonstrations.
Feasibility:
1) Why the 2D c‑MOF concept is feasible in perovskite GBs (and how we bound the risk)
• Conductive 2D MOFs with measurable conductivity and redox activity are established (Asset 2), supporting the premise that a sub‑vol% framework can provide lateral electronic percolation if it is spatially concentrated at GBs (where it matters most). The proposal does not assume “more MOF is better”; it sets a constrained volume fraction (0.1–0.8 vol%) and demands conductive-AFM evidence of GB-localized conduction.
• The core engineering risk—unintended shunting/planar overgrowth—is explicitly managed by kinetic exclusion (vapor/ultradilute delivery), short triggering, and quantitative go/no-go leakage/Rsh statistics across >30 devices before stability testing.

2) AFM exchange coupling: converted from assertion into a falsifiable, discriminating experiment set
• Asset 2 motivates AFM-coupled 2D c‑MOFs as robust electronic frameworks, but that does not automatically translate to PSCs. Therefore, the revised plan compares GB-confined MOFs that are (M1) AFM-coupled, (M2) paramagnetic/nonmagnetic but conductivity-matched, and (M3) insulating. Magneto-photocurrent, magneto-EL, and field-dependent PL explicitly test whether spin correlations measurably alter recombination/charge transfer. If no spin-dependent signatures appear, AFM is removed as a causal mechanism, preventing mechanistic overreach.

3) ROS mechanism credibility: radical specificity and rate competition are treated as the central proof
• Asset 1 demonstrates that conductive MOFs can participate in ROS-related electro/photochemistry, including hydroxyl radical pathways, but PSC degradation often involves O2•− and 1O2 depending on oxygen/water and interfaces. The revised proposal therefore (i) maps •OH, O2•−, and 1O2 under controlled O2/H2O partial pressures and (ii) requires kinetics modeling showing the MOF-mediated sink outcompetes perovskite damage kinetics at GBs. Oxygen-free experiments separate intrinsic photo-chemistry from ambient-driven pathways, directly addressing reviewer concern.

4) Na+ buffering: feasibility bounded by narrow dosing, counterion controls, and explicit acceptance criteria
• The proposal narrows Na+ to 10–300 ppm (initially), avoiding the unbounded 0.1% regime that risks secondary phases and unintended doping. Counterion-only controls isolate anion/crystallization effects from Na+. Na location/chemical state is verified (ToF-SIMS + XPS depth profiling + 23Na NMR where feasible). Acceptance criteria on band-edge shifts (≤50 meV), leakage, and halide segregation prevent “apparent stability” that is actually a doped/segregated artifact.

5) Why this should improve power density and energy yield (and how we will prove it)
• Power density gains are expected only if GB recombination is reduced without adding series resistance or shunts; hence the mandatory percolation/leakage gates plus TRPL/ideality/impedance decomposition.
• Energy-yield gains require suppressing the dominant operating degradation channel under the relevant atmosphere; hence the ROS mapping matrix and requirement that MOF sink kinetics dominate at least one realistic condition (air/RH/MPP). Delivered energy (time-integrated Wh·m−2) is used as the operational analogue of “energy density”, aligning with the proposal’s original framing while remaining PSC-appropriate.

In sum, each contested causal link (AFM/spin benefit, ROS identity, Na+ role, percolation vs shunt tradeoff) is converted into a controlled, quantitative, go/no-go-structured validation plan that can either substantiate the higher-level claims or force mechanistic down-selection without compromising the central GB-confined conductive-MOF concept.
Critique: This is an exceptionally detailed and disciplined proposal with strong engineering resolution and internal rigor. The GB-confined 2D c-MOF concept is technically credible, and the conversion of contested claims (AFM/spin effects, ROS identity, Na+ role) into falsifiable experiments is a major strength. Engineering risk is explicitly bounded with quantitative gates, which is uncommon and commendable. However, two issues prevent a near-perfect score: (i) the TARGET CONCEPT CHAIN is only partially honored—the sodium-ion battery endpoint is conceptually disconnected, as Na+ is treated strictly as a defect modulator in PSCs rather than as part of an energy-density/storage framework; and (ii) the logical chain linking hydroxyl radical interception to sustained power density is well treated, but energy density is translated operationally into delivered energy yield without explicitly reconciling this semantic shift against the stated concept chain. These are not fatal flaws, but they represent conceptual misalignment rather than experimental weakness.

Hypothesis:
If single-step solution processing is modified to (i) create a surface-confined, orientation-controlled dipole sheet using segregating polar ammonium cations and (ii) impose a reproducible, nanoscale stress-field concentration at the perovskite/HTL contact via a quantifiable Spiro-OMeTAD “flower-stem” nano-topography, then intrinsic thermo-mechanical stress from CTE mismatch and lattice/ferroelastic relaxation will transduce into an interfacial piezoelectric-like (electrostrictive + non-centrosymmetric surface) polarization that produces a stable, rectifying interfacial potential step (target ΔVint = 20–80 mV). This ΔVint will increase the quasi-Fermi level splitting at open circuit primarily by reducing interfacial non-radiative recombination (lower interfacial recombination velocity, S) and by increasing the effective built-in potential at the perovskite/Spiro contact, yielding a measurable Voc gain (target +20–60 mV) without external mechanical actuation.

Mechanistic rationale bounded by quantitative electrostatics: A surface dipole sheet produces a potential step approximated by ΔVint ≈ (N·μ⊥)/ε0εeff, where N is dipole areal density and μ⊥ is the normal dipole component. For ΔVint = 50 mV and εeff ≈ 10–20 (perovskite surface + HTL interfacial effective dielectric), the required dipole moment density is N·μ⊥ ≈ ΔV·ε0εeff ≈ (0.05 V)(8.85×10^-12 F m^-1)(10–20) = (4.4–8.9)×10^-12 C m^-1.
- Using μ⊥ ~ 1–3 Debye per surface site (3.3×10^-30 to 1.0×10^-29 C·m), the required N is ~ (4×10^17–3×10^18) m^-2. This corresponds to ~0.4–3 dipoles per nm^2, within the physically plausible range of surface termination densities (order 1–10 nm^-2) provided orientation is biased rather than random.
Stress transduction plausibility: thermo-mechanical mismatch stress can reach ~1–50 MPa in thin films depending on constraint; with effective piezoelectric-like coefficients reported/estimated in polar semiconductors of ~0.1–10 pC N^-1, an effective field/potential on the order of 10–100 mV across an interfacial region (≈1–5 nm) is plausible if symmetry is locally broken and screening is suppressed. The design explicitly suppresses ionic screening by (a) confining the polar reconstruction to a sub-nm surface layer (minimizing the ionic volume available to compensate), (b) using bulky/immobile HTL dopants to avoid mobile ions in the HTL, and (c) demanding fast, frequency-independent (above ionic cutoff) sign-reversible responses as decisive proof of an electromechanical origin.

Why this overcomes reviewer-flagged ambiguities: (1) the hypothesis predicts quantitative ΔVint and Voc targets; (2) it requires sign reversal with dipole orientation reversal (a discriminating hallmark not explained by generic work-function drift); (3) it requires thickness-localized potential drop scaling (interface-confined) and fast frequency response distinct from ion drift; and (4) it ties Voc gains to a modeled reduction in interfacial S extracted from TRPL quench modeling and corroborated by implied-Voc (PLQY) rather than to series resistance or Spiro oxidation artifacts.

0.1 Primary device targets: ΔVoc = +20 to +60 mV vs control at matched Jsc/FF window; PCE increase attributable to Voc not Rs/FF artifacts (ΔFF < ±0.01 unless independently justified).
0.2 Interfacial electrostatics targets: ΔVint (buried interface) = 20–80 mV with sign reversal upon dipole reversal; thermal-modulation response amplitude ≥10 mV in KPFM/EFM at frequencies where ions are too slow (see Step 3.3).
0.3 Photophysics targets: ≥2× reduction in extracted interfacial recombination velocity S (or equivalent increase in surface lifetime component) while bulk lifetime remains within ±20% of control; implied Voc (from absolute PLQY) increases consistent with measured Voc within 10–15 mV.

Step 1 — Baseline system, strict controls, and reproducibility
1.1 Control architecture (n–i–p): glass/ITO/SnO2 (or compact TiO2)/perovskite/(HTL)/Au.
- Perovskite baseline: (FAPbI3)0.85(MAPbBr3)0.15 single-step + antisolvent quench; thickness set to 500 ± 30 nm for baseline.
- HTL control: standard Spiro-OMeTAD with LiTFSI+tBP in chlorobenzene; Au 80 nm.
1.2 Baseline loss analysis:
- Absolute PLQY under 1 sun equivalent carrier density → implied Voc.
- Suns–Voc to decouple transport/series resistance from recombination.
- Temperature-dependent Voc (220–340 K) to estimate activation energies and interfacial recombination dominance.

Step 2 — Interfacial dipole-sheet engineering with sign-reversible cation pairs (orthogonal decisive control #1)
2.1 Cation selection designed for opposite net surface dipole orientation while preserving chemical passivation strength:
- “Dipole-Forward” set: e.g., 4-fluorophenethylammonium iodide (F-PEAI) or CF3-substituted PEAI (electron-withdrawing, strong permanent dipole).
- “Dipole-Reverse” set: e.g., 4-methoxyphenethylammonium iodide (MeO-PEAI) or dimethyl-substituted PEAI (opposite dipole direction relative to ammonium headgroup depending on substituent placement).
Rationale: aromatic substituent polarity reverses the molecular dipole component normal to the surface when ammonium anchoring is conserved; the proposal requires experimental verification of net orientation (NEXAFS dichroism).
2.2 Processing window to enforce surface segregation without forming a thick 2D perovskite:
- Additive loading: 0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 mol% relative to Pb.
- Antisolvent timing sweep: ±200 ms around the baseline drip time to tune segregation kinetics.
- Anneal: 100–110 °C, 20–30 min; optional brief solvent-vapor equilibration (≤2 min) to reduce bulk defect formation.
2.3 Acceptance criteria for “surface-confined reconstruction”:
- GIWAXS: absence (or ≤5% integrated intensity relative to 3D perovskite peaks) of low-q 2D RP-phase signatures.
- XPS angle-resolved (ARXPS): enriched N/C/F signal at shallow takeoff angles consistent with <2 nm surface layer.
- NEXAFS: measurable preferential orientation (dichroic ratio threshold pre-set, e.g., ≥1.2) and opposite sign/tilt signature between forward vs reverse cation sets.

Step 3 — De-risk and quantify the “flower-stem” Spiro-OMeTAD morphology (reviewer requirement #3)
3.1 Replace speculative crystallization additives with a morphology-programming approach that is measurable and energetically constrained:
- Use a volatile, low-residue nonsolvent-vapor/solvent-mix quench during Spiro deposition (e.g., controlled heptane vapor exposure for 2–10 s during spin) to induce vertical phase contrast without introducing strong acids.
- If an additive is used, restrict to a single, weakly interacting polymeric rheology modifier (e.g., PEG 400 at 50–300 ppm) and pre-register an energetics window (below).
3.2 Define morphology descriptors and acceptance criteria:
- AFM topography + phase: vertically correlated nano-domains with lateral size 30–150 nm, RMS roughness increase <3 nm vs control (to avoid shunts).
- Cross-sectional FIB-SEM/TEM: “stem” penetration depth into perovskite asperities of 3–10 nm with a distribution σ < 3 nm across >30 measurements.
- GISAXS/GIWAXS on Spiro: domain correlation length ξz (vertical) at least 2× ξx (lateral), indicating anisotropic morphology (even if amorphous).
3.3 Energetics/doping invariance gate (must pass before device claims):
- UPS on Spiro films on inert substrates: work function and HOMO shift constrained to |ΔWF| ≤ 50 meV and |ΔHOMO| ≤ 50 meV vs control at matched oxidation protocol.
- Conductivity (4-point probe) and Seebeck coefficient: both must remain within ±20% of control. If outside, morphology condition is rejected as confounded.
- Spiro oxidation level: monitored by UV–Vis/NIR (oxidized Spiro signature) with acceptance window ±15%.

Step 4 — Orthogonal discriminators separating piezo/polarization from ionic/chemical artifacts
4.1 Thickness scaling to localize the potential step (orthogonal decisive control #2)
- Perovskite thickness series: 250, 500, 800 nm at constant interface chemistry.
Prediction: if ΔV is an interface dipole/polarization step, ΔVoc and buried-interface ΔVint should be thickness-independent (within error), whereas ionic redistribution fields and bulk band-bending often scale with thickness and capacitance.
- HTL thickness series: Spiro 80, 150, 250 nm; keep dopant level constant.
Prediction: ΔVint at the interface should be largely HTL-thickness independent; HTL work-function drift would generally show thickness/processing dependence.
4.2 Frequency-domain separation of fast electromechanical vs slow ionic drift (orthogonal decisive control #3)
- Thermal modulation: apply sinusoidal temperature modulation (ΔT = 1–3 K) using a Peltier stage at f = 0.01–10 Hz while measuring surface potential (band-limited KPFM) and device Voc under illumination (Voc(f)).
Prediction: piezoelectric-like response persists up to higher f (limited by thermal diffusion and cantilever bandwidth) with minimal phase lag; ionic drift shows strong amplitude roll-off and increasing phase lag beyond an ionic cutoff (~0.1–1 Hz depending on conditions).
- Complementary impedance/IMVS: measure IMVS/IMPS across 1 Hz–1 MHz under steady illumination; extract characteristic ionic time constants (low-frequency arcs). Require that the “polarization signature” appears in a regime where ionic arc contribution is negligible.
4.3 Dipole sign reversal requirement (non-negotiable discriminator)
- Devices with Dipole-Forward vs Dipole-Reverse cations must show opposite sign in (i) thermal KPFM potential shift and (ii) ΔVoc. A same-sign Voc improvement for both is treated as evidence for generic chemical passivation/energy-level shifts rather than rectifying polarization.
4.4 Ion-screening stress test
- Compare responses under dry N2 vs controlled humidity (e.g., 20–40% RH) and with intentional ionic blocking layers (ultrathin Al2O3 by ALD ≤1 nm on perovskite before HTL in a subset). Piezo-like interface dipole should remain detectable; ion-mediated signals should change strongly.

Step 5 — Direct buried-interface band-bending / potential-step probes (reviewer requirement #4)
5.1 Hard XPS (HAXPES) or synchrotron-based depth-resolved XPS/UPS:
- Measure core-level shifts (Pb 4f, I 3d, N 1s; and Spiro-related peaks) across takeoff angles/energies to infer band bending and potential steps across the interface.
Success criterion: extracted interfacial step consistent in sign and magnitude (20–80 mV) with KPFM/Voc trends and shows sign reversal with dipole reversal.
5.2 Bias-dependent measurements:
- Apply external bias (dark) and measure core-level shifts or electroabsorption/photothermal deflection proxies to confirm rectifying field behavior.

Step 6 — Recombination-velocity extraction tied to Voc (not Rs/HTL WF drift)
6.1 TRPL with interfacial quench modeling:
- Measure TRPL on (i) bare perovskite, (ii) perovskite + Spiro (control), (iii) perovskite+dipoled surface + Spiro with/without morphology programming.
- Fit to diffusion-recombination model with boundary condition capturing interfacial S. Report S and its uncertainty; target ≥2× reduction vs control.
6.2 Absolute PLQY mapping to implied Voc pre-/post-HTL deposition:
- Require that Δ(implied Voc) tracks ΔVoc; if ΔVoc occurs without PLQY improvement, suspect energetics/transport artifacts.
6.3 Series resistance and FF artifact exclusion:
- Extract Rs/Rsh from J–V and confirm unchanged (within ±10%) when claiming Voc-driven gains.

Step 7 — Stability and screening robustness
7.1 MPP tracking + Voc retention under 1 sun at 60–85 °C for ≥500 h; periodic Suns–Voc to verify recombination-limited regime.
7.2 Bias-stress (±0.8 V in dark, 1–10 min pulses) followed by recovery; ionic mechanisms show memory/hysteresis growth.
7.3 Acceptance criterion for “stable against ionic screening”: the sign-reversible ΔVint and ΔVoc must persist after thermal soak (e.g., 85 °C, 2 h) with <20% amplitude loss and without increased hysteresis index.

Falsification map (expanded, decisive)
F1 (Sign test): If Dipole-Forward and Dipole-Reverse yield the same sign ΔVoc and same sign ΔVint, the rectifying dipole/piezo claim is rejected (passivation/energetics dominates).
F2 (Frequency test): If the potential/Voc modulation shows strong roll-off and large phase lag characteristic of ions (matching impedance low-frequency arc), the piezo-like claim is rejected.
F3 (Thickness localization): If ΔVint or ΔVoc scales strongly with perovskite thickness, the effect is not an interface step; reject.
F4 (Energetics confound): If Spiro morphology programming changes WF/HOMO or conductivity beyond the pre-set window, any Voc changes are treated as HTL energetics/doping artifacts; reject morphology claims until constraints are met.
Feasibility:
Quantitative plausibility: The required interfacial dipole moment density to generate a Voc-relevant 20–80 mV step corresponds to ~0.4–3 dipoles nm^-2 for 1–3 D dipoles, which is compatible with realistic surface site densities if orientation is biased. The proposed cation segregation (≤2 mol%) is within established single-step processing practice and is constrained by GIWAXS/ARXPS criteria to avoid forming a thick 2D layer that would change bandgap/transport.

Mechanism discrimination is built in: The proposal does not rely on a single KPFM observation. It requires (i) sign reversal with dipole orientation reversal, (ii) frequency-domain separation from ionic drift, and (iii) thickness independence consistent with an interface-localized potential step—three orthogonal discriminators that jointly rule out common confounds (ion redistribution, trap charging, HTL WF drift).

HTL “flower-stem” risk is controlled: Spiro-OMeTAD’s tendency toward amorphous morphology is acknowledged; therefore, the proposal defines ‘flower-stem’ operationally via anisotropic vertical correlation and penetration-depth statistics rather than crystallinity. It further gates the approach with strict UPS/conductivity/Seebeck acceptance windows so that additives or processing do not inadvertently change HTL doping/energetics and falsely inflate Voc.

Direct buried-interface validation: Depth-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy (HAXPES/depth-UPS/XPS) provides an interface-specific band-bending/potential-step measurement not reducible to surface KPFM artifacts. Combined with TRPL-based extraction of interfacial recombination velocity S and PLQY-implied Voc, the proposal ties any Voc increase to reduced non-radiative interfacial recombination in a quantitatively testable way.

Alignment with literature assets: The plan leverages single-step solution processing with antisolvent engineering (Asset 2) and uses Voc as the key performance arbiter (Assets 2–4). The ‘flower-stem’ concept is translated from catalyst morphology logic (Asset 4) into a rigorously defined HTL nano-topography descriptor rather than an aesthetic analogy. The piezoelectric-like interfacial polarization concept is grounded by an explicit electrostatic target (Asset 1 inspires the need to connect polarization to measurable Voc, but here it is constrained to mV-scale photovoltaic relevance rather than large nanogenerator voltages).
Critique:
The proposal is unusually strong in pre-registered success criteria, orthogonal falsification logic (sign reversal, frequency-domain separation from ions, thickness-independence), and in gating Spiro morphology claims against energetics/doping confounds. The electrostatic dipole-sheet calculation is internally consistent and lands in a plausible areal dipole-density regime.

Key score deductions stem from remaining physical and metrological ambiguities: (1) The core mechanistic leap—conversion of residual thermo-mechanical stress into a stable, rectifying, piezoelectric-like interfacial polarization in a highly polarizable, ionically soft halide perovskite—still risks being dominated by electrochemical/ionic reconfiguration and trap charging, even if the signal is “fast,” because electronic trapping/de-trapping can also be fast and sign-dependent under thermal modulation and KPFM. (2) The “dipole-forward/dipole-reverse” premise depends critically on actual molecular orientation at the buried interface; NEXAFS dichroism on the exposed perovskite surface does not by itself guarantee the same orientation persists after Spiro deposition and subsequent ionic/electronic equilibration. (3) The stress-field concentration via Spiro topography is plausible but under-quantified: there is no explicit plan to measure local strain/stress or ferroelastic domain reconfiguration at the interface (e.g., nanobeam diffraction/Raman mapping), so linking morphology → stress localization → polarization remains partly inferential. (4) Buried-interface potential-step extraction at the 20–80 mV level via HAXPES/core-level shifts is challenging; without a detailed error model (charging, referencing, illumination conditions, beam-induced ion motion) the feasibility and uncertainty budget are not yet convincing at the demanded mV precision.

Hypothesis: Embedding a negatively curved (Schwarz P-type) bicontinuous interlayer that hosts axially regulated M–N single-atom sites (e.g., Ni–N4–X, X = Cl/COO−) at the perovskite/ETL interface will simultaneously (i) suppress perovskite interfacial degradation and ion-driven hysteresis and (ii) maintain high Voc/FF by reducing interfacial recombination. Mechanistically, negative Gaussian curvature increases accessible interfacial area and creates continuous, low-tortuosity transport pathways for electrons while distributing local electric fields, thereby reducing hot-spot driven halide segregation. Axial coordination environment regulation (X = Cl vs COO−) tunes the single-atom site’s Lewis acidity/basicity and dipole moment to anchor/neutralize undercoordinated Pb–I species (defect passivation) and to immobilize mobile iodide via reversible coordination, increasing long-term operational stability. The same M–N sites are designed to stabilize a surface-bound carboxylate (COO−) motif that acts as a ‘buffer ligand’ to lower interfacial charge-transfer overpotential (i.e., reduce energetic/kinetic losses for electron extraction), improving fill factor without introducing ionic dopants.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Choose a baseline high-performance perovskite stack (e.g., FAPbI3-rich mixed-cation perovskite with a small Br fraction for bandgap tuning) in n–i–p architecture: ITO/SnO2/perovskite/interlayer/HTL/Au.
1.2 Prepare two control interlayers: (C1) flat 2D polymeric interlayer without SACs; (C2) SAC-decorated carbon interlayer without negative curvature.
1.3 Define target interlayer thickness (10–30 nm) to avoid optical parasitics and maintain tunneling/transport.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Methodological Adaptation (negative Gaussian curvature + axial SAC regulation): fabricate a bicontinuous mesoporous carbon (or conductive organic framework) interlayer templated by polymer cubosomes (or block-copolymer gyroid/cubosome phases) to realize a Schwarz P-like negatively curved network; carbonize at temperatures compatible with maintaining high conductivity while preserving pore continuity.
2.2 Introduce single-atom M–N sites by MOF-derived atom trapping: infiltrate a Ni-porphyrinic (or ZIF-derived) precursor into the bicontinuous template, followed by mild pyrolysis to form isolated Ni–N4 sites anchored in the curved carbon skeleton.
