- Environmental controls: oxygen exposure (quenches many organic radicals) vs inert glovebox; moisture control; dark vs illuminated; temperature-dependent linewidth analysis to separate organic radical behavior from perovskite paramagnetic centers.
- Spectral simulation: fit EPR spectra using EasySpin (or equivalent) to extract g-tensor/hyperfine tensors; require goodness-of-fit and consistency across field/illumination.
- Gate criterion G3: Unique, label-verified DCA•− spectral signature with field-dependent amplitude at fmod ≥ 10×fion.

Step 4 — Stark/electroabsorption to quantify Δμ/Δα and CT-state polarizability
4.1 Electroabsorption (EA) / Stark spectroscopy:
- Use a transparent capacitor stack (ITO/dielectric/perovskite+DCAEA-RP/transparent top electrode such as thin ITO or PEDOT:PSS with barrier) to apply known displacement fields.
- Perform lock-in detected EA at fmod (chosen from impedance) to suppress ionic artifacts.
- Extract CT-related EA features and fit to first/second derivative components to quantify Δμ and Δα; correlate EA amplitude with EPR-derived fCT.
- Gate criterion G4: measurable CT-feature Stark response consistent with EPR modulation and electrostatic model.

Step 5 — Fast (ionic-decoupled) linkage to interfacial charge extraction and recombination
5.1 Half-stack ultrafast tests under high-frequency field modulation:
- Build half-stacks: SnO2/3D/(cap) and 3D/(cap)/C60.
- Use transient absorption (TA) and time-resolved PL (TRPL) with synchronized field modulation: compare kinetics at +E and −E, using fmod ≥ 10×fion and phase-sensitive detection where possible.
- Primary observables: electron extraction time constants (ns–µs), interfacial recombination rates, and field-odd vs field-even responses (helps separate linear electrostatic vs quadratic Stark contributions).
- Require that extraction/recombination changes track ΔfCT and occur on timescales faster than ionic drift.

Step 6 — Full PSC integration with mechanistic closure
6.1 Baseline PSCs (two polarities):
- n–i–p: glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA,Cs)Pb(I,Br)3/(cap)/PTAA/Au.
- p–i–n: ITO/NiOx/(FA,Cs)Pb(I,Br)3/(cap)/C60/BCP/Ag.
6.2 Field-plate protocol on encapsulated devices:
- Apply VDC and small VAC at fmod while holding PSC at open circuit; quantify Voc/QFLS shifts and nonradiative losses via absolute PLQY.
- Confirm that observed modulation disappears at low f where ionic effects dominate, and persists at high f (electronic regime).
6.3 Quantitative causal map (pre-registered analysis):
- Regress Δkext (TA/TRPL), ΔVnr (from PLQY/QFLS), and changes in ideality factor against fCT (EPR spin density) and EA-derived Δμ/Δα under matched Eint.
- Perturbation axes: DCA loading (mixed spacer ratios), cap thickness (3/5/10 nm), and operating point (dark vs illuminated QFLS).

Step 7 — Ion-migration decoupling and stability constraints
7.1 Ionic response characterization:
- Impedance spectroscopy + bias-stress capacitance transients to quantify τion and ionic contribution to screening.
- ToF-SIMS after accelerated bias/illumination aging to detect halide migration into the RP cap and any DCAEA decomposition signatures.
7.2 ISOS-style stability (contingent on passing G1–G4):
- ISOS-L-2 / ISOS-O-2 at 65–85 °C MPP ≥ 1000 h with periodic extraction of PLQY/QFLS and EPR to assess whether CT functionality survives operational stress.

Step 8 — Saturable absorber/mode-locking arm (secondary, contingent deliverable)
8.1 Predefined SA targets (hard gate):

- Photostability target: no irreversible loss of modulation depth after exposure to representative intracavity fluence (benchmarked in pump–probe).

8.2 If G5 passes:

- Demonstrate mode-locking in a cavity only after SA metrics are met; correlate modulation depth changes to ΔfCT (EPR) and Stark coefficients (EA), leveraging the charge-transfer ↔ nonlinear optics precedent (Asset 1).

Primary success criteria (updated, gated)
- Mechanistic gates: G1–G4 all pass (interfacial field quantified; CT energetically feasible under QFLS; label-verified EPR; Stark response measurable in electronic regime).

Feasibility:
Electrostatics feasibility (addresses critique i): The revised plan explicitly computes and measures the interfacial field Eint rather than assuming the applied plate field reaches the CT layer. A multilayer Poisson/impedance framework, parameterized by measured dielectric constants and impedance-derived ionic crossover frequency, defines an electronic-only modulation regime (fmod ≥ 10×fion) where ionic screening cannot follow. This directly answers whether Stark tuning is electrostatically accessible at the buried RP/3D interface and prevents misattribution to ion motion.

Energetics/CT feasibility (addresses critique ii): CT formation is treated as a quantitative, illumination-dependent level-alignment problem. UPS provides WF/vacuum-level shifts and band edges; PLQY-derived QFLS provides EFn under operating conditions; DCAEA reduction energy from CV is mapped to the vacuum scale. These inputs feed a Marcus-type ΔG model that predicts baseline fCT and the minimum ΔECT/Δφ required to change fCT by a detectable amount. This pre-analysis creates a hard falsification gate: if ΔfCT is predicted to be below detectability at computed Eint and measured QFLS, the CT-field-adaptive premise is rejected or chemically redesigned before device-scale effort.

Spin assignment rigor (addresses critique iii): EPR ambiguities in perovskites are handled with isotope labeling (15N) to create a diagnostic hyperfine fingerprint unique to DCA•−, plus spectral simulations and environmental perturbations (O2, light/dark, temperature) to separate organic radicals from perovskite defect centers and light-induced paramagnetism. Quantitative spin counting anchors the radical density to a physically meaningful interfacial population (spins/cm2), enabling correlation with recombination metrics.

Ionic vs electronic decoupling (addresses critique iv): All field-dependent CT measurements (EA/EPR) and the causality tests to extraction/recombination (TA/TRPL) are performed with field modulation above ionic response frequencies determined by impedance. Observing consistent high-frequency (electronic) modulation of fCT and concomitant changes in ns–µs extraction kinetics provides a stringent discriminator against slow ionic redistribution artifacts.

Scope control for SA/mode-locking (addresses critique v): The SA/mode-locking arm is explicitly secondary and gated by demonstrated CT tunability (ΔfCT) and SA benchmarks (modulation depth, recovery time, photostability). This preserves proposal coherence—CT fraction remains the shared state variable—while preventing the optoelectronic demonstration from diluting the PV mechanistic objective if perovskite SA dynamics or stability prove limiting.

Literature transfer logic (Assets 1–2): Asset 2 motivates that DCA-derived CT occupancy and emergent spin signatures can be tuned by external electric fields via substrate/field coupling; we translate this to a perovskite-native, buried-interface CT equilibrium and explicitly quantify field delivery and level alignment. Asset 1 links enhanced charge transfer in ultrathin heterostructures to strong third-order nonlinear optical response and mode-locking; in our system, CT-population control is the mechanistic bridge to modulation-depth tunability, but only pursued once CT tunability is proven under electronic-only field conditions.
Critique: The proposal is unusually strong in execution planning and falsification discipline (G1–G4), with a credible strategy to decouple electronic Stark/CT effects from ionic screening—an endemic perovskite artifact. The main scientific risk is not acknowledged with enough quantitative severity: achieving a ≥kBT modulation of ΔG at the *buried* RP/3D junction may require interfacial fields that are unrealistic once geometric attenuation, electrode screening, and perovskite electronic screening are accounted for at the chosen fmod. The electrostatics section is directionally correct but under-specifies key parameters that dominate Eint (built-in fields, interfacial band bending, finite density of states/quantum capacitance of the CT layer, and whether the RP cap behaves as a simple linear dielectric versus having field-dependent polarization). Second, the Marcus/ΔG→fCT mapping is underdetermined: fCT is treated as quasi-equilibrium with EFn, but no explicit thermodynamic model is provided (e.g., Fermi–Dirac occupancy of a broadened acceptor manifold with Coulomb interactions, image-charge stabilization, and a finite areal density of DCA sites). Without that, “ΔfCT ≥ 5–10%” is not yet a rigorous prediction target. Third, the causal link from ΔfCT to reduced nonradiative recombination is plausible but currently ambiguous in sign and pathway: DCA•− could (a) drain electrons and reduce electron density at defect states, but also (b) introduce additional interfacial states, dipolar disorder, or mid-gap charge-assisted recombination depending on coupling and back-transfer; the plan lacks a decisive experiment to distinguish beneficial extraction from added recombination channels (e.g., intensity-dependent ideality analysis vs trap-assisted recombination fingerprints, or direct measurement of interfacial recombination velocity versus extraction selectivity). Finally, the SA/mode-locking arm remains conceptually attached but scientifically thin: modulation-depth tunability is asserted to correlate with fCT/EA, yet there is no quantitative linkage from CT population change to χ(3), excited-state absorption bleaching, or recovery pathways in the perovskite/RP/DCA ensemble, making this portion more of a demonstration prospect than a hypothesis-driven deliverable.

Hypothesis: Embedding a Zn‑Car_MOF–templated, transiently formed quasi‑2D/3D perovskite surface termination functions as a chemically rigid, low‑ionic‑mobility ‘ionic‑sink cap’ that suppresses *Staebler–Wronski‑like* light‑induced metastability at the perovskite/transport‑layer interface during MPP operation. Mechanistically, this approach operates via two separable but synergistic pathways: (i) **defect-chemical stabilization**—Zn2+–carboxylate/imidazole coordination and grafted carnosine/carboxylate motifs convert under‑coordinated Pb2+ and halide‑vacancy‑adjacent sites into thermodynamically stable complexes, reducing the formation probability of light‑activated metastable defects analogous to SW bond switching; and (ii) **ionic‑kinetic suppression**—the templated quasi‑2D RP‑like termination (≤10–15 nm) increases the activation energy for halide migration and polaron‑assisted bond rearrangement at the surface, thereby decoupling reversible Voc losses from fast ionic redistribution. Crucially, by removing the MOF after templating, the method decouples chemical stabilization from electronic insulation, yielding higher stabilized Voc, reduced reversible light‑soaking losses, and slower MPP power decay. The hypothesis explicitly predicts that SW‑like defect creation will exhibit distinct intensity‑ and temperature‑scaling and recovery kinetics from ion‑migration‑dominated effects, enabling unambiguous experimental discrimination.
Plan:
### Phase I – Factorial Chemical Decomposition and Surface Formation Attribution
**Objective:** Isolate which chemical components induce quasi‑2D surface formation versus which suppress metastable defect creation.

**I.1 Full factorial matrix (primary screen):**
- Variables (binary): MOF (Zn‑Car_MOF present/absent) × bulky ammonium halide (present/absent) × Zn2+ (salt present/absent) × carnosine (present/absent).
- Mandatory arms include: (a) MOF only (no ammonium), (b) ammonium only (no MOF), (c) Zn‑salt + ammonium, (d) carnosine + ammonium, (e) inert porous template + ammonium.
- Fixed perovskite: Cs0.05(FA0.83MA0.17)Pb(I0.8Br0.2)3 with 2–3% excess PbI2.

**I.2 Structural attribution:**
- GIWAXS (incident angle 0.2–0.3°) to identify RP‑like (n≤2) diffraction features confined to surface.
- Cross‑sectional STEM‑EELS to confirm thickness (<15 nm) and continuity.
- Decision gate: quasi‑2D formation must correlate uniquely with *ammonium presence*, while metastability suppression beyond standard RP caps must correlate with *MOF‑templated chemistry*.

---
### Phase II – Chemically Orthogonal MOF Lift‑Off with Mass Balance
**Objective:** De‑risk the highest‑impact failure mode (template removal).

**II.1 Lift‑off protocol:**
- Primary route: mechanical dislodgement + polarity‑orthogonal solvent wash (anhydrous anisole → dry chlorobenzene) exploiting weak MOF–perovskite adhesion post‑anneal.
- Secondary (only if needed): ultra‑dilute (≤1 mM) amino‑acid–based Zn chelator in nonpolar/alcohol‑free solvent; exposure <10 s.

**II.2 Validation and numeric thresholds:**
- ICP‑MS of rinse solutions for Zn mass balance (≥95% Zn removal relative to deposited amount).
- XPS depth profiling (Zn 2p, Pb 4f, I 3d, Br 3d): residual Zn <0.2 at.% in top 10 nm.
- AFM/ellipsometry: thickness change ≤1.5 nm post‑lift‑off.
- Electronic acceptance: no increase in Urbach energy (>2 meV), no new deep‑level signature in sub‑bandgap EQE/PDS, and ΔVoc ≤5 mV at matched QFLS compared to Zn‑free RP cap.

---
### Phase III – Discriminating Staebler–Wronski‑like Defect Creation vs Ion Migration
**Objective:** Establish causality, not correlation.

**III.1 Kinetic decision tree:**
- **Intensity scaling:** Measure reversible Voc loss ΔVoc_rev ∝ I^α. SW‑like defect creation predicts sub‑linear α<1 with saturation; ionic redistribution predicts near‑linear scaling.
- **Temperature scaling:** Extract activation energies (Ea) from stretched‑exponential fits to Voc(t) under light (25–65 °C). Ea ~0.1–0.3 eV → ionic; Ea ≥0.5 eV → bond‑switching/defect creation.
- **Recovery bias dependence:** Dark recovery at 0 V vs forward bias. Ionic effects recover bias‑dependently; SW‑like defect annealing is bias‑insensitive but thermally activated.

**III.2 Direct defect spectroscopy:**
- Operando sub‑bandgap EQE/PDS during light soaking to track mid‑gap state density evolution.
- Correlate defect density changes with Voc/QFLS decay and recovery.

---
### Phase IV – Direct Quantification of Ionic Mobility Suppression
**Objective:** Provide quantitative support beyond impedance heuristics.

**IV.1 Temperature‑dependent transient ionic current (TIC):**
- Extract ionic conductivity and Ea_ion using validated equivalent‑circuit models (separating electronic and ionic branches).

**IV.2 Tracer diffusion:**
- Bias‑assisted halide migration followed by TOF‑SIMS depth profiling; extract effective diffusion coefficients (D_eff) at interfaces.
- Success criterion: ≥3× reduction in D_eff relative to control and standard RP cap.

---
### Phase V – Device‑Level Validation under MPP and Outdoor‑Relevant Stress
- Absolute PLQY/QFLS → Voc reciprocity.
- Long‑term MPP tracking (ISOS‑L‑2+) with temperature/irradiance logging and energy‑yield modeling.
- Endpoints: stabilized Voc, reversible vs irreversible loss partitioning, T80, and Voc,stab distributions (≥25 devices/condition).
Feasibility: This refined plan directly addresses reviewer concerns by converting the proposal from a plausibility‑based narrative into a falsifiable, decision‑tree‑driven investigation. First, Staebler–Wronski‑like behavior is no longer inferred indirectly but discriminated using intensity/temperature scaling, activation energies, bias‑dependent recovery, and operando sub‑bandgap spectroscopy—approaches that can separate bond‑switching‑driven defect creation from ion redistribution. Second, the chemically orthogonal lift‑off protocol is explicitly de‑risked through mass balance (ICP‑MS), surface stoichiometry (XPS I/Pb/Br ratios), morphology (AFM/ellipsometry), and numeric residual‑Zn thresholds tied to electronic metrics (Urbach energy, deep‑level signatures, Voc at matched QFLS). Third, a full factorial chemical matrix ensures unambiguous attribution of quasi‑2D formation versus metastability suppression, preventing mechanism conflation. Finally, ionic immobilization is quantified via activation energies and tracer diffusion coefficients, not inferred solely from low‑frequency capacitance. The approach remains scalable (short post‑treatments compatible with blade coating), aligns with outdoor MPP degradation frameworks (Asset 2), and leverages coordination chemistry principles validated in Zn‑Car_MOF systems (Asset 1) while explicitly addressing SW‑type stability challenges known from thin‑film PVs (Asset 3).
Critique: The proposal is unusually strong in experimental structure (factorial attribution, quantitative lift-off thresholds, operando defect tracking, and tracer diffusion to avoid impedance-only claims). The main scientific weakness is that the “Staebler–Wronski-like” assignment is still somewhat inferential: the proposed kinetic discriminants (α intensity scaling, apparent Ea thresholds, bias-dependent recovery) are not uniquely identifying in halide perovskites because mixed ionic–electronic coupling, field-dependent ion drift, interfacial dipoles, and light-induced de-trapping can also produce sub-linear intensity response, stretched-exponential kinetics, and higher apparent activation energies. In addition, the lift-off strategy remains a high-risk integration point: mechanical dislodgement/solvent wash may alter the RP-like termination (or remove it), and XPS/ICP thresholds alone do not guarantee that residual Zn/carnosine coordination chemistry remains in the intended bound state rather than redistributed into the perovskite or transport layer. Finally, the causal linkage “MOF-templated chemistry → reduced metastable defect creation” would benefit from a more direct structural/chemical fingerprint of the proposed stabilized complexes (Pb–ligand coordination and halide-vacancy-adjacent binding) and a control demonstrating that identical quasi-2D thickness/orientation without MOF does not reproduce the effect.

Hypothesis: Embedding a carboxylic acid-based Co-MOF as an ultrathin, bicontinuous interfacial scaffold with Schwarz P (negative Gaussian curvature) at the perovskite/HTL interface will simultaneously (i) lower interfacial charge-transfer overpotential for hole extraction and (ii) suppress interfacial degradation by immobilizing iodide and coordinating under-coordinated Pb2+. The specific methodological adaptation is to convert a conventional flat MOF interlayer into a conformal Schwarz P-architected MOF film whose curved, bicontinuous channels are infiltrated with a crosslinkable ionic polymer (Nafion-like sulfonate ionomer in trace loading) to (a) tune Co-node coordination toward transient Co–OHx/Co–O motifs that act as fast redox mediators for interfacial hole transfer and (b) create steric/ionic gating that reduces halide back-diffusion and metal-ion migration. Mechanistically, negative curvature increases accessible coordination site density and optimizes intermediate adsorption/charge localization (analogous to curvature-enhanced electrocatalysis), while carboxylate-Pb binding passivates trap states; together these reduce non-radiative recombination (higher Voc) and interfacial energetic losses (lower overpotential) under operational bias.

Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1. Select a high-Voc baseline perovskite stack (e.g., p–i–n: ITO/NiOx/FA0.83Cs0.17Pb(I0.9Br0.1)3/C60/BCP/Ag or n–i–p: FTO/SnO2/perovskite/spiro-OMeTAD/Au) and define the target interface to engineer (perovskite/HTL for n–i–p or perovskite/NiOx for p–i–n).
2. Prepare a carboxylic-acid linker set enabling robust Co-MOF growth at low temperature (e.g., trimesic acid/BTC, terephthalic acid/BDC derivatives) and incorporate a small fraction (1–5 mol%) of multifunctional linkers bearing latent crosslink sites (e.g., vinyl, epoxide) to lock morphology after formation.
3. Establish a curvature template route compatible with PSC processing: polymer cubosomes or block-copolymer bicontinuous templates that yield a Schwarz P-like network at 20–80 nm length scale, stable in perovskite-compatible solvents.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
1. Schwarz P templating on perovskite: Spin-coat a thin bicontinuous polymer cubosome layer (10–30 nm effective thickness) directly on the perovskite surface under dry inert conditions; anneal mildly (<80–100 °C) to set the cubic phase without damaging the perovskite.
2. Interfacial MOF conversion (adaptation): Grow a Co-carboxylate MOF conformally within/on the cubosome channels via a vapor-assisted or low-polarity solvent-assisted coordination process (to avoid perovskite dissolution). This converts the initially polymeric Schwarz P morphology into a mechanically supported, continuous Co-MOF framework with negative Gaussian curvature and high accessible site density.
3. Trace ionomer infiltration for controlled Co–OHx formation: Introduce a very low loading of a sulfonated ionomer (Nafion-like) from an orthogonal solvent, followed by brief humidity-free activation. The ionomer provides steric hindrance and localized ionic microenvironments to favor formation of small, defective Co–OHx/Co–O motifs at/near Co nodes (without bulk insulating coverage), creating a redox-active mediator network.
4. Crosslink/lock the scaffold: Activate the multifunctional linkers (thermal/UV depending on chemistry) to crosslink the MOF/ionomer composite, preventing morphological collapse during HTL deposition and operation.
5. Deposit the transport layer: Apply HTL (spiro-OMeTAD/PTAA) or NiOx atop the Schwarz P Co-MOF interlayer; complete devices and include controls: (i) no interlayer, (ii) flat Co-MOF (no Schwarz P), (iii) Schwarz P polymer only, (iv) Schwarz P Co-MOF without ionomer, (v) ionomer only.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
1. Quantify “low overpotential” in PSC-relevant terms: Use intensity-dependent J–V, Suns-Voc, and electroluminescence quantum efficiency (EQEEL) to extract non-radiative voltage loss; use impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and transient photovoltage/photocurrent (TPV/TPC) to quantify charge-transfer resistance and interfacial recombination.
2. Mechanistic proof of curvature/function: Use GISAXS/ellipsometry/SEM-TEM tomography to confirm bicontinuous Schwarz P-like morphology; measure accessible Co-site density via chemisorption probes and XPS/EXAFS for Co coordination changes with/without ionomer.
3. Interface defect passivation: Track trap density and surface recombination velocity via thermal admittance spectroscopy, time-resolved PL (TRPL), and absolute PLQY on perovskite films with the interlayer.
4. Ion migration and chemical stability: Perform bias-stress and light-soaking tests (MPP tracking at 1 sun, 65–85 °C optional) while monitoring hysteresis, Voc drift, and EIS signatures; use ToF-SIMS depth profiles for I−/Br−/Co/S distributions before/after aging to test halide immobilization and metal diffusion.
5. Performance and scaling checks: Report stabilized PCE, Voc/FF gains, and device-to-device variance; demonstrate compatibility with larger-area substrates (e.g., 1–10 cm2) by slot-die/spin hybrid deposition of the template and vapor-assisted MOF growth.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Curvature-engineered Schwarz P architectures have been empirically shown to increase electrocatalytic turnover by maximizing accessible coordination sites and lowering reaction barriers via electronic/adsorption optimization. Separately, carboxylic acid-based Co-MOFs can be transformed/activated to Co–OHx-like active motifs and achieve low overpotential in OER when modified with Nafion due to steric hindrance yielding smaller, more defective hydroxide domains with more active sites.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): In PSCs, the dominant losses and instability often originate at interfaces (trap-assisted recombination, energetic barriers, ion migration, chemical reactions with transport layers). The proposed Schwarz P Co-MOF interlayer is not used as a bulk conductor; it is a nanometric interfacial mediator/passivator: carboxylates coordinate Pb2+ to reduce traps (boost Voc), while the bicontinuous, ionomer-tuned Co-node chemistry provides a fast interfacial redox/charge-transfer pathway (lower interfacial overpotential/charge-transfer resistance) and ionic gating (reduced halide back-diffusion under bias).
3. Comparative Advantage: Versus a flat MOF or conventional SAMs, the Schwarz P scaffold provides (i) far higher interfacial site utilization at equal thickness, (ii) continuous percolation pathways for charge transfer without requiring thick layers that impede transport, and (iii) morphological locking that resists interlayer rupture during HTL deposition and thermal cycling. Versus adding catalytic dopants directly into perovskite, the interlayer localizes Co chemistry away from the bulk absorber, minimizing deep-level defect formation while still enabling interfacial kinetic acceleration and improved operational stability.
Critique: This is an unusually sophisticated and technically ambitious interfacial engineering proposal with strong internal coherence. The engineering plan demonstrates high resolution: low-temperature Schwarz P templating, vapor-assisted MOF conversion, trace ionomer infiltration, and linker crosslinking are all actionable and largely compatible with PSC constraints. The mechanistic logic—curvature-enhanced coordination site accessibility, carboxylate–Pb2+ passivation, and Co–OHx-mediated interfacial redox facilitation—is well articulated and largely defensible by analogy to electrocatalysis and known MOF chemistry. However, two points slightly weaken the logical rigor: (i) the assumption that Co–OHx redox mediation will accelerate hole extraction without introducing mid-gap recombination channels is not quantitatively bounded (e.g., redox potential alignment vs perovskite quasi-Fermi level), and (ii) the stability of Co carboxylate frameworks under prolonged iodide-rich, biased PSC operation remains uncertain despite ionomer gating. Evidence grounding is strong and domain-relevant, though some electrocatalysis-to-PSC transfer claims rely on qualitative analogy rather than PSC-specific precedent. Overall, this is a high-risk, high-reward concept with exceptional depth, but it would benefit from tighter energetic and degradation-risk constraints.

1. These gaps do not invalidate the concept but reduce certainty that all claimed functions can be simultaneously realized in a 5–20 nm interlayer.

1.1 Select a high-Voc, stable 3D absorber (e.g., FA/Cs mixed-cation iodide-bromide tuned to ~1.55 eV) and a baseline device architecture where interfacial chemistry dominates stability losses (n–i–p: glass/ITO/SnO2/perovskite/HTL/Au; and p–i–n: ITO/NiOx/perovskite/C60/BCP/Ag for cross-validation).
1.2 Prepare a Fe–N–C precursor polymer/cubosome formulation capable of forming a Schwarz P–like bicontinuous mesophase at sub-50 nm thickness. Build a control library: (A) flat Fe–N–C layer (no bicontinuity), (B) bicontinuous carbon without Fe, (C) bicontinuous Fe present but not atomically dispersed (nanoclusters), (D) no interlayer.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Curvature templating at thin-film scale (adaptation of cubosome-templated SAC synthesis): deposit a cubosome-forming block-copolymer/phenolic-resin film (or similar carbonizable network) on the relevant transport layer (SnO2 or C60). Induce an ordered bicontinuous cubic mesophase (Schwarz P topology) via solvent-vapor annealing to lock in negative Gaussian curvature.
2.2 Introduce Fe and N coordination under confinement: infiltrate Fe and N precursors (e.g., Fe-porphyrin-like motif precursors or Fe salts + N-rich ligands) into the mesophase; then perform low-damage conversion to FeN4 sites using mild thermal treatment compatible with underlying layers (target ≤200–250 °C for ITO/SnO2, lower if on organic layers; if higher temperature needed, synthesize on a sacrificial substrate and transfer as a free-standing ultrathin network).
2.3 Densify/functionalize for PSC compatibility: apply an ultrathin wide-bandgap, ion-blocking skin (e.g., a few cycles of ALD Al2O3 or molecular crosslinking) that preserves bicontinuous porosity but prevents direct Fe contact with perovskite to avoid unwanted metal diffusion; tune work function via controlled N-speciation to maintain selective extraction (electron-selective near SnO2/C60, hole-selective near NiOx).
2.4 Interface integration: deposit perovskite atop the interlayer with crystallization control (antisolvent or gas-quench) ensuring conformal wetting into the bicontinuous topography without pinholes. Complete devices with standard HTL/ETL stacks.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural/chemical proof of adaptation: GISAXS/TEM tomography to confirm Schwarz P–like bicontinuity and curvature; BET/ellipsometric porosimetry for accessible surface area at thin-film scale; XAS (XANES/EXAFS) + Mössbauer to quantify FeN4 single-atom coordination vs clusters; XPS/NEXAFS to map N species and Fe oxidation state.
3.2 Quantify utilization ratio of FeN4 active sites in-operando: combine electrochemical redox titration (thin-film electrode in non-aqueous electrolyte) with operando spectroscopies (in-situ EPR/UV–Vis) to determine fraction of Fe sites participating in ROS scavenging and halide-redox buffering under light and bias proxies.
3.3 PSC performance and recombination diagnostics: JV (hysteresis), stabilized MPP, Suns-Voc, TRPL and absolute PLQY at 1 sun to extract quasi-Fermi level splitting; impedance spectroscopy to deconvolute interfacial charge-transfer vs recombination resistances; transient photovoltage/photocurrent to assess carrier lifetimes and extraction.
3.4 Mechanistic validation of catalytic buffering: illuminate devices in controlled O2/H2O atmospheres while tracking superoxide/iodine intermediates (EPR spin trapping; operando GIWAXS/ToF-SIMS for iodide migration and interfacial composition). Compare degradation kinetics (T80 under ISOS-L-2 / MPP tracking at 65–85 °C) across controls to attribute improvements specifically to (i) curvature (accessibility/transport) and (ii) FeN4 site chemistry (selective scavenging).
3.5 Failure analysis and guardrails: monitor Fe diffusion (ToF-SIMS depth profiles after aging), trap-density (SCLC), and band alignment (UPS/KPFM). Iterate skin-layer thickness and Fe loading to eliminate Voc penalties or shunts.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Negative Gaussian curvature bicontinuous architectures are empirically shown to increase surface area and active-site utilization ratio for FeN4 SACs, enhancing electrocatalytic activity through improved accessibility and modified adsorption energetics. In PSCs, the dominant losses often arise at interfaces via ROS-driven chemistry, halide redox, and defect-mediated non-radiative recombination—processes that can be mitigated by interfacial chemical buffering and passivation.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal does not import electrocatalysis generically; it adapts the curvature-enabled SAC concept into an ultrathin interfacial scaffold tailored to PSC constraints: low optical loss, band alignment control, ion/metal diffusion suppression, and compatibility with low-temperature processing. The FeN4 sites are positioned to act as chemically active ‘interfacial sinks’ for ROS and halide-redox intermediates while the bicontinuous topology maximizes the fraction of sites actually participating (high utilization ratio) in the confined PSC interface.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with flat passivation layers (2D perovskites, SAMs) that are chemically passive, the bicontinuous FeN4 interlayer adds an active catalytic buffering function without requiring thick layers. Compared with adding nanoparticles or redox additives, single-atom FeN4 reduces parasitic absorption/scattering and enables atom-efficient activity. The negative-curvature topology provides a unique lever—site accessibility/transport and curvature-tuned energetics—that directly targets the utilization ratio bottleneck, enabling stability gains under O2/H2O/light where conventional passivants often fail.
Critique: This is a technically ambitious and unusually well-resolved proposal that demonstrates deep cross-domain synthesis between single-atom electrocatalysis and perovskite interfacial chemistry. Engineering resolution is high: the cubosome-templated Schwarz P mesophase, FeN4 confinement strategy, low-temperature conversion constraints, diffusion guardrails, and multi-modal operando validation are articulated at a level suitable for execution in an advanced materials lab. Logical consistency is strong but not perfect: while the curvature–utilization–activity argument is convincing in electrocatalysis, the proposal partially overextends by implying curvature-tuned adsorption energetics at FeN4 sites without a clearly defined electronic-structure mechanism under solid-state, low-dielectric PSC interfacial conditions. Evidence grounding is robust: the proposal stays anchored to FeN4 SAC literature, ROS/halide chemistry in PSCs, and negative-Gaussian-curvature accessibility arguments, avoiding speculative photonic or plasmonic claims. Rationale quality is high: the work targets a real bottleneck (interfacial chemical instability under O2/H2O/light) with a non-trivial structural adaptation rather than incremental passivation. Minor deductions arise from (i) uncertain feasibility of achieving high-quality FeN4 coordination at ≤200–250 °C without sacrificing site density, and (ii) the risk that the catalytic activity window overlaps with unwanted perovskite redox pathways, which is acknowledged but not fully bounded theoretically.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a mechanically gated, ROS-scavenging “breathing electrode” built from a Zn-Car_MOF–carbon composite as the perovskite solar cell (PSC) top contact will simultaneously (i) reduce photo-oxidative degradation driven by singlet oxygen (^{1}O_{2}) by adsorption/physical removal of O2/H2O and catalytic quenching of ROS at the device surface, and (ii) preserve high power conversion efficiency by providing a low-barrier, conductive carbon current-collecting network. The methodological adaptation is to replace the conventional metal/Au (or carbon-only) top electrode with a laminated, microstructured tribo–piezoelectric hybrid nanogenerator (TPHG) electrode stack that periodically modulates the local oxygen chemical potential and interfacial charge distribution through contact–separation microcycles. Mechanistically, cyclic piezo/tribo polarization in the electrode induces reversible “gating” of O2 uptake/release within Zn-Car_MOF pores while the carnosine–Zn coordination sites chemically quench ROS (including ^{1}O_{2}) and the carbon component provides fast lateral transport; together this converts an otherwise open-air PSC surface into a self-regulating, adsorption-dominated oxygen sink that suppresses ^{1}O_{2}-initiated halide/perovskite oxidation and interfacial non-radiative recombination.
Plan:
Step 1: System setup and material preparation.
1.1 Synthesize Zn-Car_MOF microcrystals (100–500 nm) with controlled porosity and surface histidine/imidazole exposure (via modulated synthesis using carnosine:Zn ratio and pH) to maximize ROS interaction sites while maintaining chemical compatibility with iodide-rich perovskites.
1.2 Prepare a conductive carbon component as a hierarchical network: (i) few-layer graphene or CNTs for percolation, plus (ii) mesoporous carbon black for contact conformity. Form a Zn-Car_MOF/carbon composite ink where MOF is the oxygen/ROS-active phase and carbon is the continuous conductor.
1.3 Fabricate a flexible TPHG laminate that is not electrically wired into the PSC circuit: a patterned PDMS tribolayer + piezoelectric PVDF (or BaTiO3–PVDF) layer, designed for repeated contact–separation under ambient vibrations. The TPHG is used as a mechanically active cap/laminate that produces local polarization fields at the electrode surface rather than injecting current into the device.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Device architecture: inverted (p–i–n) PSC to enable low-temperature processing and stable top electrodes: glass/ITO/NiOx (or MeO-2PACz)/3D perovskite (FA/Cs mixed-cation)/C60 (or PCBM)/BCP.
2.2 Methodological adaptation—“breathing electrode” formation:
• Deposit (doctor-blade or screen-print) a 5–20 µm Zn-Car_MOF/carbon composite as the top electrode directly on BCP, optimized to be porous (gas-accessible) yet conductive.
• Laminate the TPHG film on top of this electrode with a microstructured spacer array (10–50 µm pillars) so that ambient mechanical stimuli generate periodic micro-contact without crushing the PSC.
2.3 Functional mechanism engineering:
• Engineer the MOF fraction and pore accessibility to maximize adsorption removal efficiency for oxygen/water: quantify O2 uptake isotherms and tune composite hydrophobicity (e.g., partial fluorinated binder in carbon ink) so the electrode preferentially sequesters O2 while limiting liquid water accumulation.
• Use the TPHG-induced periodic polarization to modulate adsorption/desorption kinetics: in the contact state, enhanced local fields and pressure promote O2 uptake into MOF pores and improve interfacial sealing; in the separation state, partial release prevents saturation and maintains long-term scavenging capacity.
• Ensure charge selectivity is preserved by maintaining a thin electron-selective layer (BCP) beneath the composite and by keeping the MOF electronically decoupled from the perovskite (MOF embedded within carbon matrix, minimizing direct MOF/perovskite charge extraction pathways that could introduce recombination).

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 ROS and ^{1}O_{2} quantification under operational illumination:
• Operando EPR with TEMP/TEMPO for ^{1}O_{2} and DMPO for •OH/•O2−, comparing (a) standard metal electrode, (b) carbon-only electrode, (c) Zn-Car_MOF/carbon breathing electrode without TPHG laminate, (d) full breathing electrode + TPHG laminate under mechanical actuation.
• Complement with singlet oxygen sensor green (SOSG) in a sealed optical microcell placed against the electrode surface to map ^{1}O_{2} flux.
3.2 Adsorption removal efficiency and oxygen chemical potential control:
• Measure O2/H2O uptake of the composite (gravimetric sorption, QCM) and correlate to ^{1}O_{2} suppression rate constants.
• Use operando mass spectrometry (or sealed-chamber O2 sensor) to track O2 depletion near the device surface during illumination with/without mechanical cycling.
3.3 Photovoltaic performance and recombination analysis:
• J–V (forward/reverse), stabilized MPP tracking, Suns-Voc, and impedance spectroscopy to confirm unchanged charge-selective behavior.
• TRPL and transient photovoltage/photocurrent to quantify non-radiative recombination reduction attributed to lower oxidative defect formation.
3.4 Stability testing with mechanistic attribution:
• ISOS-L-2 (light soaking) and ISOS-O-2 (oxygen-containing atmosphere) with controlled vibration spectra to activate the laminate; track Voc, FF, and PCE decay.
• Post-mortem XPS/ToF-SIMS for iodate/lead oxide formation, and GIWAXS for phase changes, linking suppressed oxidation signatures to measured ^{1}O_{2} reductions.
3.5 Controls to isolate mechanisms:
• Replace Zn-Car_MOF with an isostructural non-antioxidant MOF (same porosity, no carnosine) to decouple adsorption from chemical quenching.
• Replace carbon percolation network with low-conductivity carbon to show conductivity–stability trade-offs.
• Use a non-piezo/tribo inert laminate (same mechanical barrier) to isolate the mechanically gated adsorption effect from simple encapsulation.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Zn-Car_MOFs (carnosine–Zn bio-MOFs) provide chemically active coordination sites capable of interacting with ROS, while carbon composites are established as conductive, porous electrodes in PSCs. Literature demonstrates MOF-derived carbon systems can generate/mediate ROS and that carbon components enhance adsorption removal efficiency in oxidative environments; here we invert that logic to suppress ROS by sequestration and quenching rather than promoting AOP chemistry.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The approach targets a dominant PSC failure pathway—oxygen/light-driven interfacial oxidation—without injecting external bias or adding unstable molecular antioxidants into the perovskite bulk. By relocating ROS management into a replaceable, printable top electrode compatible with inverted PSC processing, the method aligns with scalable manufacturing (screen printing/lamination) and maintains high PCE via a continuous carbon conduction network.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike the rejected electrically addressable interlayer concept, this is a structurally novel, circuit-independent architecture: the TPHG functions as a mechanically active laminate that modulates adsorption kinetics rather than powering/biased electrochemistry. The breathing electrode provides (i) regenerative oxygen scavenging (avoids one-time antioxidant consumption), (ii) direct suppression of ^{1}O_{2} at the device/air interface, and (iii) scalable, metal-free top contacts that can improve stability and reduce cost/toxicity relative to noble-metal electrodes.
Critique: This is an unusually ambitious and well-articulated proposal that demonstrates strong command of PSC degradation physics, ROS chemistry, and functional electrode design. Engineering resolution is high: materials synthesis, device architecture, lamination strategy, and operando diagnostics are specified with actionable detail. The main score deductions arise from mechanistic overreach in the tribo–piezoelectric gating argument. While polarization-induced modulation of adsorption kinetics is plausible, the proposal does not yet quantitatively justify the magnitude, spatial extent, or timescale of the local electric fields relative to O2 diffusion and singlet oxygen lifetimes at the PSC surface. In addition, the assumption that cyclic adsorption/desorption will be regenerative rather than kinetically limited or fatigue-prone remains speculative. Evidence grounding is strong and largely disciplined, though the dual role of carbon (conductor vs. adsorption mediator) could be more clearly disentangled to avoid conceptual circularity. Overall, the logic is coherent but occasionally stacks multiple second-order effects without a clear hierarchy of dominant mechanisms.

Hypothesis: Embedding an electrochemically addressable Ni(OH)2/NiOOH-in-Zn-Car_MOF nanolayer as a wired, redox-buffering interfacial contact on the electron-selective side of perovskite solar cells will suppress oxygen-induced interfacial degradation and reduce non-radiative recombination by quantitatively lowering steady-state electron accumulation at the ETL interface rather than by invoking true oxygen evolution. Under 1-sun operation, the dominant oxygen chemistry at PSC electron contacts is oxygen reduction (O2 + e− → O2•−, E° ≈ −0.33 V vs NHE in aprotic media) and subsequent superoxide/peroxide interconversion. The Ni(II)/Ni(III) redox couple (Ni(OH)2/NiOOH, formal potential ≈ +0.45–0.50 V vs NHE in mildly hydrated environments, shifted cathodically in confined/solid-state conditions) does not drive OER under PSC conditions but instead acts as a fast, reversible electron reservoir with high areal pseudocapacitance. By providing a local redox density that can accept excess photogenerated electrons on sub-ms timescales, the Ni redox layer clamps the electron quasi-Fermi level at the ETL interface to values insufficient to sustain O2 → O2•− reduction, thereby shortening superoxide lifetime and suppressing downstream peroxide- and radical-driven perovskite oxidation. Any residual reduced oxygen species are further mitigated by rapid, catalytic electron back-transfer and disproportionation pathways occurring at the Ni sites within the MOF nanoreactor environment, spatially displaced from the perovskite by a molecular buffer. The Zn-Car_MOF is repurposed from a release medium into a programmable redox-access scaffold that controls the temporal accessibility and density of Ni active sites without ionic leaching. Quantitatively, the hypothesis predicts that achieving an interfacial pseudocapacitance ≥5–10 mF·cm−2 with a charge-transfer resistance ≤5 Ω·cm2 at ≥1 kHz will reduce the steady-state interfacial electron density by ≥3× under illumination, yielding a ≥20–40 mV increase in implied Voc and ≥2× improvement in oxygen-limited T80 lifetime, without introducing additional recombination or series resistance.
Plan:
Step 1 – Architecture and energetic baselining. (1.1) Fabricate inverted p–i–n (Glass/ITO/NiOx or MeO-2PACz/perovskite/C60/BCP/Ag) and reference n–i–p stacks to isolate polarity effects. (1.2) Establish baseline band alignment and electron quasi-Fermi level position at the C60 interface using UPS and KPFM under dark and 1-sun conditions; target EFn(C60) ≈ −3.9 to −4.0 eV vs vacuum under operation. (1.3) Synthesize 20–50 nm Zn-Car_MOF nanocrystals with 1–5 mol% π-conjugated carboxylate co-linker to enhance electronic coupling; verify porosity (BET), crystallinity (PXRD), and defect density (FTIR/XPS).

Step 2 – Wired MOF interlayer with non-alkaline Ni conversion. (2.1) Form a 3–10 nm ultrathin Zn-Car_MOF film co-deposited with 0.1–0.3 wt% carboxylated graphene quantum dots to achieve in-plane conductivity ≥10−6 S·cm−1 while keeping vertical leakage <10−7 A·cm−2 at ±1 V. (2.2) Deposit the wired MOF between C60 and BCP, or between perovskite and C60 separated by a ≤1 nm fullerene-SAM, confirmed by cross-sectional TEM. (2.3) Introduce Ni via nickel(II) acetate tetrahydrate infiltration from anhydrous ethanol with excess acetate ligand; convert to Ni(OH)2/NiOOH using a fully non-alkaline solid-state route: brief electrochemical oxidation/reduction pulses (charge density 1–10 mC·cm−2) through ITO using a solid polymer electrolyte containing bound hydroxide donors (e.g., quaternary ammonium hydroxide immobilized in PEO), followed by vacuum annealing to remove residual species. Verify absence of free OH− ingress by ToF-SIMS depth profiling.

Step 3 – Quantitative redox and capacitance tuning. (3.1) Measure Ni redox potential and kinetics in symmetric test stacks (ITO/C60/wired MOF:Ni/C60/ITO) via CV and EIS; tune Ni loading to achieve areal pseudocapacitance ≥5–10 mF·cm−2 at 1 kHz and redox time constants <1 ms. (3.2) Ensure added series/contact resistance ≤1 Ω·cm2 and DC leakage ≤10−7 A·cm−2 at operating bias. (3.3) Encode time-dependent active-site accessibility via reversible MOF pore-gating (Zn2+ back-coordination or linker protonation), monitored as gradual increases in redox charge over 10–100 h without Ni migration.

Step 4 – Oxygen-redox mechanism validation (ORR-focused). (4.1) Operando oxygen analysis in sealed micro-chambers under controlled O2 (200 ppm–air): quantify O2 consumption, H2O2 formation/decay (colorimetric or electrochemical probes), and compare superoxide lifetime using in situ EPR spin trapping on witness stacks. The discriminating signature is reduced O2•− signal amplitude and lifetime without net O2 evolution. (4.2) Correlate Ni redox state (operando Ni K-edge XAS or Raman) with transient photovoltage/photocurrent and EIS-derived recombination resistance under MPP.

Step 5 – Optoelectronic and degradation diagnostics. (5.1) Measure absolute PLQY and implied Voc of perovskite/C60/contact stacks; target ΔVoc,implied ≥20–40 mV. (5.2) Perform dark J–V (ideality factor), SCLC trap DOS, and temperature-dependent recombination analysis to verify no new trap-assisted pathways. (5.3) Conduct MPP stability at 45–65 °C under controlled oxygen; success criteria: ≥95% PCE retention after 500 h at 1% O2 and ≥2× T80 in air. (5.4) Post-mortem ToF-SIMS, XPS, and STEM-EDS to confirm suppressed iodide oxidation, Pb0 formation, and metal halide migration.

Step 6 – Controls and falsification. Compare against (i) wired MOF without Ni, (ii) Ni(OH)2 without MOF, (iii) Ni acetate without electrochemical conversion, (iv) MOF without nanocarbon wiring, and (v) oxygen-free encapsulation. The mechanism is falsified if superoxide lifetime, implied Voc, or stability gains are observed without achieving the targeted pseudocapacitance or if added redox density increases recombination or leakage.
Feasibility: The revised framework aligns the oxygen chemistry with thermodynamically accessible pathways at PSC electron contacts, replacing the unrealistic OER claim with an ORR/superoxide-suppression model grounded in known redox potentials and kinetics. MOF@Ni(OH)2 composites are empirically demonstrated to provide high pseudocapacitance and fast Ni(II)/Ni(III) redox, supporting the quantitative capacitance targets defined here. Nickel(II) acetate tetrahydrate is a validated precursor for ultrathin hydroxide phases, and the proposed solid-state, non-alkaline electrochemical conversion eliminates hydroxide ingress risks. Band-alignment (UPS/KPFM), leakage, and recombination diagnostics directly address materials-compatibility concerns, while explicit numerical thresholds for capacitance, resistance, and leakage create clear go/no-go criteria. By spatially separating the redox buffer from the perovskite and proving function through falsifiable oxygen-species signatures rather than assumed OER activity, the approach de-risks integration and tightly links electrochemical design parameters to measurable device-level gains in Voc and operational stability.
Critique: The proposal is unusually strong in mechanistic specificity and falsifiability for an interfacial-stability concept in PSCs: it correctly reframes the oxygen chemistry away from unrealistic OER toward ORR/superoxide-driven degradation, and it translates the redox-buffer idea into measurable interface-electrochemistry metrics (areal pseudocapacitance, Rct, time constants) tied to Voc and lifetime predictions. However, several high-risk elements remain under-resolved. (i) The central quantitative claim—clamping the interfacial electron quasi-Fermi level sufficiently to suppress O2→O2•−—is not rigorously linked to a device-relevant electrochemical model (e.g., coupling pseudocapacitance/kinetics to interfacial electron density and local potential under MPP), so the ≥3× reduction in electron accumulation and 20–40 mV implied-Voc gain reads aspirational without a derived relationship. (ii) Achieving ≥5–10 mF·cm−2 at ≥1 kHz in a 3–10 nm solid-state interlayer is aggressive; many Ni(OH)2/NiOOH pseudocapacitive responses are far slower (diffusion/PCET-limited) and shift to much lower effective capacitance at kHz. The proposal acknowledges confinement shifts but does not provide a clear plan to prove sub-ms PCET in the intended dry/weakly hydrated stack. (iii) The non-alkaline ‘bound hydroxide donor’ polymer-electrolyte conversion step risks introducing mobile ionic species, residual water, or quaternary ammonium fragments that can themselves accelerate perovskite/C60 interface degradation; ToF-SIMS alone may not be sufficient to exclude electrically active ionic contamination. (iv) The added nanocarbon wiring and redox sites could introduce new surface states and increase interfacial recombination; while controls are listed, there is no explicit strategy for chemical passivation of Ni/MOF surfaces toward the perovskite/ETL or for maintaining a benign density of states. (v) Some operando oxygen analytics (EPR spin trapping, H2O2 quantification) are technically challenging in thin-film device-like stacks and can generate ambiguous signals without careful calibration and oxygen mass-balance; the plan would benefit from more explicit artifacts/blank protocols and detection limits. Overall, the concept is coherent and methodologically detailed, but the key performance-enabling electrochemical kinetics and the contamination/recombination risks need tighter quantitative mitigation plans.

Hypothesis: A redox-gated, Fe-porphyrin–functionalized porous oxide contact (RG-FeN@MOF-derived contact) enhances perovskite solar cell Voc, FF, and operational stability through two *chemically and electrochemically distinct but testable mechanisms*: (1) **Specific axial coordination and dipole-mediated passivation at the buried interface**, where under-coordinated Pb2+ and halide-vacancy complexes interact preferentially with the *axial Fe center or anchoring-group oxygen atoms* of surface-grafted Fe-porphyrins (rather than porphyrin ring nitrogens), reducing interfacial trap density and non-radiative recombination; and (2) **Solid-state redox gating of interfacial ionic charge**, where reversibly addressable Fe(III)/Fe(II) centers embedded in an electrochemically accessible internal surface act as a distributed charge reservoir that buffers ionic space-charge accumulation under operation without engaging in parasitic halide redox. The hypothesis explicitly rejects nonspecific “Pb–N ring coordination” and instead posits a falsifiable binding hierarchy (Fe axial site > anchoring group > dipole-only interaction) and a requirement that Fe redox activity remains reversible, spatially confined to the contact, and electronically coupled to the oxide backbone under device-relevant quasi-Fermi levels.
Plan:
Pre-registered discriminator phase (mandatory before scaling):

**A. Chemical binding locus discriminator (go/no-go #1)**
A1. Model buried-interface system: fabricate PbI2-terminated perovskite thin films and PbI2 single-crystal surfaces contacted with RG-FeN@MOF-derived porous SnOx or NiOx films grafted with (i) Fe-porphyrin, (ii) metal-free porphyrin, and (iii) Fe-porphyrin with blocked axial site (e.g., CO- or pyridine-ligated Fe).
A2. Spectroscopic probes:
- N K-edge XAS/XANES: detect shifts indicative of axial ligation at Fe vs unchanged porphyrin ring N.
- Fe K-edge XANES/EXAFS: identify changes in Fe coordination number/bond length consistent with axial Pb–I/Pb–O interaction.
- 15N-labeled porphyrin ssNMR (where feasible) to rule out ring-N involvement.
- DFT-calibrated Pb 4f / I 3d core-level shifts to assign binding energetics (target ΔEbind ≥ 0.2–0.3 eV for specific interaction).
A3. Go/no-go criterion: proceed only if axial-Fe or anchor-mediated interaction is detected with metal-free and axial-blocked controls showing ≤20% of the effect.

**B. Solid-state redox-gating discriminator (go/no-go #2)**
B1. Solid-state operando spectroelectrochemistry: integrate the RG-FeN@MOF contact into a solid stack (ITO/contact/Al2O3(1–2 nm)/inert semiconductor) and bias across ±0.2–0.6 V vs perovskite-relevant quasi-Fermi levels.
B2. Probes: UV–Vis–NIR (Fe-porphyrin redox fingerprints), Fe Mössbauer/EPR (Fe(III)/Fe(II) ratio), or Fe K-edge XAS under bias and illumination.
B3. Correlation: simultaneously measure low-frequency capacitance (10–1–10–2 Hz) to confirm suppression of ionic accumulation concurrent with reversible Fe redox.
B4. Go/no-go thresholds: ≥90% reversibility of Fe redox signal after 100 h bias at 85 °C; no emergence of I3−/I2 spectral signatures; leakage current increase <10%.

**C. Quantified porous-contact architecture (risk mitigation)**
C1. Morphology targets: porosity 30–45 vol%, pore diameter 15–40 nm, contact thickness 30–60 nm, oxide volume fraction above vertical percolation threshold.
C2. Transport targets: sheet resistance ≤2× compact oxide; vertical conductivity ≥10−3 S cm−1; contact resistivity ≤10−2 Ω·cm2.
C3. Fabrication window: MOF-900 nanocrystals 40–60 nm; oxide:MOF volume ratio tuned 55:45–65:35; MOF removal via UV–ozone + ≤150 °C anneal.
C4. Surface functionalization density: Fe-porphyrin coverage 0.3–0.8 nm−2 (sub-monolayer) verified by QCM/XPS.

**D. Solvent and processing orthogonality**
D1. Anchoring chemistry: phosphonate/catechol binding tested for stability against DMF/DMSO/GBL exposure (<10% loss by XPS after soak).
D2. Perovskite deposition: viscosity-tuned precursor (η ≥ 10 mPa·s), brief antisolvent (<3 s) to avoid pore infiltration; confirm continuity by cross-sectional SEM/TEM.

**E. Descriptor translation and device validation (post go)**
E1. Measure EASA (Cdl) and solid-state E1/2 analogue/k0 on the same films; confirm trends persist without liquid electrolyte by solid-state charge-modulation spectroscopy.
E2. Correlate with Voc, FF, hysteresis index, ideality factor, and T80 lifetime; apply falsification logic (EASA-only vs kinetics-only regimes).
Feasibility: The revised plan directly addresses reviewer concerns by narrowing the mechanistic claims to *testable, orthogonal interactions* and embedding explicit failure criteria. Chemical passivation is no longer assumed to arise from porphyrin ring nitrogens; instead, the proposal specifies axial Fe coordination or anchor-mediated Pb interaction as the dominant pathway, supported by orthogonal spectroscopy and DFT-calibrated signatures. This sharply reduces interpretational ambiguity inherent in buried-interface HAXPES alone. Redox gating is explicitly validated in the solid state—without electrolyte—using operando spectroelectrochemistry tied to ionic-capacitance suppression, ensuring relevance to device physics and ruling out parasitic halide redox. Quantitative morphology, transport, and solvent-orthogonality windows convert porous-contact integration from a qualitative risk to a bounded engineering problem. By enforcing pre-registered go/no-go discriminators, the proposal ensures that only if specific binding and reversible solid-state redox accessibility are demonstrated will the EASA/E1/2 descriptor program be scaled to full devices, thereby aligning ambition with credible mechanistic validation.
Critique: The proposal is methodologically strong and unusually falsifiable for an interfacial-mechanism claim in perovskites: axial-site blocking controls, metal-free porphyrin controls, and multiple orthogonal spectroscopies are appropriate to reject the common but ambiguous “Pb–N ring” narrative. The redox-gating test usefully insists on solid-state operation and couples redox-state readout to low-frequency capacitance—this is a coherent device-physics discriminator. Key deductions: (i) the half-wave potential/E1/2 concept is imported from electrochemistry but the translation to a solid-state, electrolyte-free stack remains underdefined (reference scale, band-alignment dependence, and how an ‘E1/2 analogue’ is extracted reproducibly across morphologies); (ii) the ionic-buffering claim risks non-uniqueness—changes in low-frequency capacitance/hysteresis can also arise from altered interfacial recombination, dielectric response, contact selectivity, or ion-blocking by Al2O3/porosity, so the current correlation plan may not isolate ‘redox reservoir’ causality; (iii) the buried-interface binding assignment remains challenging because Pb 4f/I 3d shifts and N K-edge signatures can conflate chemical interaction with electrostatic dipoles and band bending—DFT-calibrated shifts help, but the proposal does not specify how it will deconvolute electrostatic vs chemical contributions experimentally (e.g., via thickness dependence, hard/soft XPS depth profiling, or Kelvin probe). Overall, strong engineering and logic, with the main weakness being the incomplete, quantitative closure of the half-wave-potential descriptor chain under device-relevant solid-state conditions.

Hypothesis:
A 2D RP surface cap can be converted from an electronically passivating barrier into a conductive, virtual-state–mediated charge relay if (and only if) (i) the π-acceptor spacer introduces energetically *off-resonant* (virtual) states that enhance interlayer electronic coupling without forming a real charge-transfer complex (CTC) and (ii) transport shows a decisive *distance (thickness) dependence* consistent with superexchange/tunneling rather than barrier-limited hopping. In this design, a TCNQ-like π-acceptor spacer is incorporated as the organic layer of an n=1–3 RP cap on a 3D perovskite. The spacer’s acceptor level is tuned to sit near—but not within—the perovskite band edges such that carriers traverse the RP cap via virtual-state participation (superexchange), yielding: (a) a steeper-than-activated increase in through-plane conductance with decreasing RP thickness and a weaker temperature dependence of the interfacial transfer rate, and (b) maintained or improved Voc via reduced interfacial recombination velocity from defect passivation and ionic blocking.

A sparse, chelation-anchored Ni(OH)2·x decoration is introduced *only if Ni remains in an acceptable hydroxide/oxyhydroxide speciation window* under halide exposure and bias. The Ni decoration is not intended to provide percolative conductivity; instead it functions as a localized, high-accessibility redox/ion buffer at the 2D/HTL contact where halide/radical activity initiates. By enforcing a sub-percolation, site-pinned distribution (high “utilization ratio” of accessible Ni sites analogous to high active-site utilization in bicontinuous catalysts), the interfacial redox buffering mitigates iodide/bromide oxidation products and suppresses bias-stress hysteresis and degradation without introducing shunts or creating new recombination centers.

This refined hypothesis directly addresses prior ambiguities: superexchange is claimed only if (1) conductance scales exponentially with RP thickness with a decay constant distinct from simple thermionic barrier modulation and (2) ultrafast interfacial hole-transfer kinetics are weakly temperature dependent while recombination decreases; spacer-induced electronic states are acceptable only if sensitive sub-gap and CTC probes remain below strict thresholds; Ni chemistry is accepted only if operando/ex situ speciation confirms hydroxide/oxyhydroxide dominance and negligible Ni–X formation.
Plan:
Step 0 — Pre-registered go/no-go criteria (applies throughout)
0.1 Superexchange/virtual-state “go” criteria:
- Through-plane conductance G vs RP thickness d must fit G(d)=G0·exp(−βd) over ≥3 distinct d values (quantified by n and nm), with β in the tunneling/superexchange regime (operationally: β ≥ 0.8 nm−1 and stable within ±20% across bias window where band-bending changes are minimal).
- Interfacial hole-transfer time constant (fs–ps TA) changes by <2× between 200–320 K while recombination indicators improve (ΔQFLS ≥ +20 meV at matched carrier density).
0.2 Spacer electronic “no-harm” criteria:
- Sub-gap absorption (PDS and sensitive sub-gap EQE) attributable to spacer/CTC must be below 10−4 relative EQE (or equivalent absorption coefficient threshold pre-defined per instrument) and show no new broad CTC band.
- Absolute PLQY-derived nonradiative loss must not worsen by >10 meV in implied Voc (vs alkyl-spacer RP control) at equal excitation density.
0.3 Ni chemistry “go” criteria:
- Ni speciation: ≥80% Ni(OH)2/NiOOH-like components by operando XAS linear-combination fitting (LCF) under relevant bias/illumination; Ni–X fragments in ToF-SIMS must remain below a pre-set detection ratio (e.g., NiI+/Ni+ and NiBr+/Ni+ below 0.05) after stress.
- No measurable RP/3D decomposition: GIWAXS signatures preserved; ex situ FTIR/NMR of extracted films shows no increase in common decomposition markers beyond control.

Step 1 — System definition and thickness-quantifiable RP cap formation
1.1 Device stack (isolated top interface): glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA,Cs)(Pb,I,Br)3 (high-Voc composition)/2D RP cap/HTL/Au in n–i–p; all variants share identical 3D perovskite recipe and HTL to isolate interface effects.
1.2 RP cap thickness control with explicit n/distribution:
- Form RP cap by post-treatment using π-spacer salts in orthogonal solvent (IPA/EtOAc), controlling water content <0.5 vol%.
- Target discrete RP phases: n=1, n=2, n=3 by controlling spacer concentration (e.g., 0.5–5 mM), contact time (5–60 s), and anneal (70–100 °C, 1–5 min) to avoid bulk conversion.
- Quantify d and n distribution via GIWAXS (out-of-plane RP peaks), spectroscopic ellipsometry (nm-scale thickness), and cross-sectional STEM for calibration (limited set). Only samples with narrow n distribution (pre-defined GIWAXS peak ratio window) proceed to transport tests.

Step 2 — Spacer library with bounded energetics and explicit CTC avoidance
2.1 Spacer design rules (chemically explicit):
- Use pyridinium/ammonium-anchored π-acceptors derived from TCNQ/F4-TCNQ-like motifs, but incorporate insulating “linker spacing” (e.g., short alkyl/ether spacer of 2–4 atoms) between the cationic anchor and the acceptor core to reduce direct orbital overlap that promotes real CTC formation while still enabling virtual-state coupling.
- Systematically tune electron affinity (EA) via fluorination/cyano density to scan from near-resonant to more off-resonant coupling.
2.2 Screening workflow (must pass all):
- DFT (periodic slab + dielectric embedding) to estimate level alignment and interfacial dipole; reject spacers predicted to yield real integer charge transfer at equilibrium.
- UPS/IPES in dark and under controlled illumination (to reveal photoinduced pinning) on 2D-capped perovskite surfaces to confirm no Fermi-level pinning consistent with deep acceptors.
- Sub-gap state exclusion: PDS + sensitive sub-gap EQE on complete stacks and on simplified perovskite/2D films; reject any spacer producing new broad sub-gap bands consistent with CTC.
- Quantify interface recombination velocity surrogate: absolute PLQY and QFLS vs carrier density on perovskite/2D and perovskite/2D/HTL coupons; only spacers that improve or maintain QFLS at matched density proceed.

Step 3 — Decisive transport falsification: thickness scaling + field/bias dependence
3.1 Conductance vs thickness (primary superexchange test):
- Fabricate vertical test structures: ITO/SnO2/3D perovskite/RP(π-spacer; n=1–3, quantified d)/thin inert top contact (e.g., MoOx/Au for hole collection or C60/BCP/Ag for electron collection depending on polarity) to isolate one-carrier injection.
- Measure J–V and small-signal admittance over frequency; extract G at low-field regime to minimize band-bending artifacts.
- Fit ln(G) vs d to obtain β; compare to alkyl-spacer RP controls. A genuine virtual-state pathway must show (i) robust exponential distance dependence and (ii) reduced apparent activation of transfer kinetics without relying solely on SCLC-derived Ea.
3.2 Bias-dependent admittance spectroscopy (secondary discriminator):
- Map capacitance and conductance vs frequency and bias to separate barrier-height modulation from bulk-like hopping; identify interfacial state response times. Consistency requirement: changes in β with bias must be small in the regime where superexchange dominates; strong bias sensitivity suggests barrier-limited conduction.
3.3 Ultrafast kinetics cross-check:
- fs–ps transient absorption (selective excitation) on perovskite/RP/HTL coupons to measure hole transfer and back-transfer; confirm weak temperature dependence of forward transfer for accepted spacers while recombination slows (TPV/TPC).

Step 4 — Ni(OH)2·x incorporation with non-destructive chemistry and speciation control
4.1 Replace humidity/base vapor with orthogonal, low-water alkoxide hydrolysis:
- Pre-complex Ni(II) to a chelating motif on the spacer (catechol or hydroxamate) in anhydrous alcohol (e.g., iPrOH) using Ni(OR)2 or Ni(acac)2 with controlled ligand exchange.
- After RP formation, introduce Ni via the same orthogonal solvent, then trigger *mild* hydrolysis using a precisely metered alkoxide-to-hydroxide conversion (trace water delivered via Karl–Fischer-verified micro-addition, total water <0.2 vol%) at room temperature, short exposure (<30 s), followed by immediate drying.
- Aim for sub-percolation loading: target areal Ni density defined by XPS atomic % window (pre-registered, e.g., 0.05–0.3 at% relative to Pb at surface). Verify no continuous Ni-rich phase by c-AFM (no low-resistance shorts).
4.2 Acceptable speciation window and verification:
- Ex situ Ni 2p XPS with shake-up analysis to distinguish Ni(OH)2/NiOOH from NiX2; operando XAS (Ni K-edge) under bias/illumination with LCF against Ni(OH)2, NiOOH, NiI2/NiBr2 references.
- ToF-SIMS to detect Ni–X fragments after stress; reject conditions showing significant NiX2 formation.
- GIWAXS before/after Ni incorporation to confirm RP/3D integrity.

Step 5 — Make “utilization ratio” measurable using dedicated symmetric/blank test cells
5.1 Build faradaic-isolation structures (mandatory):
- Metal/RP(π-spacer:Ni)/Metal vertical capacitors (e.g., Au/RP:Ni/Au) on inert substrates to measure Ni redox without perovskite ionic currents.
- Symmetric HTL/RP:Ni/HTL stacks and (separately) HTL/3D perovskite/RP:Ni/HTL to bound contributions.
5.2 Operational utilization ratio definition (measurable):
- Define utilization ratio U = Qredox,rev / (nNi·F), where Qredox,rev is reversible faradaic charge from CV/chronoamperometry in an inert, non-halide electrolyte or solid-state ion-gel that does not attack the RP; nNi is Ni moles (from calibrated XPS/ICP on replicate films).
- Confirm that redox peaks persist with cycling and correlate U with stability improvements in full PSCs.

Step 6 — Control matrix (expanded per reviewer directive)
Mandatory controls (in addition to original):
- Chelating spacer without Ni (isolates chelation/dipole effects).
- Ni-complexed spacer without hydrolysis trigger (isolates Ni coordination vs hydroxide cluster formation).
- Inert hydroxide/oxide analog with same chelation motif (e.g., Mg(OH)2 or Al2O3-like via alkoxide route) at matched loading (decouples redox buffering from physical ion scavenging).
- π-spacer RP with intentionally “too-strong” acceptor (expected to show CTC/sub-gap features) as a negative mechanistic control.

Step 7 — Device-level endpoints and stress protocols
7.1 Performance:
- Report Voc, FF, stabilized PCE; quantify hysteresis with forward/reverse scans and stabilized MPP.
- Correlate FF gains with thickness-scaling β and with extracted interfacial transfer rates.
7.2 Stability:
- MPP tracking under 1 sun at 60–85 °C (pre-defined), controlled RH (e.g., 20–40%), with periodic QFLS/PL checks.
- Degradation forensics: ToF-SIMS depth profiles for halide redistribution and Ni–X; GIWAXS for phase changes.

Step 8 — Decision logic to prevent post hoc fitting
- If spacer passes transport falsification but fails sub-gap/CTC thresholds → revise spacer EA downward (more off-resonant) or increase anchor–acceptor separation.
- If Ni speciation fails (Ni–X rises) → stop Ni pathway and proceed with spacer-only superexchange cap as primary deliverable; Ni branch only continues under validated speciation window.
- If neither transport falsification nor QFLS improvement is met → abandon superexchange claim and re-scope to dipole/passivation-only mechanism with explicit disclosure.
Feasibility:
Transport falsifiability is strengthened by making superexchange a *distance-scaling* claim rather than a temperature-activation inference. Exponential conductance decay with precisely quantified RP thickness (n=1–3; ellipsometry+GIWAXS calibrated) is a decisive observable that is difficult to mimic by simple Marcus hopping alone across a fixed barrier, especially when combined with bias-dependent admittance constraints and ultrafast hole-transfer kinetics that are weakly temperature dependent.

Spacer risk (CTC, Fermi-level pinning, Voc loss) is explicitly bounded by a three-layer screening gate: (i) DFT rejection of integer charge transfer propensity, (ii) UPS/IPES measured in dark and under illumination to reveal pinning/photoinduced effects, and (iii) sensitive sub-gap probes (PDS + sub-gap EQE) plus QFLS-vs-density to quantify any increase in interface recombination velocity. This converts “avoid mid-gap traps” into measurable acceptance thresholds.

Ni chemistry is de-risked by (i) replacing humidity/base hydroxylation with a low-water alkoxide-hydrolysis route in orthogonal solvent to minimize perovskite attack, (ii) pre-defining acceptable Ni speciation and proving it by complementary operando XAS (LCF), ex situ Ni 2p XPS shake-up analysis, and ToF-SIMS detection of Ni–X fragments, and (iii) enforcing sub-percolation loading verified by c-AFM so Ni does not become an electronic shunt. This addresses the reviewer concern that “few-Å clusters” are ill-defined by shifting emphasis from nuclearity claims to *speciation + loading window + spatial confinement* that can be reproducibly verified.

The utilization ratio metric becomes experimentally well-conditioned by moving its extraction away from buried PSC interfaces into dedicated metal/RP:Ni/metal and symmetric HTL/RP:Ni/HTL structures where faradaic signatures can be isolated from perovskite ionic currents. This mirrors the logic in high-utilization catalysts: accessibility and reversibility are operationally quantified, then correlated to device stabilization, rather than inferred from ill-conditioned buried measurements.

Finally, the proposal maintains coherence with the original concept chain while integrating reviewer-mandated controls (chelating-no-Ni, Ni-without-hydrolysis, inert hydroxide/oxide analog) to disentangle redox buffering from passive ion scavenging/physical blocking. The combined approach preserves the core objective—simultaneous FF and Voc gains—while adding explicit stop/go criteria to prevent post hoc mechanism assignment.
Critique: The proposal is unusually strong in engineering resolution and in pre-registered falsification logic for the superexchange claim (distance-scaling + weak T-dependence + bias-stability constraints). That said, several key deductions remain. (i) The central mechanistic discriminator—exponential conductance vs thickness—can still be mimicked by barrier tunneling through an insulator with thickness-dependent band bending or contact resistance artifacts; your current plan mitigates but does not decisively eliminate these confounds (e.g., independent extraction of barrier height and contact-limited contributions is not fully locked down). (ii) The “virtual-state–mediated relay without real CTC” hinge is conceptually plausible but under-specified quantitatively: you set strict sub-gap thresholds, yet do not provide a quantitative coupling/energy-detuning model connecting spacer EA (HOMO–LUMO gap alignment) to β and to the observed transfer kinetics, which weakens causal depth. (iii) The Ni(OH)2·x branch is chemically cautious, but the utilization-ratio construct risks being only loosely connected to halide/radical suppression at the buried PSC interface unless you define which redox couples are being buffered (I−/I2, Br−/Br2, superoxide, HTL radical cations) and demonstrate that Ni redox potential aligns under device-relevant quasi-Fermi-level splitting; otherwise it can devolve into an empirical additive. (iv) The target concept chain includes MOF and electrocatalytic activity; MOF is not actually instantiated, and “electrocatalytic activity” is inferred from reversible charge (U) rather than linked to measured interfacial reaction kinetics relevant to degradation pathways.

Hypothesis: A carnosine-anchored, nitroxide-terminated interfacial reconstruction layer can be engineered to (i) convert the 3D perovskite surface into a verifiable quasi-2D Ruddlesden–Popper-like (RP-like) slab of predefined thickness (≈1–5 nm) and (ii) act as a stoichiometrically bounded, regenerable redox buffer that suppresses interfacial ROS-triggered halide/organic oxidation, thereby increasing maximum-power-point (MPP) stabilized power density retention. Mechanistic rationale addressing reviewer limitations: (1) Strain node reframed and falsified: instead of asserting intrinsic piezoelectricity, we treat bending as a controlled accelerator of (a) ion migration and (b) interfacial redox/permeation via microcracks/permeability changes. We will only invoke flexoelectric/piezopotential contributions if directly observed as strain-dependent surface-potential signatures (KPFM/Kelvin probe under bending) that correlate with ROS formation and degradation. (2) TEMPO “ROS-gate” is kinetically/stoichiometrically constrained: TEMPO will be immobilized (no dopant-like diffusion) and monitored operando by EPR to quantify its nitroxide fraction over time. Its function is defined as a reversible one-electron redox reservoir (TEMPO•/TEMPO+) that intercepts oxidizing equivalents at the surface and suppresses the propagation steps that generate or amplify 1O2/OH-driven perovskite oxidation. We will explicitly bound side reactions by tracking iodine speciation (I−/I3−/IOx) and ensuring TEMPO does not catalyze iodine redox cycling. (3) RP-like formation is treated as an experimentally testable structural claim with pre-registered diffraction/chemical signatures and benchmarks: we will define GIWAXS peak positions/intensity ratios expected for n=1–3 RP-like phases and corroborate by FTIR/solid-state NMR/XPS depth profiling and a canonical ammonium-spacer RP reference. If those signatures fail, the hypothesis collapses to “coordination-only passivation + redox buffer” and performance/stability will be interpreted accordingly (explicit go/no-go criteria).
Plan:
Step 0 — Pre-registration of falsifiable discriminators (before fabrication)
0.1 Define three success tiers with quantitative thresholds:
  Tier A (full claim): RP-like slab + intact nitroxide + improved stability. Criteria: (i) GIWAXS shows new low-q RP-like features + shifted/quantized out-of-plane periodicity consistent with n=1–3 relative to RP benchmark; (ii) depth profiling indicates an enriched carnosine/TEMPO-containing surface layer confined to ≤10 nm; (iii) operando nitroxide EPR retains ≥50% of initial nitroxide signal after 250 h MPP in air; (iv) ≥2× increase in T80 of PMPP in air (relative control).
  Tier B (partial): no RP-like diffraction, but clear coordination + redox buffering. Criteria: (i) FTIR/NMR/XPS show Pb–N(imidazole) coordination + reduced Pb0/Iox; (ii) nitroxide EPR retention and iodine speciation show non-catalytic behavior; (iii) ≥1.5× T80.
  Tier C (fail): nitroxide consumed rapidly (<20% remaining at 100 h) or iodine cycling enhanced, or Rs penalty >0.5 Ω·cm² with no stability gain.

Step 1 — Device and materials platform (baseline + controls)
1.1 Baseline PSC stack (n–i–p): glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA,Cs)Pb(I,Br)3/HTL/Au. Target initial PCE >21%, with matched Voc deficit across batches (document via QFLS-PLQY).
1.2 Surface-treatment library (all processed from orthogonal solvent, identical thermal budget):
  A) Car–TEMPO conjugate (test).
  B) Carnosine-only (coordination without redox buffer).
  C) TEMPO-only analog (redox without anchoring/coordination; choose a neutral small molecule with comparable volatility).
  D) Imidazole-free peptide analog (anchors/sterics without Pb–imidazole coordination).
  E) Canonical cationic RP spacer benchmark (e.g., PEACl/PEAI or BA-based) to calibrate “true RP” GIWAXS and band-offset behavior.
  F) “Redox-inactive tether” control: Car–(alkyl) replacing TEMPO with similar size/dipole to isolate dipole/band-bending from redox.
1.3 Car–TEMPO synthesis and verification (expanded):
  - Confirm structure (1H/13C NMR, HRMS).
  - Confirm redox couple and stability: CV/DPV in non-aqueous electrolyte; report E1/2, ΔEp, and diffusion/film-confined behavior.
  - Quantify nitroxide fraction in films by CW-EPR (spin concentration calibration vs standard) before device integration.

Step 2 — Engineering a bounded interfacial layer (composition + thickness + electronic benignity)
2.1 Post-deposition reconstruction protocol (explicit parameter window):
  - Spin-coat Car–TEMPO from IPA:MeCN (e.g., 4:1 to 1:1; optimize to avoid perovskite dissolution) at 2000–4000 rpm for 20–40 s.
