  - Concentration series: 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0 mg mL−1.
  - Anneal: 80 °C for 2 min (primary), plus 70/90 °C brackets to map kinetics.
  - Confinement target: ellipsometry/AFM step-height on masked coupons to quantify thickness (goal 1–5 nm; hard cap ≤10 nm).
2.2 Electronic impact constraint:
  - Extract Rs and recombination parameters from J–V + impedance under 1 sun at MPP bias. Go/no-go: ΔRs ≤0.3 Ω·cm² and no >10% loss in initial PMPP vs baseline.
2.3 Adhesion and mechanical integrity of the cap (before strain tests):
  - Cross-hatch/tape test on perovskite/HTL stacks; nano-scratch if available.
  - Contact angle mapping and surface energy estimation (cap uniformity proxy).

Step 3 — Proving (or falsifying) RP-like formation vs coordination-only passivation
3.1 GIWAXS (pre-defined assignments + benchmark calibration):
  - Measure out-of-plane linecuts and in-plane texture for baseline, Car–TEMPO, carnosine-only, and RP benchmark.
  - Pre-register expected features: (i) emergence of low-q periodicity peaks associated with layered spacing (compared directly to RP benchmark); (ii) relative intensity changes consistent with preferential orientation.
3.2 Chemical coordination signatures:
  - FTIR: imidazole ring mode shifts upon Pb coordination; compare carnosine-only vs imidazole-free analog.
  - Solid-state NMR (as available): 13C/15N (or DNP-enhanced if accessible) to detect coordinated imidazole environments; otherwise use XPS N 1s chemical shift mapping as a minimum.
3.3 Composition-depth profiling:
  - Angle-resolved XPS and/or ToF-SIMS to confirm a surface-confined layer: nitrogen (carnosine) and TEMPO fragments enriched at top surface, decaying into bulk over ≤10 nm.
  - Cross-sectional TEM/EELS to exclude gross intermixing and to assess continuity (no requirement of perfect crystallinity, but continuity must be demonstrated if RP-like claim is made).

Step 4 — Quantitative redox/ROS balance for the immobilized TEMPO gate
4.1 Define the redox accounting to be tested:
  - Inputs: photogenerated holes/electrons at the interface + O2/H2O ingress.
  - Competing pathways (to be discriminated): (i) O2 reduction/ROS generation at traps; (ii) direct oxidation of I−/organic cations; (iii) nitroxide-mediated interception.
  - Readouts: nitroxide fraction (EPR), iodine speciation (XPS/Raman/UV–vis), and ROS probes (SOSG/EPR spin trapping).
4.2 Operando/aged-state nitroxide integrity tracking:
  - Operando CW-EPR on dedicated thin-film stacks under controlled illumination and bias (MPP-relevant potential), at 45–65 °C in dry air and N2.
  - Ex situ EPR before/after 100 h and 500 h MPP stress to quantify irreversible loss.
  - Complement with NEXAFS (if available) or high-resolution XPS on N/O environments to detect conversion to oxoammonium/hydroxylamine-like states.
4.3 Rule out catalytic iodine redox cycling (mandatory control set):
  - Operando/ex situ iodine speciation: XPS I 3d (I− vs higher oxidation states), Raman for polyiodides (I3−), and UV–vis of extracted films (where feasible) to detect I3−/polyiodide signatures.
  - Compare Car–TEMPO vs Car–(alkyl) dipole control and TEMPO-only control. Go/no-go: Car–TEMPO must show reduced (not increased) I3−/IOx signatures relative to baseline at equal aging dose.
4.4 Direct ROS quantification near the interface:
  - SOSG on encapsulated optical coupons (glass/perovskite/cap) with identical illumination dose; report photon-flux-normalized 1O2 signal.
  - EPR spin trapping for •OH/superoxide-related intermediates on analogous stacks; normalize to absorption and film thickness.

Step 5 — Deconvoluting strain effects: permeability/cracking vs electrostatic (flexo/piezopotential) contributions
5.1 Strain protocol (explicit) on flexible devices:
  - Substrate: ITO/PET or ITO/PI; bending radius calibrated to 0–0.5% strain.
  - Apply cyclic bending (e.g., 10^3–10^4 cycles) combined with light soaking at MPP; record Voc, FF, Rs evolution.
5.2 Crack formation and delamination monitoring (to remove ambiguity):
  - In situ optical microscopy during bending (crack onset density vs strain).
  - AFM topography before/after cycling for microcracks/roughness change.
  - Adhesion re-test post-bending.
5.3 Permeability proxies (oxygen/water ingress sensitivity):
  - Track water contact angle drift and photoluminescence quenching under controlled O2/H2O exposure.
  - If available, use Ca test (calcium corrosion) on separately prepared barrier stacks to compare relative WVTR/OTR proxies between caps.
5.4 Electrostatic signature test (only if present, to justify “piezo/flexo” node):
  - KPFM (or scanning Kelvin probe) mapping under controlled bending to detect strain-dependent surface potential/band-bending changes.
  - Correlate any observed Δsurface potential with ROS probe signal (SOSG/EPR) and degradation rate. If no reproducible Δpotential beyond noise, interpret strain effects purely as mechanical/permeation/ionic acceleration.

Step 6 — Performance/stability endpoints linked to ‘power density’
6.1 Standard PV metrics:
  - J–V forward/reverse, stabilized MPP tracking, and PMPP/area (power density) under 1 sun.
  - Report hysteresis index, ideality factor vs intensity, and temperature dependence.
6.2 Accelerated aging matrix:
  - 45–65 °C MPP in N2 and dry air (mandatory) plus controlled RH steps.
  - Encapsulated damp-heat screening (85/85) on mini-modules for barrier synergy.
6.3 Mechanistic linkage analysis:
  - Mixed-effects models across ≥25 devices/condition and ≥3 batches.
  - Regression linking PMPP decay to (i) nitroxide EPR decay, (ii) iodine oxidation markers, (iii) ROS probe signals, and (iv) crack density/permeability proxies under strain.

Step 7 — Scale-up compatibility
7.1 Slot-die/meniscus coating of Car–TEMPO on 1–10 cm² devices.
7.2 Uniformity criteria: spatial PL mapping, sheet resistance stability (no added series resistance gradients), and ToF-SIMS spot checks for nitrogen/TEMPO fragment uniformity.
Feasibility:
1) Addressing the “piezoelectric response” ambiguity with hard discriminators
Perovskite bending degradation can be dominated by ionic motion and mechanically induced permeability/cracking rather than true piezoelectric polarization. This proposal now treats strain as a controlled accelerator with mandatory measurements of crack formation, adhesion loss, and permeability proxies. Flexoelectric/piezopotential contributions are not assumed; they are tested directly via strain-dependent surface-potential mapping (KPFM/Kelvin probe under bending) and only used in interpretation if a reproducible Δsurface potential correlates with ROS generation and degradation kinetics.

2) Kinetic/redox closure for TEMPO under PSC operating conditions
The ROS-gating function is reformulated as an immobilized, regenerable redox buffer rather than an unbounded “ROS scavenger” claim. Feasibility hinges on two measurable conditions: (i) operando/ex situ EPR must show that a substantial fraction of nitroxide persists under illumination/bias, consistent with regeneration; (ii) iodine speciation must show suppression (not enhancement) of I3−/IOx signatures, ruling out catalytic iodine redox cycling. By including TEMPO-only and redox-inactive dipole/steric controls, we can separate anchoring, dipole/band-bending, and true redox-buffer effects.

3) RP-like formation is made testable rather than asserted
Because carnosine is non-ammonium and may not spontaneously yield a textbook RP lattice, we predefine structural expectations and introduce a canonical ammonium RP spacer as a calibration benchmark. GIWAXS is complemented by coordination-specific spectroscopy (FTIR/solid-state NMR or XPS chemical shifts) and depth profiling to determine whether the interfacial layer is (a) a true layered RP-like slab, (b) a mixed coordination complex, or (c) merely molecular passivation. The proposal remains scientifically valuable under Tier B (coordination + redox buffering) even if Tier A (RP-like slab) fails, preserving logical closure.

4) Coherence with the concept chain and literature assets
The proposal preserves the core chain: controlling redox chemistry to protect stabilized power density, while translating “ROS generation/quenching” logic (Asset 1) and “redox-engineered performance” logic (Asset 2) into a perovskite-native interface architecture without catalytic metal centers. The revised plan tightens causal inference by directly measuring ROS, interfacial redox state (iodine/Pb), and nitroxide integrity, and by deconvoluting mechanical strain pathways that could otherwise masquerade as electrostatic/piezo effects.
Critique: Methodological execution is strong: the proposal pre-registers falsifiable structural discriminators (GIWAXS benchmarks, depth profiling), constrains interfacial thickness, and uses operando EPR to close the redox-accounting loop—rarely done rigorously in interfacial additive work. The major scientific risk is the Tier-A claim: converting a 3D halide perovskite surface into a well-defined 1–5 nm “RP-like slab” using a non-ammonium, zwitterionic peptide (carnosine) is chemically under-justified; even if GIWAXS shows low-q features, distinguishing true RP stacking from surface texturing/solvent-induced reorganization will be difficult without decisive cross-sectional structural proof (e.g., lattice-resolved STEM with layer periodicity and composition contrast). The TEMPO gate logic is plausible, but the proposal does not fully specify the thermodynamic alignment (TEMPO•/TEMPO+ potential vs perovskite hole quasi-Fermi level, vs iodide/iodine couples) that determines whether TEMPO will be regenerative or simply sacrificial; without that, EPR retention could reflect kinetic isolation rather than functional buffering. The strain/piezo node is handled responsibly (conditional), but it becomes peripheral to the core mechanism; if piezo/flexo signals are absent, the concept chain element is effectively unused rather than integrated.

Hypothesis: If curvature in flexible inverted perovskite solar cells produces a *quantifiable* bending-induced electrostatic potential swing (Δφbend) across the absorber—arising from strain-gradient piezo/ flexoelectric polarization in the perovskite + curvature-amplified contact asymmetry—then this Δφbend will modulate the ionic electrochemical potential (μion) and interfacial band bending at the HTL-side, increasing low-frequency ionic capacitance (Cion), recombination activation, and J–V hysteresis, thereby degrading Voc under cycling. Embedding a *buried, sparse, vertically oriented* ferroelectric nanolaminate layer (sub-percolation platelet network) at a designed depth (100–250 nm from the HTL) will act as an internal electrostatic clamp that reduces ∂φ/∂κ (electric potential sensitivity to curvature κ) by (i) providing a high effective dielectric susceptibility χeff and (ii) adding a switchable remanent polarization Pr that can be oriented to oppose the curvature-induced field at the HTL-side. The hypothesis is falsifiable via (A) predicted Δφbend(κ) from an electromechanical stack model; (B) a required χeff/Pr threshold for a targeted suppression factor S = Δφbend,control/Δφbend,laminate; and (C) polarity dependence: reversing the ferroelectric dipole should *invert* the sign or increase the magnitude of Δφbend and hysteresis if screening—not generic passivation—is responsible. The refined approach overcomes feasibility concerns by (1) using platelets and passivation designed to retain switching (minimized depolarization via controlled shell thickness and partial screening), (2) aligning platelets with a demonstrably out-of-plane field geometry/dielectrophoresis rather than in-plane AC fields, (3) separating ferroelectric switching from ionic motion through blocking-layer test structures and time/frequency/temperature discrimination, and (4) employing matched-chemistry nonpolar platelet controls to isolate electrostatics from trap passivation.
Plan:
PHASE 0 — Quantitative model + go/no-go gates (mandatory before full device campaigns)
0.1 Stack mechanics: compute neutral axis (z0) and strain profile εxx(z)=κ(z−z0) for the full flexible stack (PI / TCO or Ag-mesh/IZO / HTL / perovskite / ETL / top electrode / encapsulation). Use measured layer thicknesses and elastic moduli (nanoindentation or literature) to locate z0; report uncertainty. Define curvature κ=1/R for R=3,5,10 mm.
0.2 Electromechanical-to-electrostatic mapping (order-of-magnitude + FEM):
  • Baseline source term: represent bending-induced polarization density as Pbend(z)=μβend·∂ε/∂z ≈ μeff·κ (flexoelectric-like term) plus a possible piezo-like term if texture/strain breaks centrosymmetry locally. Use μeff as an extracted parameter from dedicated bending-KPFM measurements on pristine films (Phase 1), not assumed.
  • Solve Poisson with mobile-ion screening limits: bracket two regimes—(i) fast electronic screening/slow ionic (short-time, ‘frozen ions’), (ii) partial ionic screening (long-time). Implement as an effective Debye length λD,ion fitted from EIS/impedance spectroscopy of pristine devices. Outcome: predicted Δφbend at HTL-side and its relaxation time.
  • Laminate effect: treat embedded platelet layer as an effective medium slab with thickness tL (set by second-layer deposition thickness, 50–150 nm) and permittivity εL,eff( f, field ) plus optional remanent polarization Pr,eff·cosθ (θ: platelet tilt). Use Maxwell–Garnett mixing for εL,eff(φ,εplatelet,εPVK) with volume fraction φ=0.1–0.5 vol% (global) but locally higher within the buried slab; include depolarization reduction factor Nd for thin platelets.
  • Define screening target: require S≥3 reduction in |Δφbend| at HTL-side at κ corresponding to R=5 mm under ‘frozen-ion’ conditions (the condition most relevant to scan-direction hysteresis). This translates to a required εL,eff and/or Pr,eff. Output: predicted design window {φ, tL, depth d, θ-distribution}.
0.3 Feasibility gate G0 (pass/fail): proceed to device campaign only if model predicts S≥3 with realizable θ (≤20° mean tilt), and if the required Pr,eff does not exceed what is measured in Phase 1 composites.

PHASE 1 — De-risk ferroelectric functionality inside perovskite (materials-only proof)
1.1 Nanoplatelets: prepare BaTiO3 and K0.5Na0.5NbO3 (KNN) nanoplatelets with thickness 10–30 nm (revised from 5–20 nm to reduce size-suppressed remanence risk) and lateral size 200–800 nm. Target aspect ratio >20. Confirm via AFM/TEM.
1.2 Passivation shell (engineered for partial screening + non-shunting):
  • Use a bifunctional phosphonate monolayer (e.g., alkyl/aryl phosphonic acid) with controlled thickness ~1–2 nm; verify by XPS and ellipsometry on model oxide surfaces.
  • Add a secondary wide-bandgap inorganic “spacer” only if needed (e.g., 0.5–1 nm ALD Al2O3 on platelets before ligand) to suppress interfacial traps while keeping capacitance high. Reject shells >3 nm total (would overly depolarize).
1.3 Composite ferroelectric characterization in perovskite-like dielectric:
  • Prepare perovskite/composite films on conductive substrates with a symmetric capacitor geometry using ionic-blocking electrodes (e.g., ITO/NiOx as bottom, and sputtered Au with an ultrathin blocking layer such as ALD-Al2O3 1–2 nm to suppress halide exchange) to minimize ionic current during polarization measurements.
  • Measure Pr and switching using:
    - Double-wave method (DWM) / PUND with pulse widths 1–100 µs (ferroelectric timescale) and 1–100 ms (to detect ionic contamination). Ferroelectric signature: switching charge saturates at short pulses and shows weak temperature activation; ionic: strong pulse-width/temperature dependence.
    - Charge integration under triangular wave at multiple frequencies (100 Hz–100 kHz) to separate hysteretic polarization from ionic drift.
    - Cross-sectional PFM (after focused-ion-beam cross-section prep with low-damage conditions) to map switchable domains; require reversible phase contrast localized to platelets.
  • Retention/imprint tests: track Pr, coercive field, and imprint after (i) 1 sun equivalent light soaking at 45–60 °C, (ii) thermal cycling 25↔60 °C, (iii) bias stress ±0.8 V for 5–30 min in dark. Define gate G1: ≥30% of initial Pr retained after 24 h at 60 °C + light, and DWM indicates switching charge dominated by fast component.

PHASE 2 — Alignment that is truly out-of-plane (replace in-plane AC alignment)
2.1 Revised alignment geometry (out-of-plane field / dielectrophoresis):
  • Use patterned bottom electrodes (already present TCO/Ag-mesh) plus a temporary transparent top gate during wet-film stage (e.g., a removable PEDOT:PSS-coated PET sheet or ITO-PET) separated by a calibrated spacer (10–50 µm) to apply an out-of-plane AC field across the wet precursor.
  • Apply AC 50–500 kHz at field amplitude 10^4–5×10^5 V/m. Use high frequency specifically to reduce electrode polarization and ionic screening in the wet ionic film.
  • Optionally superimpose dielectrophoretic gradient (non-uniform field via interdigitated edge features) to promote vertical standing and suppress lateral chaining.
  • Immediately lock orientation via gas-quench/antisolvent and rapid crystallization.
2.2 Alignment quantification (mandatory):
  • GIWAXS: quantify Herman’s orientation factor for platelet-related scattering (or use oxide signature peaks) and perovskite texture changes. Target: orientation factor consistent with mean tilt ≤20°.
  • Cross-sectional SEM/TEM: compile orientation statistics (N≥200 platelets/sample) at three positions across coating width (center + two edges) to verify uniformity; report distribution.
  • Gate G2: if vertical orientation fraction (>70% within ±20° of normal) is not met, iterate field amplitude/frequency and wet-film viscosity (solvent ratio, precursor concentration) before device fabrication.

PHASE 3 — Device architecture + buried laminate implementation (absorber-centric, not interfacial)
3.1 Baseline flexible inverted PSC (constant across all groups): PI / (ITO on PI or Ag-mesh/IZO) / HTL (NiOx or PTAA) / perovskite / ETL (C60/BCP or PCBM/BCP) / top electrode (evaporated Ag OR printed Ag-carbon via dry press deposition; choose one and hold constant).
3.2 Buried placement (depth-controlled):
  • Two-step perovskite deposition:
    - Layer A (seed): 100–150 nm perovskite without platelets.
    - Layer B (laminate slab): 50–150 nm perovskite containing platelets at a locally higher fraction to yield global φ=0.1–0.5 vol% but slab-local φslab ~0.5–2 vol% (derived from Phase 0 modeling). This places the electrostatic clamp 100–250 nm from the HTL, not at the interface.
3.3 Poling protocol (decoupled from ion migration):
  • Perform poling only after encapsulation and only on devices with verified ionic-blocking layers for the poling experiment subset (see Phase 4). Use short, bipolar pulses (µs–ms) at amplitudes determined from Phase 1 coercive fields, rather than a single DC ≤1 V assumption.
  • Primary poling condition: pulse train (e.g., 10–10^3 pulses, 10–100 µs width) with amplitude producing the same field across the laminate slab as used in PUND switching; estimate internal field distribution using series-capacitance model (HTL/perovskite/ETL) and validate by comparing switching charge to capacitor test structures.
  • Include reverse-poling and “sham” pulse sequences below coercive threshold.

PHASE 4 — Controls strengthened to isolate electrostatics vs passivation (expanded set)
4.1 Control matrix (all with identical ligand chemistry):
  • C1: pristine perovskite.
  • C2: ferroelectric platelets, random orientation, unpoled.
  • C3: ferroelectric platelets, vertically aligned, unpoled.
  • C4: ferroelectric platelets, vertically aligned, poled +.
  • C5: ferroelectric platelets, vertically aligned, poled −.
  • C6 (mandatory passivation-matched nonpolar): identically passivated nonpolar platelets with matched geometry and surface chemistry, e.g., SrTiO3 or CaTiO3 (high-κ but paraelectric at operating T) prepared with identical phosphonate shell; this isolates chemistry/defect effects from remanence.
  • C7 (optional): same oxide core but thermally depolarized/phase-modified (if feasible) to remove remanence without changing surface.
4.2 Trap density metrics: SCLC (electron-only and hole-only), thermal admittance spectroscopy, and PL/TRPL to quantify trap density changes across groups. Use these in regression against hysteresis to ensure improvements are not purely trap-passivation driven.

PHASE 5 — Coupled mechanical–electrical testing with model-linked endpoints
5.1 Bending protocol: radii 3, 5, 10 mm; tensile vs compressive; cycling 10^2, 10^3, 3×10^3, 10^4; hold-at-curvature dwell tests (0–60 min) for relaxation kinetics.
5.2 In-situ J–V and MPP tracking: forward/reverse at scan rates 10–1000 mV/s, fixed pre-bias; mandatory MPP tracking under curvature to avoid scan artifacts.
5.3 In-situ EIS (curved): 1 MHz–0.1 Hz at Voc and near MPP, under 1-sun, held at fixed curvature. Fit with a constrained model including Rtr, Rrec, Cgeo, Cchem, and Cion with finite-length diffusion when required. Primary readouts: curvature-induced ΔCion and ΔRrec.
5.4 Direct Δφbend measurement and relaxation: time-resolved KPFM/SKP on partial stacks (no top metal) while bending/unbending; extract Δφbend(κ,t) and compare to Phase 0 predicted ∂φ/∂κ. Expect: aligned+poled shows reduced Δφbend amplitude and faster relaxation.
5.5 Ion migration validation: bias-stress ±0.8 V (dark) + recovery; ToF-SIMS depth profiles post-cycling focusing on HTL-side accumulation; correlate ToF-SIMS gradients with Cion changes.

Success criteria (quantitative, tied to model)
• Mechanical durability benchmark: ≥90% PCE retention after 3000 cycles at R=5 mm.
• Voc retention: ΔVoc ≤20–30 mV after 3000 cycles at R=5 mm.
• Hysteresis suppression: ≥50% reduction in hysteresis index vs C1 under bending.
• Ionic response stabilization: ≤20% increase in extracted Cion under bending relative to flat state (vs much larger in C1).
• Model validation: measured Δφbend(κ) reduced by ≥3× in aligned+poled vs C1, and polarity dependence observed (C4 vs C5 diverge in sign/magnitude consistent with screening).
Feasibility:
Addresses (i) ferroelectric viability at nanoscale: the platelet thickness is revised upward (10–30 nm) to reduce remanence suppression; passivation shell is constrained to ~1–2 nm (≤3 nm total) to avoid excessive depolarization while preventing shunting. Ferroelectric switching/Pr retention is not assumed; it is gated by composite-appropriate measurements (PUND/DWM across frequency and pulse-width, cross-sectional PFM) under light/temperature/bias stress relevant to PSC operation. This directly tests depolarization, imprint, and retention in situ.

Addresses (ii) alignment realism: the in-plane AC field is replaced with an out-of-plane field geometry using a temporary top gate (parallel-plate) and high-frequency AC (50–500 kHz) to mitigate ionic screening and electrode polarization in wet precursors. Alignment is not asserted; it is quantified by GIWAXS orientation factors and cross-sectional TEM/SEM orientation statistics across the coating width, with an explicit gate (≥70% within ±20° of normal).

Addresses (iii) poling sufficiency and confounding ion migration: poling is redesigned from a low-DC-bias concept to a pulse-based protocol matched to measured coercive fields in blocking-layer capacitors. Ferroelectric switching is discriminated from ionic redistribution by (a) frequency/pulse-width dependence (fast vs slow components), (b) ionic-blocking test structures, and (c) time-resolved KPFM relaxation after poling/bending. This provides causality: if a fast, polarity-dependent Δφbend suppression occurs without slow ion signatures, the mechanism is ferroelectric screening; if only slow relaxation is seen, it indicates ionic redistribution.

Addresses (iv) missing quantitative coupling: a required, falsifiable electromechanical model is added. Neutral axis and strain are computed, a bending-induced polarization source term is introduced and *empirically calibrated* via bending-KPFM on pristine films, and Poisson + screening limits yield predicted Δφbend(κ,t). The laminate is mapped to εL,eff and Pr,eff via effective-medium theory including depolarization factors and orientation distribution. This model outputs a required screening factor S and corresponding design window for {φ, tL, depth}. The chosen 0.1–0.5 vol% global loading and 100–250 nm placement become model-derived, not arbitrary.

Addresses (v) new interfaces/traps and separating screening from passivation: controls are strengthened with a geometry- and chemistry-matched nonpolar platelet (e.g., SrTiO3/CaTiO3) using the same ligand shell, plus trap-density measurements (SCLC, thermal admittance, PL/TRPL). If hysteresis/Voc improvements correlate with polarity and Δφbend suppression but not with trap-density reduction, screening is supported. If improvements track trap reductions equally in polar and nonpolar controls, passivation is implicated.

Overall success probability is increased by staged feasibility gates (G0–G2, G1 for Pr retention) that prevent committing to full device campaigns until the key physical assumptions—(a) measurable, stable Pr in composite; (b) demonstrable vertical alignment; (c) predicted and measured Δφbend suppression—are validated quantitatively.
Critique: This is an unusually detailed and self-critical proposal with strong methodological resolution. The electromechanical-to-electrostatic model, feasibility gates (G0–G2), and polarity-dependent falsification strategy significantly elevate it above typical PSC mechanics–hysteresis studies. Engineering execution is strong but not flawless: (i) the extraction of an effective flexoelectric coefficient μeff from bending-KPFM in halide perovskites remains experimentally fragile and may conflate surface dipoles, ion redistribution, and true bulk polarization; (ii) maintaining stable, switchable Pr in a halide-rich, light-soaked perovskite environment—even with 10–30 nm platelets—remains a high-risk assumption despite the excellent gating strategy; (iii) alignment via temporary top gates at 50–500 kHz in wet ionic precursors is plausible but operationally complex and may introduce thickness nonuniformity or solvent-flow artifacts not fully addressed. Logical consistency is high, but the chain from Δφbend suppression to long-term Voc retention under cycling still partially relies on correlational evidence (Cion, hysteresis) rather than a single decisive causal observable. Evidence grounding is strong and stays within the target concept chain, with minimal disciplinary drift. Rationale quality is high: the buried electrostatic clamp is a genuinely creative adaptation addressing a known bottleneck (bending-induced hysteresis/Voc loss) rather than incremental passivation.

Hypothesis: Embedding an ultrathin dual-ligand conductive MOF van der Waals heterostructure—Cu3(HHTP)(THQ) laminated with graphene—at the buried perovskite/transport-layer interface will simultaneously (i) increase Voc by suppressing non-radiative recombination via coordinative passivation of under-coordinated Pb2+/halide-vacancy sites and (ii) enhance operational stability by creating a redox-buffered, ion-blocking interphase. The specific methodological adaptation is to convert the battery-inspired ‘active-site-rich’ Cu3(HHTP)(THQ) into a photovoltaic interfacial ‘pseudocapacitive defect-sink’ by (a) engineering partial amorphization and Cu-valence accessibility to enable fast, reversible interfacial faradaic charge accommodation (pseudocapacitance) that clamps interfacial quasi-Fermi level fluctuations and reduces hysteresis, while (b) assembling the MOF as an oriented vdW heterostructure with graphene to provide high in-plane conductivity and minimize series resistance. Mechanistically, aromatic benzene-ring π systems in HHTP/THQ provide delocalized pathways for ultrafast interfacial charge extraction, while Cu–O4 nodes act as Lewis-acid/base coordination centers that bind perovskite surface dangling bonds and immobilize migrating iodide/MA/FA species, reducing ion-accumulation-driven interfacial fields that accelerate degradation.
Plan:
Step 1: Interface and materials selection/design.
1.1 Choose a high-Voc perovskite baseline (e.g., FA0.9Cs0.1Pb(I0.9Br0.1)3) deposited on SnO2 (n–i–p) or NiOx (p–i–n) to isolate the effect at one buried interface.
1.2 Define the target interface: perovskite/ETL for n–i–p (perovskite on SnO2) or perovskite/HTL for p–i–n (perovskite on NiOx).
1.3 Synthesize Cu3(HHTP)(THQ) with controlled ligand ratio and ethylenediamine coordination moderation to ensure dual-ligand incorporation and high electrical conductivity.

Step 2: Methodological adaptation—vdW lamination + partial amorphization to induce pseudocapacitive ‘defect-sink’ behavior.
2.1 Prepare ultrathin Cu3(HHTP)(THQ) nanosheets (few-nm) and assemble a vdW heterostructure with graphene via surfactant-assisted solution synthesis followed by mild sonication-assisted exfoliation; target lateral size 0.5–5 µm to form continuous interfacial coverage.
2.2 Induce partial amorphization (key adaptation) without collapsing electronic percolation: apply a controlled solvent-vapor anneal (e.g., ethanol/water mixed vapor) or low-power plasma/UV-ozone exposure to create short-range disorder and increase accessible redox-active Cu sites while maintaining sheet integrity. Quantify amorphization by pair distribution function (PDF) and Raman D/G evolution (graphene) + MOF vibrational broadening.
2.3 Interfacial deposition protocol (buried interface compatible):
- For n–i–p: deposit the Cu3(HHTP)(THQ)/graphene heterosheets on SnO2 as an ultrathin interlayer (target 1–5 nm equivalent coverage) using Langmuir–Blodgett transfer or meniscus-guided coating to achieve oriented, low-roughness coverage; then crystallize perovskite atop.
- For p–i–n: deposit heterosheets onto NiOx before perovskite deposition.
2.4 Add a molecular-level anchoring step to ensure intimate electronic coupling while avoiding perovskite decomposition: introduce a sub-monolayer bifunctional linker (e.g., phosphonic acid or catechol-terminated aromatics) on the oxide surface to promote vdW-aligned MOF/graphene stacking and reduce interfacial voids.

Step 3: Device fabrication and rigorous validation with mechanistic tests.
3.1 Fabricate control and test devices: (i) no interlayer, (ii) graphene-only, (iii) crystalline Cu3(HHTP)(THQ) only, (iv) partially amorphized Cu3(HHTP)(THQ) only, (v) crystalline vdW heterostructure, (vi) partially amorphized vdW heterostructure (full adaptation).
3.2 Quantify optoelectronic improvements: J–V (forward/reverse hysteresis), stabilized MPP, Suns-Voc, and EQE; extract non-radiative voltage loss using absolute PLQY on completed stacks and/or quasi-Fermi level splitting on perovskite films.
3.3 Prove defect passivation mechanism: XPS/UPS to track Pb 4f shifts and halide-vacancy signatures; time-resolved PL and transient photovoltage/photocurrent to separate recombination vs extraction; Kelvin probe force microscopy for interfacial potential uniformity.
3.4 Demonstrate pseudocapacitive ‘interfacial redox buffering’: perform impedance spectroscopy under illumination over bias, fit with distribution of relaxation times (DRT) to identify a faradaic/pseudocapacitive arc distinct from ionic accumulation; conduct cyclic voltammetry on simplified stacks (oxide/interlayer/perovskite) to detect reversible redox features associated with Cu nodes.
3.5 Track ion-migration suppression and stability: operando bias-stress tests at 1 sun and elevated temperature (ISOS-L protocols), ToF-SIMS depth profiling pre/post stress for iodide and organic cation redistribution, and GIWAXS to monitor perovskite phase stability.
3.6 Establish structure–function causality: correlate amorphization degree (PDF/Raman) and accessible Cu redox fraction (XANES/EXAFS) with Voc, hysteresis index, and DRT-derived ionic time constants to identify the optimal disorder window (max passivation + buffering, minimal resistive loss).
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: HHTP-based 2D MOFs can form ultrathin vdW heterostructures with graphene that enhance charge transfer and electron cloud extension (Asset 1). Dual-ligand Cu3(HHTP)(THQ) contains abundant active sites and aromatic rings that enable fast redox-assisted ion/electron interactions and high-rate storage in LIBs (Asset 2), implying intrinsically accessible faradaic centers and high conductivity. Amorphization of MOFs is known to increase active-site accessibility and promote pseudocapacitance by improving ion migration and charge transfer (Asset 3), which can be repurposed as an interfacial charge/ion buffer in PSCs.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): PSC bottlenecks often originate at buried interfaces where under-coordinated Pb, halide vacancies, and ion accumulation drive non-radiative recombination (Voc loss), hysteresis, and accelerated degradation. The adapted interlayer converts ‘battery pseudocapacitance’ into a photovoltaic function: reversible, fast interfacial faradaic accommodation reduces local field spikes and stabilizes band alignment under operation, while Cu–O coordination sites passivate defects and immobilize mobile ions.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to conventional passivation molecules or insulating 2D perovskites, the Cu3(HHTP)(THQ)/graphene vdW interlayer adds (i) high in-plane conductivity to avoid transport penalties, (ii) a tunable density of redox-active sites (via controlled amorphization) to actively buffer interfacial charge/ion transients, and (iii) an ultrathin, conformal, solution-processable architecture compatible with scalable coating. The design is not a material swap: it is a structurally and functionally modified interphase whose disorder-engineered pseudocapacitance is directly mapped to reduced hysteresis, higher Voc, and improved operational stability.
Critique: The proposal is ambitious and unusually mechanistic for an interfacial-layer concept, with a reasonably actionable fabrication/control matrix and a good attempt to separate passivation, transport, and ionic effects (controls i–vi; PLQY/QFLS; DRT-EIS; ToF-SIMS). The main logical vulnerability is the central claim that a Cu-based MOF can act as a fast, reversible ‘pseudocapacitive defect-sink’ at a perovskite buried interface without introducing new non-radiative channels or chemical instability. In PSCs, interfacial faradaic activity is double-edged: Cu(II)/Cu(I) accessibility and halide coordination can also catalyze halide redox chemistry, promote I−/I3− formation, or enable metal migration, potentially worsening Voc and stability. The proposal does not yet specify a thermodynamic/electrochemical window (redox potentials vs perovskite quasi-Fermi levels, band edges, and halide redox couples) that guarantees the desired buffering remains benign and does not become a recombination/catalysis pathway under illumination/bias. Engineering-wise, several steps are plausible but underdetermined for reproducibility: achieving 1–5 nm ‘equivalent coverage’ of a composite MOF/graphene heterosheet with consistent orientation over rough SnO2/NiOx at scale is nontrivial; the amorphization protocol (solvent vapor vs plasma/UV-ozone) risks uncontrolled oxidation of graphene, ligand loss, and Cu–O node alteration, which could change work function and energetics unpredictably. Finally, the evidence plan would benefit from stronger discriminants between (a) true pseudocapacitance (reversible faradaic storage at Cu sites) and (b) enhanced ionic accumulation or interfacial trap charging that merely mimics capacitive signatures in EIS/DRT; as written, the electrical signatures could be ambiguous without stringent controls and rate/temperature dependence.

Hypothesis:
Embedding a tribo–piezoelectric hybrid nanogenerator (TPHG) as an opto‑mechano‑active encapsulation laminate can increase PSC short‑circuit current (Isc) and operational stability via a *quantitatively bounded, spatially confined* mechano‑chemical adaptation at the encapsulation/HTL domain (not at the perovskite). Under 1–5 Hz cyclic compression, the Zn‑Car_MOF piezoelectric layer produces an oscillatory surface potential that (after accounting for humid/oxygenated screening) induces interfacial charge accumulation at a Cu‑HHTP catalytic layer. This drives oxygen activation with *tunable ROS speciation*. We explicitly target a low ROS areal generation rate (to avoid long-range diffusion) while biasing toward singlet oxygen (1O2) by (i) operating the TPHG in open circuit to avoid Faradaic current injection into the PSC, (ii) selecting an O2‑rich, H2O‑limited microenvironment inside the encapsulation (via moisture barrier + controlled RH), and (iii) incorporating an engineered quench/consumption geometry such that 1O2 is consumed within the mesoporous HTL before reaching the perovskite interface.

Mechanistically, the 1O2 field (low-flux, short diffusion length) triggers confined oxidative coupling of thymol inside a 5–10 nm mesoporous HTL scaffold, forming an in‑situ crosslinked phenoxy/ether network that is (a) hydrophobic and oxygen-buffering, lowering O2/H2O ingress and suppressing interfacial p‑type over‑doping of the perovskite/HTL contact; (b) a local ROS sink that kinetically outcompetes transport toward the perovskite; and (c) an interfacial dipole modifier whose magnitude and sign will be *measured* (UPS/KPFM) and correlated to reduced hole-extraction barrier/contact resistance. The proposal is falsifiable because each link—(surface potential → ROS speciation/flux → spatial confinement/no ROS at perovskite → HTL percolation preserved → measured energetic shift → Isc gain)—has predefined quantitative acceptance thresholds and hard controls (inert MOF, no actuation, quencher, thymol absent, pre‑crosslinked network).
Plan:
A. Device and materials architecture (baseline + integration-ready variants)
A1. Baseline PSC (p–i–n) fabrication for reproducible Isc reference:
- Stack: glass/ITO/(SAM: MeO‑2PACz, 1.0–1.5 mg mL−1 in EtOH, 5–10 min)/(Perovskite: FA0.9Cs0.1Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3, target 500–650 nm)/(HTL variant set below)/Au (80–100 nm).
- Acceptance: baseline champion PCE ≥ 19% and stabilized Isc within ±5% across n≥12 devices.

A2. Mesoporous HTL scaffold that is reproducible and electronically percolating:
- Replace dense spiro‑OMeTAD with *mesoporous organic HTL scaffold* formed by templated spiro‑OMeTAD (or PTAA) using removable porogen (e.g., PS-b-PEO micelles) to yield 5–10 nm pores, thickness 50–120 nm.
- Two HTL arms to de-risk: (i) mesoporous spiro‑OMeTAD scaffold; (ii) mesoporous PTAA scaffold (dopant-free), to avoid dopant volatility.
- Acceptance (before thymol): hole-only device mobility ≥ 10−4 cm2 V−1 s−1; sheet resistance within 2× of dense control.

A3. Encapsulation laminate with mechano-active ROS generator but PSC electrically isolated:
- Laminate (outer→inner): patterned PDMS triboelectric film (micro-pyramids 5–20 µm)/Zn‑Car_MOF piezoelectric film (thickness 10–50 µm)/Cu‑HHTP catalytic layer (100–500 nm) on inert support.
- Separation from PSC: a gas-permeable, ion/solvent-blocking fluoropolymer membrane (Teflon AF 2400, 0.5–2 µm) plus an additional *ROS quench interlayer* on the PSC side (see Section C) if needed.
- Mechanical actuation: 100 kPa peak pressure, 1–5 Hz, matched to Asset 1 regime; operation strictly open-circuit (no galvanic connection to PSC).

B. Quantify piezo/tribo surface potential at Cu‑HHTP and link to speciated ROS (Mandatory Milestone 1)
B1. Model the effective surface potential delivered to Cu‑HHTP:
- Use a capacitor/screening model: Zn‑Car_MOF polarization → surface charge density σ(t); include dielectric stack (PDMS, membrane) and Debye screening length in humid air film.
- Output: predicted ΔVsurf(t) at Cu‑HHTP for 1–5 Hz, 30–70% RH, and O2 0.21–1 atm.

B2. Measure ΔVsurf(t) under realistic encapsulation conditions:
- Kelvin probe (macroscopic) + EFM/KPFM (microscale) on the Cu‑HHTP surface while cyclically loading the laminate (1–5 Hz, 50–200 kPa), under controlled RH (30%, 50%, 70%) and O2 partial pressure.
- Quantitative milestone M1a (go/no-go): achieve |ΔVsurf| ≥ 0.3 V peak-to-peak at 1–5 Hz at 50% RH (or revise laminate thickness/materials to reach this threshold).

B3. Quantify ROS speciation and areal flux vs ΔVsurf:
- 1O2: 1270 nm phosphorescence (time-resolved), calibrated with a chemical actinometer.
- O2•−/•OH: EPR spin trapping (DMPO for •OH/O2•− adduct discrimination; TEMP/TEMPO for 1O2 corroboration); include dark controls.
- Define selectivity metric: f(1O2)=R1O2/(R1O2+RO2•−+R•OH) based on calibrated rates.
- Quantitative milestone M1b: f(1O2) ≥ 0.70 at total ROS areal generation rate Rtotal ≤ 1×10−9 mol m−2 s−1 under 1–5 Hz actuation (adjust Cu‑HHTP thickness, O2 availability, RH, and surface modifiers if off-target).
- Competing pathway bounding: map f(1O2) as a function of RH and O2; if superoxide dominates at RH≥70%, impose encapsulation RH spec ≤50% using desiccant perimeter + moisture barrier topcoat.

C. Demonstrate spatial confinement and ‘no ROS at perovskite’ with built-in kinetic consumption (Mandatory Milestone 2)
C1. Introduce a sacrificial reporter layer at the perovskite-side interface:
- Insert a thin 1O2 reporter film (e.g., SOSG immobilized in PMMA, 10–30 nm) at (i) HTL/perovskite interface (test coupon devices) and (ii) immediately under the fluoropolymer membrane on PSC side.
- Operate under actuation and illumination (1 sun) and quantify reporter response.
- Quantitative milestone M2a: reporter signal at perovskite-side interface ≤ LOD (≤3σ of blank) after 10^5 cycles at 1–5 Hz.

C2. Kinetic quenching/consumption calculations + engineered quench placement:
- Use 1O2 lifetime and diffusion length estimates in organic matrices; require Ld(1O2) << membrane-to-perovskite path length.
- If M2a fails, add a dedicated quench interlayer *above HTL but below perovskite* is impossible; therefore implement on the PSC-facing side of the membrane: a nanometric scavenger coating (e.g., hindered amine/physical quencher like DABCO derivative immobilized in fluoropolymer, 10–50 nm) to consume 1O2 before it reaches PSC.
- Quantitative milestone M2b: with quench interlayer, maintain Cu‑HHTP-side 1O2 generation while perovskite-side reporter remains ≤ LOD.

D. Thymol confinement and oxidative coupling inside mesoporous HTL without loss of electronic percolation (Mandatory Milestone 4)
D1. Thymol loading into mesoporous HTL (controlled uptake):
- Vapor infiltration at 30–50 °C (below perovskite thermal stress) to target 5–20 wt% thymol in HTL; quantify via QCM/gravimetry and FTIR.
- Ensure no thymol reaches perovskite by using dense interlayer at HTL/perovskite (already present in p–i–n via SAM/perovskite interface; confirm by ToF-SIMS depth profiling on test stacks).

D2. Mechanically gated oxidative coupling protocol:
- Encapsulate with TPHG laminate; actuate 1–5 Hz for defined cycle counts (10^3, 10^4, 10^5) under controlled O2 and RH.
- Confirm coupling: FTIR/Raman (phenoxy/ether features), solid-state NMR on peeled HTL films, and GPC/solubility change (crosslinking proxy).

D3. Electronic percolation and series resistance constraints:
- Build hole-only devices (ITO/SAM/HTL/Au) from identical mesoporous HTL films pre/post coupling; measure SCLC mobility and conductivity.
- Impedance (Nyquist) under 1 sun for full PSCs to extract Rs and Rrec.
- Quantitative milestone M4: post-coupling HTL conductivity drop ≤ 30% and PSC series resistance increase ΔRs ≤ 0.5 Ω·cm2 (else reduce thymol loading or pore volume).

E. Replace qualitative ‘dipole improves extraction’ with measured energetic shifts and barrier extraction (Mandatory Milestone 3)
E1. Measure work function / VBM alignment changes:
- UPS on HTL surfaces (before and after coupling) to extract work function shift ΔΦ and VBM position; complement with KPFM maps on cross-sections for spatial localization.
- Define directionality requirement: shift must reduce hole extraction barrier at perovskite/HTL (sign determined from baseline alignment).

E2. Quantify contact barrier/resistance changes:
- Temperature-dependent J–V and TPC/TPL to extract activation energy for extraction and contact-limited behavior.
- Quantitative milestone M3: achieve either (i) ΔΦ (or ΔVBM) ≥ 0.10 eV in the barrier-reducing direction, or (ii) ≥ 30% reduction in extracted contact resistance (from impedance/TPC fits) sufficient to explain targeted ΔIsc.

F. Photovoltaic validation + stability under mechanochemical conditioning
F1. Isc-centered PV metrics:
- J–V (forward/reverse), stabilized Isc at 0 V, and EQE integration before/after conditioning.
- Target effect size: ΔIsc ≥ +3% absolute relative to passive encapsulation control at matched light soaking history.

F2. Operational stability:
- 1-sun MPP tracking in O2-rich atmosphere (controlled RH ≤50%) for ≥1000 h, with and without actuation periods (duty cycle defined, e.g., 10 min actuation per hour).
- Track PbI2 formation (XRD), interfacial oxidation states (XPS), and metal migration indicators.
- Acceptance: Isc retention ≥ 90% at 1000 h with actuation, and no increased PbI2 relative to passive control.

G. Hard controls to isolate causality (Mandatory Milestone 5)
- C1: Cu‑HHTP present, no mechanical actuation (tests electrostatic necessity).
- C2: Mechanical actuation with inert MOF (replace Cu‑HHTP with non-catalytic porous carbon/MOF) (tests catalytic necessity).
- C3: Mechanical actuation + 1O2 quencher interlayer on PSC-facing side of membrane (tests 1O2 dependence).
- C4: Thymol absent (tests polymer network necessity).
- C5: Pre-crosslinked thymol network (prepared ex situ in HTL) without TPHG (tests whether actuation-formed chemistry is uniquely beneficial).
- C6: Replace thymol with a non-coupling hydrophobe (tests whether simple hydrophobization explains results).

Go/No-Go logic (decision points)
- Gate 1 (after B): if M1a or M1b fails, redesign laminate (thickness, dielectric, Cu‑HHTP surface) before PSC integration.
- Gate 2 (after C): if M2a/M2b fails, implement/optimize quench interlayer or abandon ROS route.
- Gate 3 (after D/E): if M4 fails or M3 fails, adjust thymol loading/pore fraction or pivot to alternative coupling chemistry that preserves mobility.
- Gate 4 (after F): if ΔIsc < +3% or stability worsens vs control, terminate integrated approach and publish negative mechanistic findings as boundary conditions.
Feasibility:
1) Addressing ‘open-circuit polarization → selective 1O2’ with quantitative boundaries: Asset 1 supports strong piezoelectric response (high Voc under pressure) and Cu‑HHTP ROS generation under electrifying conditions, but reviewers correctly demand the *effective surface potential* at Cu‑HHTP under humid screening and the *speciated* ROS yields. The revised plan makes this a first-class milestone: ΔVsurf(t) is modeled and measured (Kelvin probe/EFM) under RH/O2 control, then directly correlated to ROS speciation using orthogonal methods (1270 nm for 1O2; EPR spin traps for O2•−/•OH). We predefine selectivity and flux targets (f(1O2) and Rtotal) so the approach is falsifiable and tunable (via RH, laminate dielectric thickness, Cu‑HHTP thickness/surface).

2) Spatial confinement is no longer asserted; it is tested with a perovskite-side sacrificial reporter and enforced by design: The critique that gas-permeable membranes do not block 1O2 is explicitly handled by (i) short-lived/short diffusion-length kinetics for 1O2, (ii) a consumption geometry where thymol in mesopores acts as the primary sink, and (iii) an engineered scavenger coating on the PSC-facing side of the membrane if required. Acceptance is ‘no detectable ROS at the perovskite-side reporter after 10^5 cycles’, which is decisive.

3) ‘Dipole improves extraction’ is converted into measurable energetics and barrier parameters: UPS/KPFM quantify ΔΦ/ΔVBM and its sign; temperature-dependent JV plus TPC/impedance extract barrier/contact resistance changes. A minimum energetic/contact-resistance change is defined to plausibly account for the targeted ΔIsc, preventing narrative-only interpretation.

4) Mesoporous HTL risk is mitigated by dual HTL arms and strict percolation constraints: The plan recognizes that crosslinking within 5–10 nm pores could impede transport. Therefore, thymol loading is controlled (vapor infiltration, wt% targets), and post-coupling mobility/conductivity plus ΔRs thresholds are enforced (go/no-go). A PTAA mesoporous option de-risks spiro‑OMeTAD reproducibility and dopant-related instability.

5) Integration/materials risks (outgassing, moisture uptake, Cu proximity) are converted into controls and gates: Encapsulation RH is specified; MOF proximity is buffered by fluoropolymer + optional scavenger; and hard control experiments isolate each causal step (actuation, catalysis, 1O2, thymol chemistry, pre-formed networks). This ensures that if performance changes occur, they can be causally assigned rather than conflated.

Overall, the revised proposal maintains the original concept chain (TPHG open-circuit → gated ROS → confined thymol coupling → dipole/hydrophobic buffer → improved Isc) but replaces unbounded assertions with measurable fields, speciated ROS selectivity/flux targets, confinement acceptance criteria, electronic percolation thresholds, energetic-shift quantification, and decisive controls.
Critique: The proposal is unusually well engineered for a mechanochemical/ROS-driven PSC concept: it replaces qualitative claims with measurable intermediates (ΔVsurf, f(1O2), Rtotal, reporter LOD, ΔΦ, ΔRs) and hard controls. The primary scientific risk remains the physical plausibility of sustaining ≥0.3 Vpp effective surface potential at the Cu-HHTP interface under realistic humid, oxygenated encapsulation boundary layers while avoiding unintended electrochemical pathways; Kelvin probe/KPFM under cyclic loading helps, but translating that field into reproducible, selective 1O2 at the stated low areal flux is still uncertain. Second, the confinement argument hinges on kinetics in complex multilayers: 1O2 lifetimes/diffusion lengths are highly matrix- and impurity-dependent, and the membrane is explicitly gas-permeable; the sacrificial reporter is good, but fluorescence-based 1O2 probes (e.g., SOSG) can be artifact-prone under illumination and in the presence of redox-active surfaces, requiring stringent calibration and orthogonal confirmation. Third, the mesoporous HTL scaffold introduces a large variability/stability axis independent of the ROS concept (pore formation reproducibility, mechanical integrity under cyclic stress, dopant/oxidation sensitivity, and long-term morphological drift), which could dominate Isc/stability trends and complicate attribution even with controls. Finally, the mechanistic link from confined thymol coupling to a beneficial interfacial dipole that measurably reduces extraction barriers is plausible but not guaranteed; dipole sign/magnitude could be heterogeneous and may instead increase energetic disorder or trap densities, depressing FF/Voc even if Isc rises.

Hypothesis:
A mechanochemically synthesized, 2-methylimidazole–rich ZIF-8 nanophase can improve the thermal stability and optoelectronic quality of α-FAPbI3 perovskite solar cells not by acting as a bulk ion conductor, but by acting as a *surface-accessible coordination micro-reservoir* at grain boundaries and interfaces. The falsifiable central mechanism is:
(1) **Interfacial Pb2+ coordination buffering (surface-limited)**: Accessible imidazolate/2-MI motifs at the external surface and defect sites of nano-ZIF-8 (not necessarily internal micropores) form reversible Pb–N coordination to undercoordinated Pb2+ at perovskite grain boundaries/CTL interfaces, measurably shifting Pb 4f binding energies and imidazole vibrational modes. This reduces deep trap formation and suppresses thermally accelerated interfacial decomposition.
(2) **Guest-ion hosting (verified, not assumed)**: Only ions demonstrably incorporated/retained in ZIF-8 (after rigorous washing) contribute to stabilization. Mn2+/Rb+/I− “loading” is treated as an experimentally bounded variable with explicit rejection criteria (amorphization, salt microcrystallites, Zn-exchange/etching). Any observed device benefit must track *framework-hosted uptake* (ICP-MS + XAS/XPS) rather than physical salt admixture.
(3) **Ion-migration mitigation via boundary chemistry, not pore transport**: The expected reduction in halide/vacancy migration arises from passivated grain-boundary pathways and reduced interfacial electric-field hot spots (lower interfacial defect density), which should produce causally linked changes in impedance spectra, operando EL/Voc stability under bias-thermal stress, and TOF-SIMS depth profiles.
Given ZIF-8’s small pore windows and hydrophobicity, the proposal explicitly limits claims of “ultra-high ionic loading” to the *experimentally verified* uptake that preserves crystallinity/porosity. The working design target is a <50 nm ZIF-8 population with high external surface area and controlled surface chemistry, enabling coordination buffering without imposing transport barriers.

Option on emission/CRI is made falsifiable and architectural: the core deliverable is PV thermal stability; a secondary, gated aim explores Mn2+-enabled down-conversion as an *optical* color-conversion layer (remote phosphor concept) rather than claiming intrinsic broadband/high-CRI EL from a FAPbI3 PV stack unless a dedicated LED sub-architecture is built and benchmarked.
Plan:
Step 0 — Define acceptance criteria and control matrix (pre-registered)
A0. **ZIF-8 nanophase targets**: particle size D50 = 20–50 nm; BET surface area retained ≥70% of pristine after any loading step; XRD crystallinity retained (no broad amorphous halo dominance); no detectable crystalline salt impurities by XRD/PDF above detection limit.
A1. **Integration window targets**: additive loading in perovskite ≤0.05–0.5 vol% (screened); interfacial layer thickness 2–10 nm equivalent (spin-coated ultra-dilute dispersion) to avoid series resistance.
A2. **Perovskite film metrics to hit**: α-FAPbI3 phase fraction (GIWAXS) ≥95% post-anneal; grain size distribution tracked (SEM) and no δ-phase increase after 85–120 °C aging.
A3. **Controls required (mandatory)**: (i) free 2-MI additive; (ii) imidazole-poor ZIF-8 (stoichiometric 2-MI, lower linker excess); (iii) amorphous Zn–2MI gel (same chemistry, no reticular order); (iv) inert SiO2 nanoparticles (20–50 nm, similar size); (v) physical salt mixing without MOF uptake (Mn/Rb salts mixed post-synthesis).

Step 1 — Mechanochemical synthesis of nano-ZIF-8 with tunable surface-accessible 2-MI
1.1. **Ball-milling recipe**: ZnO or Zn(OAc)2·2H2O with excess 2-MI (2-MI:Zn = 8–20 molar) to bias toward 2-MI-rich surfaces/defect sites; milling frequency/time systematically varied (e.g., 20–30 Hz; 10–60 min). If liquid-assisted grinding is needed, use minimal water/ethanol (green, ≤50 µL per g) and document.
1.2. **Size control**: post-milling size selection by centrifugation/antisolvent fractionation to obtain <50 nm fraction; verify by DLS + TEM.
1.3. **Baseline characterization**: PXRD (Rietveld where feasible), total scattering/PDF for short-range order, BET (N2 at 77K and CO2 at 273K for ultramicropore accessibility), TGA/DSC (thermal stability and guest content), FTIR/Raman (linker modes), XPS (Zn 2p/N 1s baseline).

Step 2 — Define and verify “ion loading” vs physical admixture (explicit falsification)
2.1. **Loading methods compared** (two orthogonal routes):
(a) *Co-milling loading*: add MnCl2/MnI2, RbI, KI at controlled mole fractions during milling.
(b) *Post-synthetic incipient wetness*: expose nano-ZIF-8 to minimal-volume ethanolic or aqueous salt solutions, then dry under mild vacuum (to reduce framework damage and isolate adsorption/coordination effects).
2.2. **Rigorous washing protocol**: repeated washing (ethanol/water sequence) until supernatant conductivity and ICP signal plateau; only then proceed.
2.3. **Quantify uptake**:
- ICP-MS of digested solids to quantify Mn/Rb/K/I loading (mmol g−1) *after washing*.
- TGA/DSC to corroborate guest mass and identify decomposition changes.
- PXRD + PDF/total scattering to detect amorphization and exclude salt microcrystallites.
- XPS for Mn 2p/Rb 3d/I 3d presence; depth-sensitive angle-resolved XPS to distinguish surface-enriched vs bulk.
- EXAFS/XANES (Mn K-edge; Zn K-edge as needed) to determine Mn coordination environment and detect Zn↔Mn exchange or framework etching.
2.4. **Pore accessibility before/after**: N2/CO2 sorption changes interpreted as (i) pore blocking by true inclusion, (ii) collapse/amorphization (ruled in/out by XRD/PDF), or (iii) external adsorption.
2.5. **Go/no-go criteria**: any loading condition that causes (i) >30% BET loss *with* strong amorphization signatures, or (ii) detectable crystalline salt peaks, is rejected for device integration and kept only as a negative control.

Step 3 — Engineer perovskite integration without transport penalties
3.1. **Two deployment modes (kept distinct)**:
Mode A (Interfacial): ultrathin nano-ZIF-8 layer between perovskite and CTL (select architecture: n–i–p or p–i–n). Target thickness 2–10 nm equivalent; confirm via ellipsometry/AFM step edge and cross-sectional TEM.
Mode B (Bulk additive): disperse nano-ZIF-8 at 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5 vol% into FAPbI3 precursor (or FA/Cs mixed-cation for phase robustness). Use dispersants only if they do not bind Pb2+ strongly (document); verify colloidal stability by DLS in solvent.
3.2. **Morphology/phase control readouts**:
- SEM (top-view and cross-section) for grain size and pinholes.
- GIWAXS for α/δ phase fraction, texture/orientation, and thermal evolution.
- PL/TRPL mapping to identify whether improvements localize to grain boundaries.
- Electrical transport: SCLC trap density (electron-only/hole-only devices) and series resistance tracking.
3.3. **Upper bound selection**: choose maximum ZIF-8 vol% that does not degrade mobility/FF (quantified) and does not increase haze/scattering beyond set threshold (UV–vis haze measurement).

Step 4 — Prove the interfacial coordination mechanism (not inferred)
4.1. **In-situ/operando vibrational spectroscopy**:
- In-situ FTIR/Raman during perovskite crystallization on ZIF-8-coated substrates to detect imidazole mode shifts consistent with Pb–N coordination.
4.2. **XPS evidence of Pb–N interaction**:
- Compare Pb 4f, I 3d, N 1s spectra for: (i) baseline perovskite, (ii) perovskite on ZIF-8, (iii) perovskite with free 2-MI, (iv) perovskite on amorphous Zn–2MI gel, (v) perovskite on SiO2.
- Expectation: reproducible Pb 4f binding-energy shift and N 1s component consistent with coordinated N in ZIF-8 case; absence or different signature in SiO2 control.
4.3. **Competitive binding falsification**:
- Add a competing Lewis base (carefully chosen to not dissolve perovskite) in a controlled experiment; if Pb–N coordination is central, trap density and interfacial recombination should revert toward control.

Step 5 — Establish causality for migration/defect suppression under bias-thermal stress
5.1. **Operando bias-thermal protocol**: apply forward bias near Voc and reverse bias conditions at 85–120 °C under 1-sun equivalent illumination; track degradation kinetics.
5.2. **Coupled diagnostics**:
- Impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to extract interfacial recombination resistance/capacitance evolution.
- Thermal admittance spectroscopy for defect activation energies.
- TOF-SIMS depth profiling *pre/post stressing* to quantify halide and cation redistribution; compare against controls.
- Correlate changes with Voc loss rate and (if measured) EL turn-on shift—linking migration suppression to device physics rather than co-variation.

Step 6 — Clarify the emission/CRI claim with a gated, architecture-specific model
Primary deliverable: PV stability + reduced non-radiative recombination.
Secondary (optional, gated by Step 2 success):
6.1. **Replace intrinsic high-CRI EL claim with a feasible path**:
Option (preferred): Mn2+-loaded ZIF-8 as a *down-conversion color conversion layer* (remote or on-glass), optically pumped by a separate UV/blue source or by a dedicated perovskite LED sub-stack, not by a standard FAPbI3 PV junction. Measure photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY), thermal quenching, and CRI of converted emission.
Option (only if pursuing true PV–LED): build a separate wide-bandgap perovskite LED stack (e.g., Br-rich or quasi-2D) adjacent to Mn@ZIF-8 conversion, define energy-transfer pathway (host exciton → Mn2+), and benchmark EL spectra, EQE, and operational stability. Otherwise, CRI is removed from PV claims.
6.2. **Benchmarks**: report CIE coordinates, CRI, and thermal drift for the conversion layer; for EL, report EQE and spectral stability at fixed current density and temperature.
Feasibility:
1) Addressing ZIF-8 pore/ion-access skepticism: The refined hypothesis explicitly treats ZIF-8 as a *surface coordination buffer* rather than a bulk ion conductor. Ion “loading” is no longer assumed; it is experimentally bounded by ICP-MS (after rigorous washing), sorption (N2/CO2), and structural integrity checks (PXRD + PDF). This directly answers the reviewer concern that ZIF-8’s small apertures/hydrophobicity may limit true uptake.

2) Decoupling true framework-hosted loading from physical mixing: The plan includes orthogonal loading routes (co-milling vs incipient wetness), strict washing, and rejection criteria based on salt crystallites (XRD/PDF) and amorphization (total scattering). EXAFS/XANES and XPS explicitly determine whether Mn2+/Rb+ are coordinated/adsorbed or simply present as residues, and whether Zn2+ exchange/etching occurred.

3) Preventing nanoparticle-induced transport/morphology penalties: The integration window is engineered with explicit constraints (particle size <50 nm; ≤0.5 vol% bulk additive; 2–10 nm interfacial layer). Film morphology/phase targets are enforced by GIWAXS (α/δ-FAPbI3), SEM/TEM (grain boundaries), haze/scattering metrics, and SCLC/EIS to quantify whether any passivation benefit is offset by transport losses.

4) Interfacial mechanism is made falsifiable with competitive controls: Pb2+–imidazolate coordination is verified via in-situ FTIR/Raman and Pb 4f / N 1s XPS shifts, with mandatory controls (free 2-MI, imidazole-poor ZIF-8, amorphous Zn–2MI gel, inert SiO2). This disambiguates effects of chemistry vs nanofiller morphology.

5) Migration/defect causality beyond correlation: TOF-SIMS is paired with operando bias-thermal stressing and impedance/admittance analyses. The claim becomes: reduced migration signatures must coincide with stabilized Voc/EL metrics and improved recombination resistance evolution, establishing causal linkage.

6) CRI claim is no longer overstated: The proposal either (i) focuses on PV stability, or (ii) treats Mn2+-related high-CRI output as a separate, explicitly architected down-conversion/LED sub-system with appropriate excitation physics and benchmarking. This removes the weakest speculative link while preserving the mechanochemical loading concept as a testable materials platform.

Overall, mechanochemical synthesis remains the enabling route (green, solvent-minimizing, scalable) consistent with literature on reticular-framework encapsulation/loading capacity, while the perovskite-relevant mechanism is reformulated around *surface-accessible coordination chemistry* and rigorously verifiable guest states.
Critique: Methodologically, the proposal is unusually well-resolved: it pre-registers quantitative go/no-go criteria (BET retention, crystallinity, salt-impurity exclusion), separates interfacial vs bulk-additive deployment, and provides a control matrix that can actually disambiguate chemistry (2-MI/Pb–N) from morphology (nanofiller) and from non-framework salt mixing. The mechanistic claim is also made testable via paired spectral signatures (Pb 4f/N 1s XPS; imidazole vibrational shifts) and stress-coupled causal diagnostics (bias-thermal + EIS/admittance + TOF-SIMS). The main remaining weaknesses are (i) ambiguity in what constitutes “2-MI–rich surface” in ZIF-8 (defect density, missing-linker vs dangling linker, protonation state) and how it will be quantitatively controlled/normalized across batches; (ii) risk that mechanochemical excess-2-MI conditions produce non-ZIF amorphous Zn–imidazolate phases or persistent surface-adsorbed 2-MI that could mimic the intended buffering mechanism, complicating attribution even with washing; (iii) the competitive-binding falsification experiment is underspecified and may be chemically unrealistic without perturbing the perovskite (most strong Lewis bases/chelators will also solvate PbI2/FAI or alter surface termination); and (iv) the ion-loading branch (Mn/Rb/I) still carries a nontrivial probability of framework damage or surface salt residues at the low aperture size—this is acknowledged and gated, but it may consume significant effort relative to the primary PV-stability objective. Evidence grounding is strong and stays within the concept chain; the only mild drift is the breadth of characterization (EXAFS, operando Raman/FTIR, TOF-SIMS, TAS) which is appropriate but may be resource-intensive and vulnerable to underpowered execution if access/time is limited.

Hypothesis: A photo-inert, electronically selective, and ion-blocking interlayer can be created at the perovskite/HTL interface by a de-risked two-step dry process: (i) perovskite-benign, purely coordinative tethering of atomically precise Ag44 nanoclusters (APNCs) to undercoordinated surface Pb2+ sites via multidentate phosphonate (or halide-agnostic chelating) ligands—without generating new vacancies or Pb0—and (ii) subsequent self-limited growth of an ultrathin conjugated reticular overlayer by solvent-free interfacial oligomerization using a vapor-infiltration Knoevenagel pathway that avoids free base exposure at the perovskite surface (latent/base-free chemistry or base-quench cycling). Mechanistically, immobilized and electronically decoupled Ag44 clusters function as sub-monolayer ‘polarizable defect-screeners’ by increasing local interfacial dielectric response and stabilizing charged point defects (e.g., halide vacancies) electrostatically, thereby lowering interfacial capture cross-sections and suppressing trap-assisted recombination—provided that Ag44/ligand frontier levels are kept outside the perovskite bandgap and the coupling is tunneling-limited. The reticular network (3–6 nm target) provides a rigid, hydrophobic, size-selective barrier that increases the activation energy for halide/organic-ion migration and suppresses interfacial redox degradation, while its ionization potential/work-function shift is tuned into a quantitative window that maintains hole extraction and blocks electrons without raising contact resistance beyond a predefined series-resistance budget. The central feasibility risk (interfacial chemistry damage, redox activity of Ag species, and incomplete vapor-phase condensation) is addressed upfront via hard go/no-go gates: (a) orthogonal quantification of Ag44 anchor density and bonding chemistry without relying on PL, (b) electronic-structure and photoredox risk assessment (UPS/IPES + DFT + operando XANES/XPS in iodide contact), (c) staged validation of vapor Knoevenagel growth first on inert analogs and then on perovskite under strict base-exposure limits with in situ QCM/FTIR tracking, and (d) quantitative design targets (interlayer thickness, work-function shift, allowable Rs increment, and percolation/shunt threshold) enforced as kill-criteria before full device statistics.
Plan:
PHASE 0 — Quantitative design targets + kill-criteria (must pass before device integration)
0.1 Energy-level/selectivity targets (hard targets):
- Interlayer thickness (ellipsometry/AFM): 3–6 nm (kill if >8 nm or <2 nm with persistent pinholes).
- Work-function shift at perovskite surface (Kelvin probe/UPS): +0.10 to +0.30 eV (toward higher WF to aid hole extraction). Kill if |ΔWF| <0.05 eV (no measurable dipole) or if ΔWF shifts in the wrong direction.
- Interlayer ionization potential (UPS): within 0–0.4 eV deeper than HTL HOMO to preserve hole injection; electron-blocking: LUMO/EA at least 0.3 eV above perovskite CBM (from IPES or optical gap + UPS). Kill if predicted electron barrier <0.2 eV.
- Series resistance budget: ΔRs ≤ 0.5 Ω·cm^2 relative to no-interlayer control at matched HTL (kill if ΔRs > 1.0 Ω·cm^2 or FF drops >3% absolute at matched Jsc).
- Shunt/percolation constraint: Jleak(0.1 V reverse) increase ≤ 2× control; Rshunt ≥ 1 kΩ·cm^2. Kill if leakage indicates percolation.

0.2 Percolation/shunt model to pre-define safe Ag44 areal density:
- Treat clusters as conductive inclusions separated by tunneling barriers through ligand shells + framework. Use a conservative 2D percolation threshold p_c ≈ 0.59 for random disks; convert to areal density N via effective inclusion radius r_eff = r_core + 2·t_ligand.
- With Ag44 core ~1.2–1.6 nm and ligand shell t_ligand ~0.7–1.0 nm, r_eff ~2.0–2.6 nm. Set maximum N_max to keep area fraction p = N·πr_eff^2 <0.05 (large safety factor vs p_c). This gives N_max ~ (0.05)/(πr_eff^2) ≈ 2.3×10^11 cm^-2 for r_eff=2.6 nm; adopt N_max = 1×10^11 cm^-2 as safe upper bound; explore 1×10^10, 3×10^10, 1×10^11 cm^-2.
- Validate experimentally by conductive-AFM current maps + device leakage.

PHASE 1 — Perovskite-benign tethering chemistry and orthogonal anchor-density quantification (no plasma/UV-ozone vacancy generation)
1.1 Perovskite and architecture (kept constant through Phase 1):
- Absorber: FA0.8Cs0.2Pb(I0.8Br0.2)3 (or closely matched high-Voc composition), n–i–p: ITO/SnO2/perovskite/interlayer/HTL/Au.
- HTL for screening tests: dopant-free PTAA (primary), spiro-OMeTAD (secondary) to test contact-resistance sensitivity.

1.2 Define a tethering reaction that is selective and non-damaging:
Option A (primary): Multidentate phosphonate coordination to surface Pb2+.
- Ligand design on Ag44: mixed-thiolate shell Ag44(SR)30 where 5–10% of SR are ω-phosphonic-acid-terminated aryl/alkyl thiolates (e.g., HS–(CH2)n–Ar–PO(OH)2) and the remainder are inert thiolates chosen to keep Ag44 atomically precise.
- Rationale: phosphonate–Pb2+ binding is coordinative, does not require generating radicals/vacancies, and is halide-agnostic.
- Implementation (dry): deposit Ag44 onto perovskite by vacuum soft-landing (electrospray deposition into vacuum with differential pumping) at low kinetic energy; immediately anneal 40–60 °C under N2 for 10–20 min to promote coordination without driving ion migration.

Option B (backup): Neutral chelating anchors (e.g., pyridyl/terpyridyl) that bind undercoordinated Pb2+ without strong basicity.
- Avoid strongly basic amines; prefer weakly basic aromatic N donors to minimize perovskite deprotonation.

1.3 Orthogonal quantification of Ag44 anchor density (mandatory):
- QCM-D (or QCM) during soft-landing onto a perovskite-analog QCM crystal (same surface chemistry; see 1.4) to quantify mass uptake per area and infer cluster density using known Ag44 molecular weight.
- XPS absolute quantification on films: Ag 3d/Pb 4f ratio converted to areal density using sensitivity-factor correction and attenuation-length model; cross-check with angle-resolved XPS.
- ToF-SIMS with standards: prepare calibration samples by depositing known Ag44 areal densities on inert substrates; use Ag-containing fragment counts vs known density to build a transfer function; apply to perovskite samples.
- Kill-criterion: if the three methods disagree by >2×, halt and resolve metrology before proceeding.

1.4 Prove tethering is perovskite-benign (no deep trap creation / stoichiometry damage):
- Surface chemistry: XPS for Pb0/PbOx signatures (Pb 4f), I/Br ratios, and emergence of phosphate binding shifts (P 2p).
- Optical/electronic: absolute PLQY at 1-sun equivalent (QFLS extraction) before/after tethering; kill if QFLS decreases >10 meV relative to pristine.
- Trap density: SCLC on electron-only/hole-only test structures; kill if trap density increases.
- Morphology: AFM roughness; kill if RMS increases >20%.

1.5 Controls for Phase 1:
- No interlayer.
- Same ligand shell without Ag44 (free ligand deposition) to decouple ligand vs cluster effect.
- Non-atomically-precise Ag nanoparticles at identical Ag mass loading (dry deposited).

PHASE 2 — Electronic-structure + photoredox risk assessment of Ag44 at iodide-rich perovskite interface (mandatory before framework growth)
2.1 Frontier-level alignment and electronic decoupling assessment:
- UPS (and IPES if available) on perovskite surfaces: pristine vs tethered Ag44 vs ligand-only.
- Kelvin probe mapping for WF uniformity.
- PDS and EL reciprocity/Suns-Voc to detect sub-gap absorption or increased J0.
- DFT (computational gate):
  - Compute Ag44-ligand cluster frontier levels and density of states; evaluate whether states fall within perovskite bandgap.
  - Model cluster–surface binding motif (phosphonate–Pb) and electronic coupling; require that any new states are outside gap or sufficiently localized without enhancing nonradiative recombination.
- Kill-criterion: evidence of mid-gap state formation (new sub-gap PDS feature correlated with increased J0 or reduced QFLS) or UPS/IPES indicating interfacial states near mid-gap.

2.2 Photostability/redox assay under iodide contact:
- Prepare perovskite/Ag44 samples and expose to 1-sun equivalent at 45–65 °C under N2 and under dry air; monitor for 24–100 h.
- Operando or quasi-operando XANES/XPS: track Ag oxidation state (Ag0/Ag+), iodide oxidation signatures, and any AgI formation.
- Complement with GI-XRD for AgI.
- Kill-criterion: detectable AgI formation or systematic Ag oxidation correlated with PLQY/QFLS decline.

PHASE 3 — Solvent-free reticular framework growth: de-risk vapor Knoevenagel with base-free/latent-base strategies and staged substrates
3.1 Stage A: demonstrate SVI-Knoevenagel on inert analog surfaces (mandatory):
- Analog substrates: ALD-Al2O3, SnO2, and PbI2 thin films (less fragile than perovskite) to validate chemistry and thickness control.
- In situ monitoring: QCM mass gain per cycle + in situ FTIR (C=O consumption; vinylene C=C formation).
- Outcome: establish a cycle window (temperature, pulse time, purge time) that yields monotonic growth with minimal residual aldehyde.

3.2 Stage B: translate to perovskite under strict base-exposure limits:
- Replace continuous base vapor with one of the following (priority order):
  (i) Base-free activated-methylene system: choose linkers with sufficiently acidic methylene groups enabling condensation via surface-assisted catalysis or intrinsic polarization at Ag44 sites (screen multiple candidates; proceed only if FTIR confirms conversion).
  (ii) Latent base strategy: co-dose a thermally labile base precursor that releases trace base only after monomer adsorption (e.g., blocked amidines or carbonate-protected amines) and is fully purged after reaction.
  (iii) Base microdosing + quench cycling: if a base is unavoidable, use ppm-level pyridine dosing for <1 s pulses followed by extended purge and an immediate acidic-scavenger pulse on chamber walls (not on sample) to prevent base carryover; validate no perovskite compositional shift by XPS.
- Temperature: 30–60 °C (cap at 60 °C during growth to limit ion migration).
- Kill-criterion: any measurable perovskite decomposition markers (loss of FA/Cs signatures, halide loss, Pb0 increase) or QFLS drop >10 meV after growth.

3.3 Site-directed nucleation test (must be proven, not asserted):
- Compare framework growth kinetics and film closure on: (a) perovskite-only, (b) ligand-only, (c) Ag44-tethered.
- Metrics:
  - Nucleation density/closure: AFM pinhole statistics + conductive-AFM current maps.
  - Growth per cycle: QCM (mass/cycle) and ellipsometry (thickness/cycle).
  - Chemical conversion: FTIR ratio of vinylene/aldehyde peaks.
- Acceptance: Ag44-tethered samples must show either faster closure (lower pinhole density at same thickness) or higher conversion at the same thermal/base budget.

3.4 Reticular framework design parameters for electronic selectivity:
- Monomers: volatile multi-aldehyde node + activated-methylene aromatic linker to form vinylene-linked conjugated network.
- Substituent tuning: incorporate moderate electron-withdrawing substituents (e.g., F, CN) to deepen IP and create an interfacial dipole; screen 2–3 monomer sets.
- Thickness control: terminate growth at 3–6 nm; if growth continues linearly, introduce a bulky “capping” monomer cycle (steric stop) to enforce self-limitation.

PHASE 4 — Mechanism-first validation on films (before full device statistics)
4.1 Recombination/QFLS mechanism:
- Absolute PLQY under 1-sun equivalent to quantify QFLS; target: +20–40 meV vs control after Ag44 + framework.
- Suns-Voc to extract J0 and ideality factor changes; require reduced J0.
- TRPL/transient photovoltage to isolate interfacial lifetime gain.

4.2 Ion-migration barrier mechanism:
- Temperature-dependent impedance spectroscopy to extract ionic activation energy; target: increase by ≥0.05–0.10 eV relative to control.
- Bias-stress hysteresis and operando PL mapping for interfacial degradation initiation.

PHASE 5 — Device integration and benchmarking (only after gates pass)
5.1 Device set and controls (≥30 devices/condition):
- (i) no interlayer, (ii) framework-only (SVI-Knoevenagel), (iii) Ag44-only tethered, (iv) Ag nanoparticles (same Ag mass), (v) ligand-only.

5.2 Electrical targets and diagnostics:
- Maintain FF within 3% absolute of control; ΔRs within Phase 0 budget.
- Voc gain must correlate with QFLS gain (reciprocity check).

5.3 Stability and beta metric:
- beta(t)=PCE(t)/PCE(0) under MPP tracking, 1 sun, 65–85 °C; report beta@200 h and beta@1000 h + T80.
- Post-mortem: ToF-SIMS for Ag/halide redistribution; XPS for interfacial chemistry; check for AgI or halide depletion signatures.

Decision tree / go-no-go summary (enforced):
- Gate 1: Tethering benign + anchor density metrology consistent.
- Gate 2: No mid-gap states / no increased J0; Ag photoredox stable in iodide contact.
- Gate 3: Vapor Knoevenagel works on analogs, then perovskite with no QFLS penalty; demonstrable pinhole closure advantage with Ag44.
- Gate 4: Film-level mechanism metrics achieved (QFLS gain, J0 reduction, ionic Ea increase) before scaling to full device statistics.
Feasibility:
This revision converts the highest-risk links flagged by reviewers into constrained, testable steps with orthogonal metrology and explicit kill-criteria.

(1) Perovskite-benign tethering: The proposal removes plasma/UV-ozone ‘reactive-site creation’ and replaces it with a selective, coordinative anchoring mechanism (multidentate phosphonate–Pb2+ binding or weakly basic chelation). This directly addresses the risk of deep-trap creation, stoichiometry drift, and vacancy inflation. Anchor density is quantified independently of PL via QCM (mass uptake), XPS absolute quantification (Ag/Pb with attenuation modeling), and ToF-SIMS calibrated with standards—meeting the directive for orthogonal validation.

(2) Physical grounding of ‘dielectric defect-screening’ without mid-gap penalties: The hypothesis is conditioned on electronic decoupling: Ag44 must remain atomically precise, isolated below percolation, and have frontier levels outside the perovskite bandgap. This is enforced by a mandatory electronic-structure risk assessment (UPS/IPES + PDS/EL reciprocity) combined with DFT of Ag44/ligand and cluster–surface binding motifs.
