- Perform EPR spin trapping with TEMP to detect TEMPO formation under NIR; compare (i) ZnPor-COF with each axial ligand, (ii) carbon-only, (iii) ZnPor-COF + physical 1O2 quencher barrier (e.g., immobilized DABCO derivative or HALS additive in a thin overlayer).
- Acceptance criterion: NIR-on condition increases ORR current/lowers interfacial peroxide signal while 1O2 signal remains unchanged (≤10% change) or is reduced with quencher without loss of ORR benefit.
3.3 Confirm NIR changes ORR kinetics at fixed overpotential (not via increased η):

Energy-level alignment feasibility: UPS/KPFM/SPV are standard, quantitative tools for mapping work function and illumination-induced potential changes; coupling these to a microkinetic ORR model directly answers the reviewer’s concern that “outside the quasi-Fermi level” was underdefined. Using a single reference framework (vacuum level) and reporting explicit thresholds (≥150 mV separation; ≥10× reduction in a_H2O2 at the perovskite boundary) converts the concept into falsifiable criteria.

Peroxide transport/selectivity feasibility: Sulfonation-dependent water uptake and D_eff can be quantified (QCM-D/porosimetry/SECM), enabling a transport-informed optimization rather than an assumption. Critique: The proposal is unusually strong on operational definitions, falsifiable milestones, and control logic. The main technical weaknesses are (i) the claimed ≥150 mV “E_Fn,illum(contact) vs E_onset,app” separation is not yet convincingly measurable on a single absolute scale under identical chemical potentials: KPFM/UPS/SPV provide work functions and photovoltages, but mapping these to an electrochemical ORR onset in humid O2 without a rigorously defined interfacial reference state (water activity, local pH, double-layer potential, carbon doping/adsorbates) risks systematic offsets larger than the 150 mV threshold; (ii) the microkinetic/transport model is still underconstrained—selectivity and Tafel data alone will not uniquely identify k2/k4 and H2O2 boundary activity without independent calibration of local water content, O2 permeability, and potential distribution through the COF; (iii) the NIR mechanism as written (“triplets accelerate back-electron transfer / interfacial charge-exchange with O2 increasing j0 at fixed η”) is plausible but ambiguous—triplet–O2 interactions commonly *increase* 1O2 unless explicitly quenched, so the plan needs a clearer mechanistic discriminant (e.g., outer-sphere ET vs energy transfer) tied to measurable spectroscopic signatures; (iv) PCP deposition feasibility on/near perovskite stacks is a risk: even ‘pre-integration’ deposition on ETL can alter ETL energetics, introduce dipoles, and add ionic functionalities affecting hysteresis—this could confound attribution to ROS suppression unless additional electrical controls (dark JV, electron-only mobility/contact resistance) are built in. Overall, deductions are for metrology traceability at the ORR/energetics interface and parameter identifiability, not for lack of rigor.

Hypothesis:
A perovskite-compatible, electronically benign bicontinuous passivation manifold can be realized by combining: (i) an ultrathin (3–6 nm) *metal-free* aminated coordination glass (aIRMOF-3 chemistry translated into a Zn-free, carboxylate-free, dipole-controlled network) that immobilizes undercoordinated Pb–(I/Br) surface species and pins halide-vacancy migration; (ii) a *Schwarz P–class* (P-surface–targeted) bicontinuous minimal-surface morphology that increases interfacial area and homogenizes interfacial electric-field/ionic-flux distributions; and (iii) wall-confined Fe–N4 single-atom redox centers positioned in the *gas-accessible* internal walls but *energetically and kinetically gated* to avoid acting as recombination sites.

Mechanistic resolution of reviewer risks:
1) **Composition control / ionic contamination:** Replace Zn2+/carboxylate motifs with a neutral, coordinatively saturated, aminated “coordination-glass analogue” built from (a) multidentate amines/ureas/guanidiniums (Lewis bases for Pb2+), (b) non-ionic covalent crosslinking (thiol–ene or SPAAC click), and (c) optional zwitterion buffering groups to tune interfacial dipole to ~0. This maintains the aIRMOF-3 *functional logic* (high-density donor sites + amorphous conformality) while avoiding Zn2+ leaching, carboxylate-driven interfacial dipoles, and photochemical metal–ligand rearrangements.
2) **Curvature suppresses ionic hot spots (quantified):** In perovskites, mobile halide vacancies and ionic defects drift under local fields and accumulate at transport interfaces, accelerating field-assisted defect formation and interfacial recombination. A Schwarz P–class bicontinuous interface imposes negative Gaussian curvature and spatially distributed surface normals. Under a coupled Poisson–Nernst–Planck (PNP) model using realistic dielectric contrast (εperovskite ~ 20–30; εorganic ~ 3–5), this geometry reduces peak interfacial electric-field magnitude and the variance of the normal field component En at the perovskite contact, lowering the steady-state ionic concentration polarization (Δc/c0) and the accumulation time constant (τacc) relative to a flat film at identical thickness and applied bias. This provides a *predictive* reduction in experimentally observable KPFM potential pile-up and bias-stress impedance signatures.
3) **Fe–N4 ROS sink without halide oxidation or recombination:** Fe–N4 sites are introduced with (a) a ligand field designed to place Fe(III/II) redox below halide-oxidation thresholds and (b) an ultrathin tunneling/kinetic barrier that permits ROS interception (requiring only local electron availability) but suppresses electronic back-transfer into perovskite bands. The key is to ensure: (i) Fe redox levels are off-resonant from perovskite band edges at operating quasi-Fermi-level splitting, (ii) no additional subgap absorption is introduced, and (iii) carrier recombination metrics (PLQY at 1-sun carrier density, ideality factor, subgap EQE) do not degrade. If these quantitative gates are met, the Fe–N4 centers operate as a selective redox sink for superoxide/peroxide intermediates in oxygen-containing environments, reducing oxygen-driven interfacial chemistry without becoming a recombination-active manifold.

Net expected outcome: higher Voc/FF through reduced interfacial nonradiative recombination and reduced ionic accumulation, plus improved oxygen/light/heat operational stability through ROS interception—achieved without the series-resistance penalty of insulating crystalline MOFs, because the manifold is ultrathin, bicontinuous, and electronically tuned by dipole control and barrier-gated redox centers.

Hypothesis: Embedding an ultralow-volume-fraction (≤0.5 vol%) third-order NLO–active molecular network into a compact TiO2 ETL can *measurably and reversibly* modulate the ETL’s low-frequency dielectric response (εeff, 10–10^3 Hz) and effective electron conductivity (σe) under solar illumination, thereby reducing interfacial charge accumulation and J–V hysteresis. The refined mechanism explicitly bridges ultrafast χ(3)/saturable absorption (SA) physics with slow electrodynamics as follows: under steady-state illumination (~1 sun), partial saturation of the NLO chromophores induces a population-averaged, intensity-dependent polarization ⟨P⟩ that renormalizes the Maxwell–Wagner interfacial polarization of the nanocomposite ETL. This produces a *DC-relevant increase in εeff* via field-averaged χ(3) contributions (Δε ≈ 3χ(3)⟨E^2⟩) and a concomitant reduction in space-charge field gradients at the perovskite/ETL junction. The resulting field flattening lowers the interfacial charge density (Δσint) and suppresses the driving force for ionic redistribution without relying on permanent chemical passivation. The hypothesis is falsifiable: if illumination does not induce a reversible Δεeff ≥ 10–20% at 10–10^2 Hz and a correlated reduction in low-frequency EIS capacitance/arc area and hysteresis index, the dynamic χ(3)-based mechanism is invalidated.

4.1 Quantify interfacial charge accumulation via low-frequency EIS arc area and capacitance; target ≥30% reduction relative to pristine TiO2.
4.2 Correlate Δεeff with reduced HI, scan-rate dependence, and bias-stress recovery.
4.3 Use IMPS/IMVS and light-biased EIS to demonstrate that transport/capacitance changes track illumination intensity rather than permanent chemical modification.

Step 5: Controls and decoupling experiments.
5.1 Non-NLO analog control: chemically similar additives with comparable dipole moments but χ(3) ≪ 10^−10 esu.
5.2 Stoichiometry control: match TiO2 oxygen vacancy density across samples (XPS, EPR) and band alignment (UPS/KPFM).
5.3 Mobility control: Hall/4-probe and SCLC to ensure μe reduction ≤20%.

Step 6: Go/no-go criteria.
- Δεeff(10–100 Hz, 1 sun) ≥ 10% (go).
- Reduction in low-frequency EIS capacitance ≥30% (go).
- ΔJsc ≤ −2% and μe ≥ 80% of reference (go).
Failure to meet these thresholds terminates the dynamic χ(3) hypothesis.
Feasibility: The proposal now explicitly reconciles ultrafast NLO physics with slow hysteresis phenomena by invoking field-averaged χ(3)-induced dielectric renormalization rather than direct ultrafast carrier dynamics. This approach is grounded in Maxwell–Wagner polarization theory for nanocomposites and supported by empirical χ(3) magnitudes demonstrated in ultrathin MOF/graphene systems (Asset 1). The quantitative model yields clear, testable predictions for Δεeff and σe under 1-sun illumination, directly addressing the reviewer’s concern regarding mechanistic overreach. By predefining strict go/no-go thresholds (Δεeff, μe, ΔJsc, EIS features) and employing chemically matched non-NLO controls alongside stoichiometry and band-alignment matching (Assets 2 and 3 context), the plan rigorously decouples dynamic optical nonlinearity from static passivation or doping effects. Finally, SPD compatibility and electron percolation are explicitly validated with in-film mapping and mobility measurements, ensuring scalability and preserving the comparative advantage of a bulk-modulated, illumination-adaptive ETL over conventional interfacial strategies.
Critique: This is a technically ambitious and unusually rigorous proposal that stands out for its falsifiability and quantitative discipline. The engineering plan is detailed, SPD-compatible, and supported by appropriate in-film diagnostics. The primary weakness lies in the logical leap between ultrafast χ(3)/SA saturation physics and a sustained, DC-relevant increase in ε_eff at 10–100 Hz under 1-sun illumination. While the Maxwell–Wagner framework is invoked correctly, the proposal does not yet convincingly demonstrate that the field-averaged ⟨E_opt^2⟩ under solar flux is sufficient to drive a ≥10–20% dielectric renormalization at sub-kHz frequencies, especially given the extremely low volume fraction (≤0.5%) and post-anneal survival constraints. The χ(3)-to-ε translation, though mathematically stated, risks overestimating the effective contribution without a more explicit treatment of relaxation times, chromophore orientation averaging, and thermal vs optical saturation under steady-state conditions. Evidence grounding is strong and remains within the optoelectronic/NLO domain, but empirical precedent for such large low-frequency dielectric shifts in oxide ETLs under 1 sun remains sparse. The rationale is creative and addresses hysteresis without chemical passivation, yet its success hinges on a narrow and demanding physical window.

Hypothesis:
Target use-case and failure mode: In humid, soiling-prone deployments where microbial colonization is documented and plausible—specifically agrivoltaics (leaf litter, irrigation aerosols), coastal installations (salt + bioaerosols), and floating PV—biofilms can form on module backsheets/edges and at imperfect seals, creating hydrated, ion-conducting matrices that (i) increase local water residence time at edges/pinholes, (ii) trap ionic contaminants (Cl−/NO3−/NH4+) and organic acids, (iii) lower surface resistivity and promote electrochemical shunting/corrosion at contacts, and (iv) accelerate encapsulant/interlayer interfacial delamination. We hypothesize that converting a PVDF interfacial/edge-encapsulation layer into an ‘active catalytic sink’ by embedding hierarchically porous UiO-66(Zr/Ce) nanoparticles will improve perovskite solar cell (PSC) operational stability through two falsifiable, device-relevant mechanisms executed in spatially separated domains:

Mechanism A — Biofilm-to-ingress suppression (outer/edge domain): The Zr/Ce Lewis-acid sites (and Ce-associated redox buffering when properly passivated) catalyze hydrolysis/cleavage of phosphorus–oxygen (P–O) bonds in extracellular DNA (eDNA), weakening biofilm cohesion and reducing persistent hydrated coverage on the polymer surface. This lowers effective water residence time and ionic conductivity at edges/pinholes, thereby decreasing moisture-assisted ion migration and shunt formation. Falsifiable linkage: reduced biofilm coverage (%) and eDNA signal must correlate with improved shunt resistance (Rsh), lower leakage current, and higher Voc retention under damp-heat + biological exposure.

Mechanism B — Interfacial ion/byproduct immobilization without electronic penalty (inner domain): At the device-side interface, defect-rich UiO-66(Zr/Ce) nodes (Zr6O4(OH)4 and Ce-oxo clusters) provide coordinatively unsaturated metal sites and μ3-OH/μ3-O that can bind migrating halides (I−/Br−), Pb–halide complexes (PbIx(2−x)), and oxidized HTL dopant byproducts (e.g., LiTFSI-related species, tBP-derived fragments) through inner-sphere coordination or acid–base interactions. This creates a ‘sink’ that reduces halide accumulation at the HTL/metal interface and suppresses interfacial chemical steps that drive Voc loss (interfacial recombination, contact corrosion). Crucially, electronic de-risking is built in: the MOF is confined in a PVDF matrix with controlled loading/percolation and is surface-passivated (fluorinated phosphonate/fluoroalkyl carboxylate ligands) to reduce exposed Lewis acidity toward the perovskite and to stabilize Ce in a non-catalytically aggressive state (minimize uncontrolled Ce3+/Ce4+ redox). Falsifiable linkage: depth profiling must show reduced halide/metal/dopant accumulation at critical interfaces after stress, while UPS/KPFM/TRPL/impedance confirm unchanged (or improved) band alignment and reduced non-radiative recombination relative to PVDF-only controls.

Acceptance metrics (predefined): (1) Under combined damp-heat (85 °C/85%RH) + soiling/bioaerosol challenge, biofilm surface coverage on encapsulation/edge region ≤10% after 14 days and ≥2× reduction vs PVDF-only; (2) ΔVoc ≤ 30 mV and ΔRsh ≤ 20% after 500 h ISOS-D-3-like damp-heat (device-level) with quantified WVTR; (3) ToF-SIMS/XPS shows ≥50% reduction in I−/Br− accumulation at HTL/metal interface and reduced Li+/TFSI− signatures (if spiro used) relative to PVDF-only after identical stress; (4) No penalty in initial PCE beyond 2% relative and no increase in trap density (SCLC) beyond 10% relative to controls across optimal loading.
Plan:
A. Define deployment-relevant biological/soiling scenario and acceptance tests
1) Target scenario definition: agrivoltaic / floating PV proxy conditions—intermittent wetting, nutrients, and bioaerosols. Use a controlled ‘bio-soiling chamber’ combining: (i) high RH cycling (40–85% RH), (ii) periodic misting with dilute nutrient solution (e.g., 0.1× LB or defined mineral medium), (iii) inoculation with representative strains (Pseudomonas aeruginosa + mixed environmental consortium optional), and (iv) particulate soiling (standard Arizona dust) to promote adhesion.
2) Acceptance metrics (locked before experiments): quantify biofilm coverage (confocal microscopy/fluorescent staining), eDNA content (PicoGreen assay), and relate to device electrical metrics (ΔVoc, ΔRsh, leakage current at reverse bias).

B. Materials design: UiO-66(Zr/Ce) catalyst engineered for catalytic function + electronic safety
3) Synthesize hierarchically porous UiO-66(Zr/Ce) nanoparticles (HMUiO-66(Zr/Ce)):
   - Target particle size: 50–150 nm (to avoid optical scattering in thin layers).
   - Hierarchical porosity: micro+mesopores via templating (microemulsion/soft template) to keep active sites accessible when embedded.
   - Zr:Ce feed ratios: screen 100:0, 90:10, 70:30, 50:50 (molar at node level) guided by DNase-mimetic literature; keep identical crystallinity/size as much as possible.
   - Defect engineering: modulator (acetic/formic acid) control to tune missing-linker density (quantify by TGA + 1H NMR of digested MOF) because defect sites govern adsorption/coordination.
4) Surface passivation/compatibilization to PVDF and to mitigate electronic penalties:
   - Ligand shell: fluorinated phosphonate (e.g., perfluoroalkyl phosphonic acid) at low surface coverage to (i) anchor in PVDF, (ii) increase hydrophobicity, (iii) cap the most aggressive Lewis sites.
   - Ce redox control: optional thin inert overlayer (sub-nm Al2O3 by solution ALD-like route or molecular layer deposition analogue) OR catechol-like chelator at low density to suppress undesired redox while maintaining halide affinity. Verify Ce3+/Ce4+ ratio by XPS (Ce 3d) pre/post stress.

C. Device architecture choices and placement logic (separating inner and outer functions)
5) Baseline PSC stack (two representative HTLs to generalize):
   - n–i–p: Glass/ITO/SnO2/perovskite (FA/Cs/MA–Pb–I/Br)/HTL (PTAA and spiro-OMeTAD as separate cohorts)/Au.
   - Control encapsulation: PVDF-only and commercial thin barrier (if available) as benchmarks.
6) Two placements to disentangle mechanisms:
   - Inner interfacial layer (ion-sink emphasis): ultrathin PVDF:MOF (30–80 nm) coated on top of HTL before Au (requires solvent orthogonality; use PVDF in low-damage solvent system; validate HTL integrity by UV–vis/UPS).
   - Outer/edge encapsulation layer (biofilm emphasis): PVDF:MOF film (5–25 µm) laminated as edge-seal/backs-side encapsulation (low-temperature lamination ≤80 °C). This allows biofilm tests without directly contacting perovskite.
   - A ‘decoupling matrix’: four groups—(i) no PVDF, (ii) PVDF-only, (iii) PVDF:MOF inner only, (iv) PVDF:MOF outer/edge only, (v) both inner+outer—to attribute effects.

D. Composition/process window with explicit targets
7) MOF loading and PVDF phase control:
   - Loadings: 0.5, 1, 3, 5 wt% (avoid >5 wt% in inner layer to minimize dielectric discontinuity and trap formation).
   - PVDF β-phase induction: solvent/anneal protocol fixed (e.g., DMF/acetone blend + 60–80 °C anneal) and quantified by FTIR (β-phase fraction) to ensure reproducibility and consistent dipole environment.
   - Film QC: ellipsometry/profilometry for thickness; SEM/TEM cross-sections for dispersion; contact angle for surface hydrophobicity.

E. Binding/catalysis map (chemical specificity) + decisive measurements
8) Predefine target species and binding hypotheses to test:
   - Halides: I−/Br− binding at Zr(IV)/Ce(IV) open sites and μ3-OH via inner-sphere coordination; monitor via XPS (I 3d/Br 3d shifts), solid-state NMR where feasible, and halide uptake isotherms on free MOF powders.
   - Pb complexes: PbIx(2−x) capture by node oxy/hydroxo groups; verify by XPS Pb 4f chemical shifts and ToF-SIMS fragments (PbI+, PbI2− etc.).
   - Organic cations (MA+/FA+): weaker electrostatic association; primarily tracked as suppression of their accumulation at electrodes via ToF-SIMS depth profiles.
   - HTL dopant/byproducts: Li+ and TFSI− (spiro cohort) and oxidized spiro fragments; quantify by ToF-SIMS + XPS (F 1s/S 2p for TFSI; Li 1s), and correlate with impedance-derived interfacial charge transfer resistance.
9) Depth-resolved diagnostics before/after stress (immobilization vs catalyzed degradation):
   - ToF-SIMS depth profiling across Au/HTL/perovskite with and without MOF layers after aging.
   - GIWAXS/GIXRD for phase stability (δ-phase/ PbI2 emergence) to ensure MOF is not accelerating decomposition.
   - XPS with gentle sputter for interface chemistry; specifically monitor Pb0 formation and halide depletion.

F. Electronic de-risking: explicit energetics/defect/recombination plan
10) Energetics alignment:
   - UPS to extract HTL work function and valence onset with/without PVDF:MOF.
   - KPFM surface potential mapping to detect local band bending and heterogeneity induced by MOF clusters.
11) Recombination and traps:
   - TRPL on perovskite/HTL stacks with and without PVDF:MOF to quantify interfacial quenching and non-radiative recombination.
   - Impedance spectroscopy under illumination to separate recombination resistance and ionic contributions.
   - SCLC (electron-only/hole-only) test structures to quantify trap density vs MOF loading and Ce content.
   - Criteria for ‘no sacrifice’: initial Voc and quasi-Fermi level splitting (via absolute PL, if available) must be unchanged within experimental uncertainty.

G. Operationally relevant stability protocols (replace TGA-centric validation)
12) Stability testing matrix (device level):
   - ISOS-L-2 (MPP tracking under 1 sun, 25–45 °C) for intrinsic operational stability.
   - ISOS-D-3-like damp-heat (85 °C/85% RH) with encapsulation; include bias-stress (±0.8 V or MPP) to accelerate ion migration.
   - Thermal cycling (−20 to 80 °C) for delamination/edge-seal robustness if targeting field-like conditions.
13) Barrier quantification:
   - Measure WVTR of PVDF vs PVDF:MOF films (MOCON or equivalent) and helium leak/edge seal integrity for laminated samples.
14) Operando / in-situ attribution:
   - Operando PL mapping during damp-heat to spatially locate degradation (edges vs active area).
   - In-situ XRD (where feasible) during heating/humidity to correlate phase change timing with device metrics.

H. Biofilm module with explicit linkage to device failure modes
15) Biofilm formation assay on films and laminated edges:
   - Quantify biomass (crystal violet), live/dead staining, confocal thickness, and eDNA concentration.
   - Surface energy/roughness changes: contact angle + AFM.
16) Electrical impact linkage:
   - Measure surface insulation resistance (SIR) across encapsulated test coupons under humidity with/without biofilms.
   - For devices, track ΔRsh, leakage current, and edge-related failure via EL imaging; correlate with biofilm coverage.

I. Recyclability demonstration with quantification (not qualitative)
17) Delamination protocol:
   - Engineer a defined release interface (e.g., thin sacrificial layer or controlled adhesion primer) so delamination is repeatable.
   - Quantify adhesion energy (peel test) pre/post aging.
18) Recycling metrics:
   - Recovery yield: % of devices successfully delaminated without electrode damage; quantify via SEM cross-sections and sheet resistance of contacts.
   - Performance statistics: re-encapsulate and report PCE/Voc/FF distributions over ≥3 delamination cycles (n≥10 per group).
   - Chemical cleanliness: XPS/ToF-SIMS check that residues from PVDF:MOF are not left on Au/HTL in damaging amounts.

Decision points / down-select criteria:
- If inner-layer PVDF:MOF increases trap density or worsens Voc beyond thresholds, shift MOF function primarily to outer/edge encapsulation and retain PVDF-only inner layer.
- If Ce redox signatures correlate with accelerated perovskite degradation (PbI2 increase, Voc drop), reduce Ce fraction and/or increase surface passivation density while maintaining Zr-driven Lewis acidity for binding.
Feasibility:
1) Use-case plausibility (addresses critique i): Biofilms are not claimed as universal PSC stressors; they are positioned for specific wet/soiling-prone deployments (agrivoltaics/floating/coastal). The proposal includes a controlled bio-soiling chamber and acceptance metrics that explicitly link biofilm coverage/eDNA to device-relevant shunting and edge-driven degradation (ΔRsh, leakage, EL hot spots).

2) Mechanistic closure from DNase-mimetic activity to PSC metrics (addresses critique ii): The DNase-mimetic P–O cleavage is not treated as intrinsically improving PCE; it is mapped to reduced hydrated conductive films and reduced edge/pinhole ingress, which are directly measurable via SIR, WVTR/leak tests, leakage current, and spatial PL/EL mapping. This creates a falsifiable chain: catalytic eDNA disruption → lower biofilm cohesion/water residence → reduced shunting/edge degradation → Voc and Rsh retention.

3) Chemical specificity of immobilization (addresses critique iii): The plan enumerates target migrating species (I−/Br−, Pb-halide fragments, Li+/TFSI− and oxidized HTL byproducts) and hypothesized binding motifs at Zr/Ce nodes/defects, then commits to depth-resolved spectroscopy (ToF-SIMS, XPS) plus phase probes (GIWAXS/GIXRD) to distinguish ‘immobilization’ from MOF-catalyzed decomposition. Uptake tests on powders provide independent confirmation of binding capacity and selectivity.

4) De-risking electronic penalties (addresses critique iv): The proposal anticipates Lewis acidity/redox risks by (i) limiting MOF loading and controlling dispersion/percolation in PVDF, (ii) surface-passivating MOF particles with fluorinated anchors, (iii) monitoring and controlling Ce3+/Ce4+ chemistry, and (iv) implementing an explicit interfacial energetics/recombination/trap-density metrology suite (UPS, KPFM, TRPL, impedance, SCLC) with quantitative ‘no sacrifice’ criteria and down-select rules.

5) Operational relevance beyond TGA (addresses critique v): TGA is demoted to materials QC (defects/thermal robustness) rather than a primary stability proof. Device claims are validated under ISOS-aligned operational protocols (light soaking, damp-heat, bias stress), with WVTR/leak quantification and operando mapping (PL/EL) plus in-situ structural probes (XRD) to attribute lifetime gains.

6) Recyclability is quantified, not asserted: The proposal defines delamination engineering, adhesion-energy measurement, recovery yield, multi-cycle performance statistics, and interfacial damage checks (SEM cross-sections, sheet resistance, XPS/ToF-SIMS), meeting the directive for decisive evidence.

Overall feasibility: All synthesis, thin-film processing, PSC fabrication, and characterization methods are standard in advanced PSC and porous materials laboratories. The key novelty—an active PVDF:UiO-66(Zr/Ce) catalytic interface—has built-in go/no-go criteria and modular placement (inner vs outer) to ensure that if electronic penalties arise, the biofilm/edge protection function can still be retained without compromising charge extraction.
Critique: This is an unusually detailed and technically mature proposal with strong methodological closure. Engineering resolution is high: synthesis, processing windows, device architectures, diagnostics, and go/no-go criteria are all explicitly defined and aligned with PSC best practices. Logical consistency is strong, particularly in mapping DNase-mimetic biofilm disruption to measurable electrical failure modes (Rsh, leakage, EL hot spots) rather than overstating direct efficiency gains. Minor logical risk remains in the assumed persistence and relevance of biofilms at PSC edges under accelerated lab conditions; while the proposal carefully scopes the use-case, the causal strength between eDNA cleavage and long-term moisture ingress reduction is still partly inferential and will require careful controls. Evidence grounding is solid: the concept chain is respected, with no obvious disciplinary hallucinations, though TGA’s inclusion in the chain is somewhat orthogonal to the central hypotheses and could be misread as overstated by less careful reviewers. Rationale quality is high due to the creative reframing of MOFs from passive scavengers to spatially programmed catalytic/immobilization interfaces, but the recyclability component, while quantified, is incremental rather than transformative relative to existing delamination strategies.

Hypothesis:
A perovskite-safe, covalently crosslinked phthalocyanine “electrostatic coupling skin” (ECS) can be formed *without oxidants, bias, or polar solvents* by initiating an ultrathin (1–3 nm) surface-confined coupling reaction from pre-anchored Pc monomers. The ECS will act as a self-limiting electrostatic boundary condition—defined by a tunable fixed-charge density (σ0), interfacial capacitance (Cint), and suppressed ionic mobility (μion)—that (i) passivates under-coordinated Pb–X sites via multidentate carboxylate/sulfonate anchoring and macrocycle–Pb coordination, (ii) raises the energetic/entropic penalty for halide and metal-cation accumulation at the selective contact by reducing local ionic permittivity and available solvation volume (ion-blocking), and (iii) imposes a controlled interfacial dipole that shifts band alignment *without inducing carrier pile-up*, because the sign/magnitude of σ0 is chosen to counter the built-in field at the relevant contact and is validated against drift–diffusion + ionic transport predictions.

Mechanistic rigor (addressing reviewer concerns):
1) Feasibility and chemical compatibility are ensured by replacing oxidative electropolymerization with a “click-like” surface-confined crosslinking route (copper-free SPAAC or thermal azide–alkyne cycloaddition) executed in orthogonal, perovskite-benign solvents (anisole/chlorobenzene) or solvent-free vapor exposure at ≤60 °C, eliminating pathways for halide extraction, Pb0 formation, and surface amorphization.
2) The demetallation is not treated as a vague post-process; instead, it is bounded to a thermodynamic/kinetic window using non-aqueous, non-halogenating ligation chemistry (chelator-driven Cu removal) where Cu is immediately sequestered by tethered multidentate ligands whose stability constants for Cu(I/II) exceed those of Cu–halide and Cu uptake into perovskite. A decisive tracer protocol (ToF-SIMS Cu depth profiles under bias/heat) falsifies/validates the immobilization claim.
3) Electrokinetics is elevated from correlation to mechanism by explicitly mapping streaming/zeta outputs onto (σ0, Cint, μion) using a calibrated slip-plane assumption for the polymer skin, and by cross-validating σ0 and Cint with independent solid-state electrostatic measurements (MOS-cap C–V and KPFM/EFM under controlled ionic environments). The proposal pre-registers the *sign* of expected trends: σ0 sign → band bending direction (KPFM) → ideality factor change and Voc deficit; μion ↓ → hysteresis area ↓ and bias-stress drift ↓.

Outcome: The ECS becomes a quantitatively tunable interfacial “electrostatic boundary layer” rather than a generic passivator, enabling a transferable design rule: choose σ0, Cint, μion to minimize non-radiative recombination (Voc), reduce ionic accumulation (hysteresis), and suppress bias-stress degradation (T80), while preserving efficient electronic coupling (FF).
Plan:
Step 0 — Materials and baseline definition (locks the reference frame)
0.1 Device stack (baseline): glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA0.83Cs0.17)Pb(I0.8Br0.2)3/ECS/HTL (NiOx or PTAA)/metal.
0.2 Baseline perovskite acceptance window (pre-registered, must be met after every ECS process step):
- GIWAXS/XRD: no new PbI2 peak growth >2% relative integrated intensity; no peak broadening >10% (FWHM) vs untreated.
- SEM/AFM: RMS roughness change <1.5 nm; no pinhole density increase.
- XPS: Pb0 fraction <0.5 at.% (Pb 4f deconvolution); halide/Pb ratio change <5%.
- Steady-state PL (film on SnO2): PL intensity not decreased relative to untreated (to rule out gross new quenchers).

Step 1 — Perovskite-safe formation of an ultrathin, continuous covalent ECS
1.1 Replace oxidative electropolymerization with surface-confined “click” crosslinking (two viable routes; select based on meeting Step 0 thresholds):
Route A (preferred, copper-free): SPAAC crosslinking.
- Monomer set: Pc bearing (i) multidentate anchors: 2–4 carboxylates and/or sulfonates (for Pb2+ binding), and (ii) strained cyclooctyne (DBCO) or azide handles for SPAAC.
- Process: (a) anchor-layer deposition by spin-coating 0.1–0.5 mg mL−1 monomer in chlorobenzene or anisole, 2000–4000 rpm, 20–40 s; (b) mild bake 50–60 °C, 2–5 min; (c) vapor-phase or solution exposure to the complementary azide-/DBCO-functional crosslinker (bifunctional, nonpolar solvent), 1–10 min; (d) rinse in dry chlorobenzene.
Route B (thermal azide–alkyne cycloaddition, no catalyst):
- Use azide + alkyne functionalized Pc/crosslinker; react at 50–70 °C for 5–15 min in solvent-free vapor exposure to minimize perovskite contact with liquids.
1.2 Thickness/continuity control (hard metrics):
- Target thickness: 1.0–3.0 nm (ellipsometry on planar witness Si; cross-checked by XPS attenuation length on perovskite).
- Continuity criterion: no exposed perovskite signal increase after solvent rinse (XPS: Pb 4f intensity attenuation consistent with ≥90% coverage; AFM phase uniformity).
1.3 Chemical anchoring confirmation:
- Angle-resolved XPS: quantify Pb–O bonding (carboxylate/sulfonate) vs physisorbed; threshold: ≥30% of O 1s assigned to bound species.
- NEXAFS/linear dichroism (if available): constrain Pc orientation to interpret dipole direction.

Step 2 — Controlled, bounded demetallation + Cu immobilization (or elimination) with decisive tracer tests
2.1 Decision tree (risk-managed):
Option 1 (lowest Cu risk): start from metal-free H2Pc monomers and omit demetallation entirely; use tethered cation chelators to trap *extrinsic* Cu/metal impurities from contacts.
Option 2 (original concept, but bounded): partial CuPc → H2Pc conversion post-crosslinking.
2.2 Demetallation chemistry (Option 2): chelator-driven, non-halogenating, non-aqueous.
- Medium: dry acetonitrile or propylene carbonate with ≤10 mM neutral chelator additive; exposure ≤60 s (dip) or ≤5 min (vapor/gel contact), temperature 20–40 °C.
- Chelator tether: iminodiacetate (IDA) or higher-denticity ligand (e.g., NTA-like) covalently built into ECS (pendant groups) to immediately bind liberated Cu.
- Bounding measurements (must pass):
  (i) UV–vis on witness films: Q-band shape retained (macrocycle integrity); allowed shift consistent with metallated→free-base fraction.
  (ii) XPS Cu 2p: quantify demetallation fraction (target 10–60% removal; do not exceed level that increases interfacial redox activity).
  (iii) EPR/ICP-MS (on extracted solution): confirm Cu captured/removed; no evidence of ongoing Cu redox cycling.
2.3 Thermodynamic/kinetic justification package (generated in project year 1):
- Measure (or compile) Cu binding constants of tethered chelator vs Cu–halide complexes in the chosen medium; requirement: Kchelator/Khalide >> 10^3 under relevant conditions.
- Diffusion-length constraint: estimate Cu diffusion length during worst-case bias/heat using DCu in perovskites (literature range) and impose design requirement that ECS chelation + low permeability yields LCu << perovskite thickness over 100 h.
2.4 Decisive falsifiable tracer experiment:
- ToF-SIMS depth profiling with isotopically enriched 65Cu in the Pc precursor (or distinguishable Cu signature): map Cu distribution after (a) 1 sun, 60 °C, MPP tracking 100 h; (b) ±1 V bias in dark, 60 °C, 24 h.
- Pass criterion: no Cu accumulation peak inside perovskite bulk beyond near-surface noise; Cu remains confined within ECS region.

Step 3 — Quantitative electrokinetic model and cross-validation (replace IESI with σ0, μion, Cint)
3.1 Define the electrokinetic measurement as a calibrated proxy (not a direct replica) for buried interface electrostatics:
- Build model surfaces: perovskite (same composition) coated with ECS on insulating substrates; encapsulate edges to avoid dissolution.
- Use non-reactive, low-donor-number solvents (dry ACN) with controlled salt (e.g., 1–10 mM tetrabutylammonium PF6) to set Debye length; maintain water <50 ppm.
- Slip-plane assumption: treat the ECS as a porous polyelectret layer with slip plane at outer ECS surface (validated by thickness independence tests: zeta should saturate beyond ~2–3 nm if slip plane is external).
3.2 Extract physically interpretable parameters:
- Fixed charge density σ0: from streaming potential/current vs pressure using modified Smoluchowski including ECS thickness and dielectric constant; calibrate with a reference surface of known σ0.
- Interfacial capacitance Cint: from MOS-cap style C–V on metal/ECS/perovskite stack (small-signal, frequency sweep) and from EFM/KPFM force-gradient methods.
- Ionic mobility μion: from time-resolved electrokinetic relaxation after field reversal + corroboration by impedance spectroscopy DRT (ionic arc time constants) on full stacks.
3.3 Cross-validation (required):
- σ0 cross-check: KPFM surface potential shifts under controlled ionic atmosphere (dry N2 vs controlled polar vapor) and compare inferred band bending direction with σ0 sign.
- Cint cross-check: compare MOS C–V extracted Cint with capacitance from impedance fits of full devices (separating geometric, interfacial, and ionic contributions).
3.4 Pre-registered mechanistic predictions (make it falsifiable):
- If σ0 is negative at the perovskite/HTL interface, expect reduced hole accumulation (or enhanced electron blocking depending on contact), manifested as: ideality factor trending toward 1 (radiative/bulk-limited) and reduced low-frequency capacitance rise under bias.
- If μion decreases (ECS more blocking), expect: smaller J–V hysteresis index, reduced bias-stress Voc drift rate, and higher ionic activation energy from temperature-dependent impedance.
- If Cint increases excessively (too polar/soft ECS), expect increased interfacial charge storage and possibly *worse* hysteresis—this defines an optimization constraint, not a guaranteed improvement.

Step 4 — Device validation mapped explicitly to σ0, μion, Cint (not multi-technique correlation)
4.1 Voc deficit and non-radiative recombination:
- Absolute PLQY on complete stacks to extract quasi-Fermi level splitting; success: ΔVoc,nr reduced by ≥30 mV vs control at matched Jsc.
- TRPL + transient photovoltage: separate interfacial recombination velocity change; correlate specifically with σ0 sign/magnitude (not with “IESI”).
4.2 Hysteresis and ionic drift:
- Stabilized MPP power and forward/reverse J–V at controlled scan rates; correlate hysteresis with μion and Cint.
- Temperature-dependent impedance (DRT) to extract ionic activation energy; success: increase by ≥0.1 eV relative to untreated.
4.3 Stability:
- ISOS-L-2 and ISOS-D-2 plus 65 °C damp-heat on encapsulated devices.
- Success: T80 >2× baseline with <1% absolute FF loss and no new mid-gap signatures (checked by sub-gap EQE or photothermal deflection if available).
4.4 Interfacial chemistry integrity:
- Operando or staged ex-situ XPS: verify Pb0 remains below threshold and halide/Pb ratio within ±5% after aging.
- Depth profiling (ToF-SIMS): confirm suppressed metal-halide interdiffusion (e.g., Au, Ag, Cu if present in contacts) compared to controls.

Step 5 — Controls (must isolate each mechanism)
- C0: no treatment.
- C1: physisorbed (non-crosslinked) Pc monomer layer at same optical density.
- C2: crosslinked ECS without ionic anchor groups (tests dipole-only).
- C3: crosslinked ECS with anchors but no dipole-tuning substituents (tests passivation/ion-blocking without alignment).
- C4: (if Option 2 used) demetallated ECS without tethered chelator (tests Cu immobilization necessity).
- C5: standard passivator (PEAI/2D) thickness-matched.

Go/No-Go gates (risk-managed milestones)
- Gate 1 (after Step 1): perovskite acceptance window met + continuous 1–3 nm ECS proven.
- Gate 2 (after Step 2): ToF-SIMS shows no Cu ingress under stress (or switch to Option 1 H2Pc-only route).
- Gate 3 (after Step 3): σ0, Cint, μion extracted with cross-validation; predicted sign trends match KPFM/ideality-factor direction.

Hypothesis:
A perovskite-benign, ultrathin reticular Zn–imidazolate interphase can be fabricated as a conformal “Reticular Proton‑Sponge Dipole (RPSD)” by (i) low-reactivity Zn precursor pulsing that avoids Pb–X disruption, (ii) linker-driven conversion to a ZIF‑8–like (sodalite-topology) microporous network or a deliberately defined amorphous Zn–imidazolate (aZIF) analog, and (iii) nanoconfined immobilization of sulfonate-tethered GQDs (GQDs–PSS) that provides a controllable population of Brønsted sites and bound water. The refined mechanism is explicitly falsifiable and risk-bounded: (1) Electronic passivation is supplied by a spatially ordered 2D/3D surface heterojunction (n=1–2) that reduces SRH recombination by saturating undercoordinated Pb2+ and suppressing halide vacancy percolation at the topmost grains (Voc/QFLS increase, reduced ideality factor). (2) Ionic-field stabilization is supplied by a nanoconfined protonic screening pathway inside the reticular interphase that is kinetically fast (sub‑second to seconds) and low-mobility compared to halide drift (10–10^3 s), thereby stabilizing the interfacial electric double layer (EDL) under bias without enabling net halide transport. Proton donors/acceptors are pre-defined as: (i) sulfonate acid/FA+ counterion pairs on PSS (tunable acidity without free strong acid), (ii) adsorbed H2O forming hydrogen-bond networks, and (iii) imidazolate/imidazole equilibrium at the Zn–mim nodes. Under humidity, these sites support Grotthuss/vehicular proton motion confined to the MOF/aZIF volume, producing a measurable increase in low-frequency interfacial ionic capacitance (Cion) and a distinct relaxation time constant (τp) that shifts with H2O→D2O isotope substitution, while TOF-SIMS confirms reduced halide redistribution under identical bias stress (decoupling proton screening from halide migration). (3) Process-order risk on 2D-skin formation is removed by explicitly benchmarking two sequences (2D-first vs MOF-first) and selecting the one that yields a verified depth ordering: 3D perovskite → 2D (n=1–2) → reticular Zn–imidazolate (with embedded GQDs–PSS) → C60, rather than an intermixed damaged region. (4) Fluorescence quenching is converted from a qualitative indicator into a pre-registered photophysical diagnostic by fitting a multi-channel kinetic model (radiative + SRH + energy transfer + charge transfer) across temperature and distance-control samples, so “interphase integrity” corresponds to a stable, model-resolved transfer rate (kET or kCT) without emergent nonradiative channels (kSRH increase).

This hypothesis overcomes reviewer-identified limitations by (i) replacing aggressive Zn precursors with demonstrably perovskite-benign chemistries and proving, pulse-by-pulse, that Zn–N coordination forms without Pb–X loss; (ii) defining acceptance criteria that explicitly separate crystalline ZIF‑8 from amorphous Zn–imidazolate and allowing either to be a valid reticular proton-sponge provided porosity/proton response targets are met; (iii) making the proton-screening claim quantitative via isotope-dependent EIS/KPFM time constants and capacitance changes correlated with halide-stability metrics; and (iv) de-risking 2D-layer formation by an order-of-operations study plus depth-resolved structural confirmation.
Plan:
Step 0 — Pre-registration of acceptance criteria (go/no-go gates)
0.1 Define “perovskite-benign Zn pulsing” acceptance: after Zn pulse sets (no linker), the perovskite surface must show (i) no detectable Pb0 growth by XPS (Pb 4f metallic component <1 at%), (ii) no net halide loss by XPS (I/Pb and Br/Pb within ±5% of baseline), (iii) unchanged near-surface crystallinity by GIWAXS (no new PbI2 peak above detection) and AFM RMS roughness change <0.5 nm.
0.2 Define “reticular Zn–imidazolate” classification:
- Crystalline ZIF-8: GIWAXS shows characteristic sodalite reflections (e.g., (011), (002), (112) at expected q); FTIR/Raman indicates Zn–N(imidazolate) coordination (imidazolate ring modes shifted vs Hmim); ellipsometry thickness 0.7–3.0 nm target; porosity proxy confirmed on reference substrates (Kr adsorption or ellipsometric porosimetry with water/methanol).
- aZIF (amorphous Zn–imidazolate): no GIWAXS reflections but FTIR/Raman confirms Zn–N coordination; must still show measurable porosity proxy and proton-response signature (humidity-dependent impedance with isotope shift).
0.3 Define “proton-screening” quantitative targets at device-relevant RH (30–50%):
- A low-frequency capacitance increase ΔCion ≥ 2× vs baseline (same bias and RH), with a dominant relaxation time τp in 0.1–10 s range.

1.2 Prepare matched substrates for process-chemistry studies: (i) perovskite on ITO/MeO‑2PACz for in-vacuo characterization; (ii) perovskite on inert TiO2/Si for depth profiling; (iii) reference inert substrates (Si, Al2O3, quartz) for porosity and growth metrology.

Step 2 — De-risked reticular growth chemistry (precursor benchmarking + in-situ metrology)
2.1 Benchmark Zn precursors (replace Zn(Et)2 as non-default):
- Primary: Zn(tmhd)2 (Zn(2,2,6,6‑tetramethyl‑3,5‑heptanedionate)2) or Zn(hfac)2 is avoided due to fluorinated acidity/corrosion risk; prioritize non-fluorinated β‑diketonates.

- Tertiary (only if benign in Step 2.3): Zn(acac)2.

2.2 Linker delivery and mobility: 2‑methylimidazole (Hmim) delivered by controlled vapor dosing (heated reservoir) with short pulses and purge to minimize residence time; RH kept <1% during growth (dry N2/Ar) to prevent uncontrolled perovskite hydration.
2.3 Pulse-by-pulse surface reaction study (mandatory):
For each Zn precursor: perform (Zn pulse → purge → in-vacuo XPS; Hmim pulse → purge → in-vacuo XPS) over 1–5 cycles on perovskite.
Measured endpoints after each half-cycle:
- XPS: Zn 2p, N 1s (imidazolate), Pb 4f, I 3d, Br 3d, C 1s; track Pb–X integrity and Zn–N formation.

Step 3 — Formation of the RPSD interphase (two validated architectures)
3.1 Architecture A (MOF/aZIF-first, then 2D):
3.1.1 Grow ultrathin reticular Zn–imidazolate (target 0.7–3.0 nm) by alternating Zn/Hmim pulses (2–10 cycles). Temperature: 40–60 °C. Stop when ellipsometry indicates target thickness and QCM indicates diminishing uptake (self-limiting regime).
3.1.2 Incorporate GQDs–PSS by one of two solvent-orthogonal routes (benchmarked for perovskite compatibility):
- Route A (preferred): dry aerosol deposition of GQDs–PSS (size 2–5 nm) with controlled dose, followed by 1–2 Zn/Hmim “capping” cycles to immobilize sulfonate-tethered domains at pore mouths/defects.

4.2 2D-only: PEA-I/FPEA-I vapor.

Critique: The proposal is unusually well-engineered for an interphase-chemistry problem: it replaces the highest-risk chemistry with a gated precursor screen and builds falsifiability into the central “proton-sponge” claim via isotope-sensitive time constants tied to halide redistribution readouts. However, several deductions remain. (i) The physical plausibility of forming a continuous, functionally porous 0.7–3.0 nm ZIF-like network on a heterogeneous perovskite/2D surface at 40–60 °C is still uncertain; the porosity proxy is largely demonstrated on inert substrates, not on the actual perovskite stack where densification/partial collapse is likely at sub-3 nm thickness. (ii) Equivalent-circuit extraction of ΔCion and τp is non-unique; without a stronger impedance identifiability plan (model selection, Kramers–Kronig compliance, parameter correlation analysis), the claimed protonic element can be confounded with interfacial dipoles, contact inhomogeneity, or slow electronic trapping—especially because humidity also changes perovskite surface energetics. (iii) The mechanism assumes “fast-but-confined” proton screening that stabilizes the EDL without enabling net anion transport; yet the proposal does not specify an upper bound on protonic/ionic conductivity that would avoid new shunt pathways, nor does it define how to separate genuine proton motion inside the reticular phase from water-mediated surface conduction along grain boundaries or pinholes. (iv) The 2D (n=1–2) passivation layer is treated as simultaneously electronic passivator and halide-vacancy suppressor, but direct proof of reduced vacancy percolation at the topmost grains is indirect; TOF-SIMS post-stress is helpful but not sufficient to attribute the effect specifically to vacancy percolation suppression vs changed interface fields or altered electrode reactions.

Hypothesis: Embedding an ultrathin (20–60 nm) triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) interlayer with controlled negative Gaussian curvature at the perovskite/charge-transport interface increases the *effective utilization ratio* of passivation and extraction sites by jointly optimizing geometry, electrostatics, and interfacial chemistry. Specifically, (i) a bicontinuous Schwarz P or gyroid architecture with 5–12 nm necks maximizes specific surface area per projected area while preserving continuous electronic percolation and low contact resistance; finite-element Poisson–drift–diffusion modeling predicts that such curvature redistributes interfacial electric fields from localized asperity-driven hot-spots into a more spatially homogeneous field landscape, reducing field-assisted non-radiative recombination and ion-migration nucleation. (ii) The same geometry enhances accessibility of tethered amine passivants and radical-scavenging motifs, ensuring that a larger fraction of chemically present sites are kinetically contacted by photo-generated radicals and under-coordinated defects. (iii) Photo-induced oxidative coupling of selectively designed aromatic amines into a sparse, conjugated imine network proceeds with kinetics and thermodynamics that outcompete perovskite, SnO2, or C60 oxidation under tightly bounded oxidant chemical potential, thereby converting otherwise destructive ROS/free-radical chemistry into a self-limiting crosslinking reaction. The resulting imine network immobilizes mobile ionic species, passivates emergent defects, and introduces a controlled interfacial dipole that improves band alignment without creating deep trap states. Collectively, curvature-enabled electrostatic homogenization plus chemically selective, operation-triggered radical consumption raises Voc and operational stability while preserving FF, providing a quantitatively testable structure–property–utilization relationship rather than an empirical passivation effect.
Plan:
1. TPMS interlayer fabrication with explicit process window and electrical validation.
1.1 Block-copolymer (BCP) cubosome templating: Use PS-b-PEO (Mn_PS ≈ 32 kg mol⁻¹, Mn_PEO ≈ 11 kg mol⁻¹, Ð < 1.1) dissolved at 1.2–1.5 wt% in toluene/THF (7:3 v/v). Add 8–12 vol% swelling agent (1,3,5-trimethylbenzene) to access Schwarz P/gyroid phases with target lattice parameter 25–40 nm. Spin-coat at 2000–3000 rpm in 40–45% RH, 22–25 °C. Thermally anneal at 80 °C for 10 min to equilibrate the mesophase. Expected neck size: 5–12 nm after infiltration and shrinkage.
1.2 Sol–gel infiltration and shrinkage control: Infiltrate with an anhydrous ethanol solution containing (i) methyltriethoxysilane (MTES) as the backbone, (ii) 3-aminophenyltriethoxysilane and 4-aminobenzyltriethoxysilane (molar ratio MTES:amine-silane = 7:3), and (iii) 2 mol% bis-silane crosslinker. Water content fixed at H2O:Si = 1.2; acid catalysis with 0.01 M acetic acid. Condense at 60 °C for 30 min. Expected linear shrinkage ≤18%, yielding final TPMS thickness 20–60 nm.
1.3 Template removal and interface compatibility: Remove BCP by selective extraction in ethanol/THF (9:1) at 40 °C for 15 min. Verify no SnO2 etching (XPS Sn 3d) and no perovskite exposure at this step (TPMS fabricated only on SnO2 or on completed perovskite using orthogonal solvents). RMS roughness tolerance: <5 nm over 5 µm AFM scan to avoid shunting.
1.4 Electrical continuity and contact resistance: Lightly infiltrate (≤10 vol% pore filling) with the adjacent transport material (SnO2 sol for n–i–p or C60 by thermal evaporation) to ensure electronic percolation across the TPMS without blocking pores. Measure contact resistance by TLM; target Rc < 0.5 Ω·cm².

2. Geometry-resolved modeling and validation (mandatory mechanistic closure).
2.1 3D geometry reconstruction: Acquire electron tomography of TPMS interlayers (voxel size ≤2 nm). Reconstruct realistic meshes for Schwarz P and flat controls.
2.2 Finite-element simulations: Solve Poisson + drift–diffusion equations on reconstructed geometries to map electric-field magnitude, recombination rate sensitivity, and carrier extraction vs curvature and SSA. Include experimentally measured dielectric constants and trap densities. Output quantitative metrics: field variance (σ_E), local recombination enhancement factor, and effective contact resistance.
2.3 Experimental validation: Correlate modeled Rc and σ_E with TLM, impedance spectroscopy under bias, and Mott–Schottky analysis.

3. Chemically selective oxidative coupling with hard stop-criteria.
3.1 Amine design and selectivity: Use predominantly aromatic amines (aniline/benzylamine) with oxidation potentials 0.3–0.5 V lower than iodide oxidation, plus 5 mol% sterically hindered diamine to limit over-crosslinking.
3.2 Oxidative protocol: Pre-form a sparse imine network using trace O2 (10–50 ppm) under 1-sun illumination for 5–10 min, or 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁴ M ammonium persulfate in an orthogonal solvent followed by vacuum drying. During operation, rely only on photo-generated ROS.
3.3 Selectivity controls: Measure rate constants for amine→imine vs perovskite/SnO2/C60 oxidation on model films using in-situ FTIR and XPS. Hard stop-criteria: no detectable Pb⁰/PbOₓ growth (<1% XPS sensitivity), no iodide depletion by ToF-SIMS depth profiling after treatment.
3.4 Electronic impact assessment: Track band offsets (UPS/KPFM) and trap formation (DLTS/TRPL). Abort condition: emergence of new deep traps (>10¹⁵ cm⁻³).

4. Redefined utilization ratio with spatial calibration.
4.1 Site tagging: Incorporate 15N-labeled amines (20%) or F-tagged analogues. Use angle-resolved XPS and ToF-SIMS to spatially locate total vs reacted sites.
4.2 Quantitative definition: Utilization ratio = (number of tagged sites participating in defect passivation or radical quenching, inferred from proportional reduction in interfacial recombination velocity and EPR radical decay constant) / (total tagged sites present at the interface).
4.3 Calibration experiments: Systematically cap 25%, 50%, 75% of amines with inert acyl groups and demonstrate linear scaling between active-site fraction and implied Voc / EPR decay.

5. Device integration, yield, and failure modes.
5.1 Thickness/penetration limits: Confirm perovskite penetration into TPMS <5 nm by cross-sectional ToF-SIMS.
5.2 Yield analysis: Fabricate ≥30 devices per condition over 1 cm²; track shunt incidence and FF spread.
5.3 Stability testing: ISOS-L-2, ISOS-O-2, and 85 °C thermal aging correlated with EPR and chemical signatures.
Feasibility: This revised plan directly addresses the reviewers’ feasibility and mechanistic concerns. (i) The TPMS fabrication route is now bounded by explicit BCP molecular weights, solvent systems, humidity, condensation chemistry, shrinkage limits, and roughness tolerances, with defined strategies (partial transport-layer infiltration and TLM validation) to ensure electrical continuity and low series resistance. (ii) Geometry-resolved electrostatic and drift–diffusion modeling on reconstructed TPMS meshes replaces qualitative curvature arguments, yielding testable predictions for field variance, recombination sensitivity, and contact resistance that are experimentally validated. (iii) The oxidative coupling strategy is de-risked by a selectivity-first design: aromatic amines with favorable oxidation potentials, ultralow oxidant chemical potential, and explicit stop-criteria based on Pb/iodide speciation ensure that amine-to-imine formation kinetically outcompetes deleterious oxidation pathways. (iv) The utilization ratio is redefined with isotopic/elemental tagging, spatial localization, and site-blocking calibration, preventing narrative flexibility and enabling stoichiometric closure. Collectively, these refinements transform the concept from an ambitious architectural idea into a quantitatively constrained, manufacturable interfacial strategy aligned with high-efficiency PSC process windows.
Critique: This is an unusually detailed and disciplined proposal that substantially exceeds the typical architectural-passivation narrative in PSC interfaces. Engineering resolution is high: the TPMS fabrication window, shrinkage control, electrical percolation strategy, and failure thresholds are explicitly bounded, reducing execution ambiguity. Logical consistency is strong overall, particularly in the closure between curvature-induced field homogenization and reduced recombination/ion-migration; however, the causal separation between electrostatic homogenization and increased chemical utilization occasionally blurs, and the proposal assumes additive benefits without fully interrogating potential antagonism (e.g., increased SSA vs. ionic accessibility). Evidence grounding is solid and remains within perovskite/interfacial chemistry without conceptual drift, though the oxidative selectivity claims rely heavily on assumed kinetic hierarchies that, while plausible, are not yet benchmarked against known halide-rich radical environments. Rationale quality is high: the redefinition of utilization ratio with spatial and stoichiometric calibration is genuinely creative and addresses a recognized bottleneck in passivation research. Minor deductions reflect residual risk in oxidative chemistry control and the manufacturability of BCP-derived TPMS at scale.

Hypothesis: Embedding a MOF-derived, Schwarz P surface (bicontinuous negative-Gaussian-curvature) single-atom catalytic interlayer between the perovskite absorber and electron-transport layer will simultaneously (i) suppress interfacial non-radiative recombination and ion-migration-driven degradation and (ii) enable controllable electrochemical redox buffering measurable via half-wave potential shifts, thereby increasing Voc, FF, and operational stability. The methodological adaptation is to repurpose the Schwarz P bicontinuous architecture—originally used to maximize utilization of FeN4 active sites and raise ORR half-wave potential—into an ultrathin, electronically percolating interphase that couples (a) curvature-enhanced charge extraction and field homogenization, (b) Lewis-acid/base defect passivation through coordinatively unsaturated metal nodes, and (c) redox-stable single-atom centers whose half-wave potential is tuned to sit outside the perovskite operating Fermi-level window, preventing parasitic interfacial redox while still buffering transient charge and halide radicals.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a benchmark high-performance perovskite stack (e.g., n–i–p: FTO/SnO2/perovskite/Spiro-OMeTAD/Au and p–i–n: ITO/NiOx/perovskite/C60/BCP/Ag) using a mixed-cation perovskite (FA-Cs, I/Br) to ensure state-of-the-art baseline PCE.
1.2 Define the interlayer target: 5–20 nm thickness, continuous bicontinuous channels, and electronically connected to ETL (or HTL in inverted) without introducing deep traps.
1.3 Prepare methane/biogas-relevant test atmospheres (dry CH4, CO2/CH4 mixtures, and humid CO2/CH4) for stability stress tests to evaluate whether the interlayer mitigates gas- and moisture-accelerated interfacial degradation.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Schwarz P template-to-interlayer conversion (methodological adaptation):
- Synthesize polymer cubosome templates that encode a Schwarz P minimal surface; infiltrate with a MOF precursor solution to form a conformal MOF network along the bicontinuous template.
- Convert the MOF/template composite into a MOF-derived N-doped carbon/metal-node hybrid with isolated single-atom M–N4 sites (M = Fe or Co) while preserving bicontinuous Schwarz P morphology (controlled pyrolysis with curvature-preserving ramp + sacrificial template removal).
- Post-functionalize residual metal nodes/defects with perovskite-compatible Lewis base groups (e.g., pyridine/thiophene-like moieties) via vapor-phase infiltration to avoid solvent damage to perovskite.
2.2 Half-wave-potential-guided interlayer energetics design:
- Use rotating disk electrode (RDE) electrochemistry on interlayer films to measure half-wave potential (E1/2) for a chosen redox probe and/or ORR surrogate; tune M identity, coordination environment, and N-doping to shift E1/2 so that the interlayer is redox-inert across the perovskite device operating electrochemical potential range (minimizing interfacial redox degradation).
- Implement a compositional series (Fe–N4, Co–N4, and mixed Fe/Co–N4; plus metal-free N-doped Schwarz P carbon) to decouple curvature vs. redox contributions.
2.3 Device integration:
- Deposit the Schwarz P interlayer by gentle, orthogonal processing (e.g., dry transfer/lamination or low-polarity dispersions with rapid evaporation) onto the ETL (or perovskite surface depending on stack) and complete PSC fabrication.
- For comparison, fabricate controls: (i) no interlayer, (ii) non-bicontinuous flat carbon/M–N4 layer, (iii) MOF-derived hollow carbon spheres (MOF-templated but not Schwarz P), and (iv) conventional molecular passivators.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Optoelectronic validation (mechanism: recombination/passivation):
- Quantify Voc gains via quasi-Fermi level splitting (absolute PL and QFLS mapping) and time-resolved PL; correlate with reduced non-radiative recombination at the interface.
- Perform impedance spectroscopy and intensity-dependent JV to separate transport, recombination, and interfacial capacitance changes attributed to the bicontinuous interlayer.
3.2 Structural/chemical validation (mechanism: defect coordination + ion blocking):
- Use XPS/UPS to confirm band alignment and chemical coordination (Pb–N, Pb–O, halide–metal interactions) and to measure interfacial dipole changes.
- Track ion migration using TOF-SIMS depth profiling (I−/Br−/MA+/FA+/Cs+), thermal bias stressing, and Kelvin probe force microscopy under illumination to test whether the Schwarz P interlayer reduces field hotspots and ion accumulation.
3.3 Half-wave potential as a predictive stability descriptor (mechanism: redox buffering vs parasitic redox):
- Establish a correlation between interlayer E1/2 and operational stability (MPP tracking at 65–85 °C, 1 sun, controlled O2/H2O/CH4/CO2 atmospheres). Hypothesis test: interlayers with E1/2 tuned away from device operating potentials show lower interfacial redox signatures (EPR for radicals, in situ Raman for iodide/iodine species).
3.4 Methane/biogas-relevant robustness:
- Expose completed devices to CH4 and CO2/CH4 mixtures with controlled humidity and trace H2S (ppm-level, optional) to emulate biogas; quantify PCE retention, Voc drift, and interfacial chemistry evolution. Evaluate whether the MOF-derived interlayer acts as a gas/moisture diffusion modulator without sacrificing charge extraction.
3.5 Scale-up check:
- Demonstrate coating/transfer on ≥25 cm2 substrates; evaluate uniformity (photoluminescence imaging, sheet resistance) and module-relevant metrics (aperture-area PCE, interconnect losses).
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Schwarz P bicontinuous architectures are empirically linked to higher electrocatalytic activity and elevated half-wave potential through enhanced active-site utilization and curvature-driven lowering of reaction barriers; MOF-templated hollow/carbonized structures are established routes to produce M–N–C catalysts with high E1/2. Translating these principles to PSC interfaces is feasible because PSC performance is strongly limited by interfacial recombination, ion migration, and interfacial redox/chemical instability.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The adapted interlayer is not used as an ORR catalyst in the PSC; instead, E1/2 becomes a tunable descriptor for interfacial redox inertness/buffering. The Schwarz P morphology provides a continuous, thin, high-surface-area contact that improves electronic percolation and homogenizes local electric fields, while MOF-derived coordinatively unsaturated sites and N-rich motifs passivate under-coordinated Pb2+ and halide vacancies.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to flat passivation molecules or non-bicontinuous carbons, the Schwarz P interlayer offers (i) curvature-enabled bicontinuous charge pathways with minimal thickness penalty, (ii) a higher density of accessible passivation/coordination sites without blocking transport, and (iii) a quantifiable, electrochemically measurable tuning knob (half-wave potential) to engineer interfacial redox stability. Relative to conventional MOF additives dispersed in perovskite, an engineered interphase localizes functionality where degradation is most severe and can be implemented as a scalable coating/transfer step compatible with large-area fabrication.
Critique: This is an unusually deep and technically ambitious proposal with strong mechanistic intent. The engineering plan is largely credible, particularly the compositional series and control matrix to decouple curvature, chemistry, and redox effects. However, two issues weaken full confidence: (i) preservation and defect-free transfer of a 5–20 nm Schwarz P bicontinuous architecture onto a delicate perovskite interface is nontrivial and under-justified experimentally, and (ii) the conceptual leap from ORR half-wave potential measured by RDE to a predictive descriptor of PSC interfacial redox stability, while intriguing, lacks a clear quantitative mapping to the perovskite quasi-Fermi-level landscape. The methane/biogas angle is interesting but partially tangential; CH4 is chemically inert toward perovskites, so its role risks appearing as an environmental stress proxy rather than a chemically motivated degradation pathway unless more rigorously justified.

Hypothesis:
An ultrathin, percolative Cu3(HHTP)2 or Ni3(HHTP)2 conductive-MOF (c‑MOF) nanonetwork grown by surfactant-confined, low-temperature interfacial synthesis at the buried perovskite/transport-layer contact will improve Voc and operational stability primarily through coordination-driven defect passivation and selective charge extraction, and—under explicitly defined PV-relevant transient high-irradiance stress—secondarily through ultrafast third-order nonlinear optical (χ(3)) response that suppresses hot-carrier–driven interfacial damage.

Mechanistic rationale (tightly bounded to reviewer critique):
1) Interface chemistry (dominant under 1-sun CW): catecholate O donors in HHTP chelate undercoordinated Pb2+ and interact with halide-vacancy-rich motifs, reducing surface recombination velocity and non-radiative losses; concurrently, the π-conjugated 2D MOF plane and metal–catecholate nodes provide electronically percolative extraction pathways and a tunable interfacial dipole that improves contact selectivity without introducing an insulating barrier.
2) PV-relevant stress scenario where χ(3) can matter: PSCs in the field and in module operation experience short, high-irradiance excursions that can locally exceed steady-state 1-sun due to (i) specular “sun-glint” and reflective focusing from nearby glass/metal surfaces and module frames, (ii) arc/partial-discharge events in strings and connectors producing ms–µs optical bursts, and (iii) manufacturing/inspection exposures (class-1–3R alignment lasers; LiDAR/ToF sources; pulsed indoor LED drivers) that can deliver kW–MW·cm−2 peak intensities in µs–fs windows on localized areas. While rare, these events are disproportionate drivers of interfacial hot-carrier spikes, local heating (ΔT), and accelerated ion-migration-assisted degradation at already defect-rich buried contacts.
3) χ(3) pathway (activated only during transients): the c‑MOF’s large χ(3) (manifesting as nonlinear absorption β and Kerr coefficient n2) introduces intensity-dependent loss and phase response at the interface, effectively clamping transient carrier generation near the contact and accelerating carrier/phonon dephasing (reduced hot-carrier lifetime and peak carrier temperature). This reduces the amplitude of the transient quasi-Fermi-level/field overshoot that otherwise increases interfacial recombination, local Joule heating, and defect formation. The proposal explicitly tests whether measured β/n2 at PV-relevant wavelengths and pulse widths quantitatively reduces (a) peak interfacial carrier temperature (ΔTe), (b) peak ΔT in the first 10–50 nm near the contact, and (c) the rate constant for a chosen degradation proxy (Voc loss rate under combined bias/light stress with superimposed pulses).

Critical boundary conditions to avoid over-claiming: under pure 1-sun CW without transient spikes, χ(3) is not expected to measurably contribute; thus, success criteria for the χ(3) novelty are defined only under the specified transient-stress protocol and must be supported by ultrafast spectroscopy at the buried interface plus a degradation-rate correlation.
Plan:
A. Device stacks, controls, and interlayer acceptance criteria (defined up-front)
A1. Baseline stacks (two architectures to generalize interface physics):
- n–i–p: glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA,Cs)Pb(I,Br)3/HTL/Au.
- p–i–n: glass/ITO/PTAA/(FA,Cs)Pb(I,Br)3/C60/BCP/Ag.
A2. Perovskite surface termination control: generate iodide-rich vs PbI2-rich terminations by (i) slight precursor stoichiometry offsets (±1–2% PbI2), (ii) antisolvent timing shifts, and (iii) brief post-anneal variations. Baseline mapping: XPS (Pb 4f, I 3d), UPS, KPFM, absolute PLQY, and TRPL.
A3. Hard acceptance criteria for the c‑MOF interlayer (go/no-go gates):
- Added contact resistivity (ρc) from TLM or J–V/Rs extraction: ≤ 0.5 Ω·cm2 (stretch goal ≤ 0.2 Ω·cm2).
- Work-function (WF) shift window by UPS/KPFM: |ΔWF| ≤ 0.30 eV unless accompanied by improved selectivity (verified by reduced leakage current and improved ideality factor).
- Optical parasitics: ΔJsc loss from transmission/reflection modeling + EQE ≤ 0.3 mA·cm−2.
- Physical thickness/percolation: effective thickness 1–5 nm, surface coverage 30–80% (percolative but not blocking), verified by cross-sectional HR-TEM/EDX, AFM step-height on masked samples, and GIWAXS for 2D ordering.
- If any criterion fails: branch to (i) reduced coverage, (ii) alternate metal node (redox-inert MOF), or (iii) organic conjugated reference (see C3).

B. Surfactant-confined interfacial synthesis (methodological specificity and residue control)
B1. Design principle: confine MOF nucleation to an ultrathin 2D network while preventing bulk crystallites and avoiding perovskite dissolution.
B2. Surfactant templating parameters (explicit):
- Non-ionic amphiphile: Brij-58 or Triton X-100.
- Concentration: 0.05–0.20× CMC (sub-CMC) to form patchy/lamellar adsorption without micellar solubilization of perovskite organics.
- Deposition: dynamic spin-coating (e.g., 2000–4000 rpm, 20–40 s) of surfactant solution in anhydrous IPA:EA (70:30 v/v) with water ≤0.1 vol%.
- Residue removal: two-step rinse (anhydrous IPA then EA), followed by 60–80 °C vacuum bake (10–20 min). Residue check: ATR-FTIR (C–O–C bands), XPS C 1s deconvolution; acceptance: surfactant signal ≤5% of initial adlayer.
B3. MOF growth chemistry (perovskite-compatible window):
- Metal precursor: Cu(OAc)2 or Ni(OAc)2 at 0.5–2 mM in IPA:EA with water ≤0.1 vol%.
- Ligand: HHTP (2,3,6,7,10,11-hexahydroxytriphenylene) at 0.2–1 mM in EA with minimal base.
- Volatile base: triethylamine (TEA) 0.5–2 mM equivalent in vapor-assisted or trace liquid dosing; objective pH-equivalent: sufficient to partially deprotonate catechols while avoiding perovskite etching.
- Confined growth: sequential dosing (metal then ligand) with a 10–60 s reaction window at room temperature; quench by immediate rinse.
- Ultrasound: optional, only for precursor stock pre-mixing (not directly on perovskite) to avoid mechanical damage; if used during deposition, limit to <1 W·cm−2 equivalent, <10 s.
- Mild anneal: ≤90 °C, 5–10 min in N2.
B4. Percolation tuning knobs:
- Control surface coverage via (i) surfactant concentration, (ii) total precursor dose (mM·s), (iii) sequential cycle number (1–3 cycles).
- Target: sheet-like domains with lateral size 20–200 nm, forming a connected network but leaving transport-layer wetting intact.

C. Active-site engineering with bounded risk (avoid midgap states)
C1. Replace the original “co-ligand dilution to create unsaturated nodes” with a bounded, spectroscopy-gated strategy:
- Primary mode: pristine HHTP-MOF (no intentional unsaturation) as the default.
- Secondary mode (only if needed for binding density): introduce 1–3 mol% of a redox-inert, sterically hindered catechol analog (e.g., alkyl-substituted catechol) to modulate nucleation and binding density rather than creating open metal sites.
C2. Spectroscopic gating (must pass before devices):
- Sub-gap absorption/photothermal deflection spectroscopy (PDS) and UPS: no new deep sub-gap features >10% increase vs control.
- Time-resolved PL and absolute PLQY: QFLS must increase or remain unchanged; if QFLS decreases, abandon co-ligand approach.
C3. Mandatory redox-inert and “electronically similar” references beyond Zn:
- Redox-inert conductive MOF alternative: a Mg/Al-based catecholate-like framework is likely non-conductive; therefore use a two-pronged reference set:
  (i) A redox-inert, fully conjugated organic interlayer with strong Pb–O binding and π-system (e.g., a catechol-terminated oligothiophene or triphenylamine-catechol SAM/polymer) matched to similar thickness and optical density.
  (ii) A c‑MOF with less redox-active node chemistry relative to Cu/Ni: e.g., a Ni-based vs Cu-based comparison plus a metal-free conjugated covalent network (2D COF) thin interlayer where feasible, to separate “conjugation/percolation” from “metal redox.”

D. Quantifying χ(3) under PV-relevant transient scenarios + order-of-magnitude modeling
D1. Define the PV-relevant transient illumination protocol (two tiers):
- Tier-1 (module/field-like microsecond–millisecond bursts): superimpose high-intensity LED/laser diode pulses (e.g., 405/532/808 nm) with pulse width 1–1000 µs, duty cycle ≤1%, peak irradiance 10–200 suns equivalent on a 0.1–1 mm spot to emulate hot-spot/glint/arc optical bursts; keep average power near 1 sun.
- Tier-2 (inspection/laser exposure femto–nano pulses): 1030 nm or 800 nm pulses, 100 fs–10 ps, spot 50–200 µm, fluence adjusted below ablation but high enough to probe nonlinearities (device-safe window determined empirically).
D2. Measure β, n2, χ(3) on complete perovskite/interlayer/transport stacks (not standalone films):
- Open/closed aperture Z-scan at 532, 808, 1030 nm on representative buried-interface stacks on glass.
- Pump–probe reflectance/transmittance under device-like layering to extract intensity-dependent absorption and refractive index changes.
D3. Minimal quantitative link (order-of-magnitude) from β to reduced transient heating:
- Use Beer–Lambert with nonlinear absorption: dI/dz = −αI − βI^2.
- For a transient spike with peak intensity I0 at the interface, the incremental absorbed energy density in the first δ (10–50 nm) is ΔU ≈ ∫0^δ (αI + βI^2) dz × τpulse.
- If β<0 (saturable absorption/bleaching) or if the effective nonlinear response clamps I in the perovskite near the interface (via interlayer absorption/dispersion), predict a reduced ΔU in the perovskite and lower ΔT = ΔU/(ρCp). The sign and magnitude will be determined experimentally; the proposal will not assume bleaching vs RSA a priori.
- Map ΔT(t) into an Arrhenius acceleration factor for an interfacial degradation proxy kdeg ∝ exp(−Ea/kBT) (Ea extracted from separate temperature-accelerated tests). The goal is to show that the measured nonlinear response changes peak T by even a few K during spikes, producing a measurable change in kdeg under repeated bursts.
D4. Define a degradation-rate metric tied to the transient protocol:
- Track ΔVoc/Δt and ΔPLQY/Δt under ISOS-L-2-like bias+light at 65 °C with superimposed Tier-1 pulses; compare slopes with/without c‑MOF at matched initial Voc.

E. Mandatory ultrafast evidence at the buried interface (causality)
E1. Ultrafast transient absorption (TA) with interface sensitivity:
- Use front/back excitation geometries and selective probing to emphasize the buried interface (e.g., excite through transport layer if transparent; compare with excitation through glass).
- Extract hot-carrier cooling time constants and band-edge bleach recovery; acceptance: c‑MOF must reduce hot-carrier lifetime or reduce peak hot-carrier signature amplitude under high-fluence excitation without degrading low-fluence carrier lifetime.
E2. Terahertz (TRTS) or time-resolved microwave conductivity (TRMC):
- Quantify sub-ps to ns photoconductivity and momentum scattering time (proxy for dephasing).
- Acceptance: faster early-time decay (dephasing) plus equal or improved long-time extraction (in device-relevant stacks).
E3. Correlate ultrafast metrics to degradation:
- Across a small matrix (no interlayer / organic conjugated reference / Ni-MOF / Cu-MOF), correlate (i) hot-carrier lifetime reduction and/or peak photoconductivity suppression under spikes with (ii) reduced ΔVoc/Δt under superimposed-pulse aging.

F. Standard interface passivation/extraction validation (anchored, not optional)
F1. Energetics and passivation:
- Absolute PLQY → QFLS; compare QFLS–Voc (non-radiative voltage loss).
- UPS/KPFM band alignment, dipole formation.
- XPS for Pb–O coordination signatures; ToF-SIMS depth profiles for Cu/Ni/HHTP distribution.
F2. Recombination/extraction kinetics:
- TPV/TPC, EIS (recombination resistance, chemical capacitance), Suns-Voc, ideality factor vs intensity.
- Series resistance/contact selectivity: dark J–V, S-shaped curve screening, TLM on dedicated test structures.

G. De-risk Cu/Ni electrochemistry and diffusion (mandatory operando/after-stress diagnostics)
G1. Operando or quasi-operando bias+illumination spectroscopy:
- Near-ambient-pressure XPS (NAP-XPS) or operando XAS (Cu/Ni K-edge) under applied bias and illumination to detect oxidation state shifts indicative of redox shuttling.
- If operando is unavailable: staged bias+light exposures with rapid transfer to XPS/XAS (glovebox-integrated transfer).
G2. Metal diffusion/catalysis checks:
- ICP-MS of dissolved layers after selective etch; ToF-SIMS depth profiling pre/post stress (ISOS-L-2 and pulsed protocol).
- Acceptance: no measurable Cu/Ni migration into perovskite beyond detection threshold or a predefined limit (e.g., <10^19 atoms·cm−3 equivalent in the perovskite bulk region, adjusted to instrument sensitivity).
G3. Chemical stability controls:
- Monitor iodide oxidation/catalysis signatures: XPS I oxidation states, UV–vis changes, and any emergence of iodine-related species after stress.
- If redox activity observed: pivot to Ni-only (if Cu problematic) or to conjugated organic reference as the primary “χ(3) + passivation” platform.

H. Statistics and deliverables
- Device batches: n≥20 per condition; report stabilized PCE (MPP tracking), hysteresis index, Voc distribution.
- Deliverable 1: passivation/extraction benefit under CW 1-sun (baseline claim).
- Deliverable 2 (novelty claim): under defined transient protocol, demonstrate reduced degradation rate with quantitative linkage: measured β/n2/χ(3) + ultrafast dephasing/hot-carrier suppression + reduced ΔVoc/Δt.

Decision tree (explicit go/no-go)
- If Rs/ρc exceeds threshold or S-kink appears → reduce coverage/thickness; if persists → abandon c‑MOF for organic conjugated reference.
- If Cu shows diffusion/redox signatures → switch to Ni-only and/or redox-inert conjugated reference; repeat stability.
