- If χ(3) measurable but no ultrafast or aging correlation → restrict claims to passivation/extraction only; χ(3) becomes a characterization side-result, not a central novelty.
Feasibility:
1) Why the χ(3) angle is now PV-relevant (anchored scenario): The revised plan no longer assumes χ(3) matters under steady 1-sun. Instead, it targets quantified short-duration, high-irradiance excursions (glint/hot-spot optical bursts, arc events, inspection/laser exposures, pulsed indoor drivers) that can create localized carrier and temperature spikes at buried interfaces—precisely where defect density and ion migration sensitivity are highest. This is the only regime where intensity-dependent absorption/dispersion can plausibly produce a measurable benefit.

2) Quantitative causality is built in: β and n2 will be measured on device-relevant stacks and inserted into a minimal absorption/heating model (nonlinear Beer–Lambert + ΔT estimation). The proposal then tests whether the predicted reduction in peak ΔT/ΔTe correlates with a directly measured reduction in degradation rate (ΔVoc/Δt) under an ISOS-like baseline plus superimposed pulses. This addresses the reviewer’s demand that Z-scan outputs map onto a device-relevant kinetic consequence.

3) Direct ultrafast evidence at the buried interface is mandatory: TA + TRTS/TRMC on layered stacks will quantify hot-carrier cooling/dephasing and early-time photoconductivity changes specifically attributable to the c‑MOF. The novelty claim is accepted only if these ultrafast signatures correlate with slower degradation under the transient protocol.

4) Electrochemical and diffusion risks are explicitly de-risked: Cu/Ni redox activity and diffusion are treated as primary failure modes. Operando/quasi-operando XPS/XAS plus ToF-SIMS/ICP-MS post-stress are included with explicit acceptance limits. A broader redox-inert, electronically similar reference set (conjugated organic interlayer; alternative conjugated network) ensures that any observed benefit can be separated from unintended metal-catalyzed chemistry.

5) Interlayer engineering is bounded by device constraints: The proposal specifies thickness (1–5 nm), percolation/coverage targets, WF shift windows, maximum allowed contact resistance, and optical-loss limits, all verified by cross-sectional TEM/EDX, GIWAXS, UPS/KPFM, TLM, and EQE. A go/no-go decision tree prevents over-optimization loops and ensures the interlayer cannot “win” by adding series resistance or parasitic absorption.

6) Interface-chemistry plausibility remains strong: Independent of χ(3), Pb–O chelation and defect passivation by oxygen-rich catecholate ligands are well-aligned with known perovskite defect chemistry. The c‑MOF adds percolative conductivity and tunable interfacial dipoles—addressing a common weakness of insulating passivators—while the surfactant-confined growth strategy is explicitly designed to avoid bulk crystallites and to minimize chemical damage/residue on sensitive perovskite surfaces.
Critique: This is an unusually rigorous and over-constrained proposal that demonstrates strong command of both perovskite interface physics and nonlinear optical materials. Engineering resolution is high: synthesis parameters, acceptance criteria, diagnostics, and failure pivots are defined with rare precision. Logical consistency is strong but not flawless: while the χ(3)-mediated mitigation of transient interfacial damage is carefully bounded, the causal chain from measured β/n2 to materially significant ΔT or ΔTe reduction under realistic PV transient events remains ambitious and may yield marginal signal-to-noise. The proposal mitigates this risk with ultrafast spectroscopy and degradation-rate correlation, but the physical leverage of χ(3) at nm-scale interlayers is still near the lower bound of plausibility. Evidence grounding is solid: the concept chain is largely respected, though terms like 'mode-locking' appear only metaphorically and are not physically instantiated in the device context, slightly weakening conceptual tightness. Rationale quality is high: the work directly targets a known bottleneck (buried-interface instability under non-ideal illumination) with a structurally novel combination of conductive MOF passivation and transient nonlinear optical clamping, while explicitly avoiding over-claiming under 1-sun CW operation.

Hypothesis:
A low-temperature (≤70 °C substrate) sublimation–vapor phase pseudomorphic transformation (SVPT) of an ultrathin NiFe–LDH seed on mixed-halide FA/Cs perovskite can yield a conformal, electronically benign interlayer whose *function is conditional on its verified material identity*. We hypothesize two mutually exclusive, pre-registered outcomes with distinct, falsifiable mechanisms:

(A) **Crystalline Ni/Fe–imidazolate framework (true MOF) outcome**: If GIWAXS indexing and TEM/SAED confirm an oriented Ni/Fe–imidazolate lattice (or a known/topologically assignable Ni–imidazolate with Fe substitution) at 1–5 nm thickness, then (i) under-coordinated Pb2+ and halide-vacancy-adjacent Pb will be passivated primarily by N-donor coordination (Pb–N) from imidazolate, producing measurable Pb 4f / N 1s chemical shifts and a correlated increase in quasi-Fermi level splitting (QFLS) and Voc; (ii) ionic motion (I− and A-site cations) will be suppressed by a reduction in the *effective interfacial diffusion coefficient* (Deff) under bias due to a continuous, rigid, nanoporosity-controlled barrier plus strengthened surface binding that lowers vacancy-mediated exchange; (iii) any claimed piezotronic benefit will be treated as a **separate hypothesis test** and is only expected if the converted layer is demonstrably non-centrosymmetric (SHG-positive and polar-domain PFM with consistent phase), producing an interfacial field of order 10^5–10^6 V m−1 under realistic device strain (≤0.1%), sufficient to cause a strain-correlated, contact-resistance-independent modulation of nonradiative recombination.

(B) **Amorphous metal–imidazolate/oxyhydroxide hybrid outcome (pivot)**: If SVPT yields an amorphous or poorly indexed Ni/Fe–imidazolate hybrid (no definitive MOF peaks; diffuse GIWAXS; local M–N/M–O coordination by XAS/XPS), we explicitly pivot the claim: the layer functions as a *metal–imidazolate coordination glass* where (i) passivation is dominated by Pb–N adducts and residual M–OH anchoring that increases surface formation energy for halide vacancies; (ii) ionic suppression is expected mainly from increased activation energy for ion exchange at the top interface (measurable from temperature-dependent drift/diffusion), rather than strict “size-selective” sieving; and (iii) piezotronics is not expected unless SHG indicates polar order.

Across both outcomes, Ni/Fe redox chemistry is treated as a risk: the interlayer is only viable if it does not catalyze iodide oxidation, does not inject deep traps, and does not produce an extraction barrier. Therefore, we hypothesize that a *chemically buffered* Ni:Fe ratio and controlled partial conversion (retaining ≤30% interfacial –OH spectral signature) will keep the work-function shift within ±0.2 eV and suppress formation of I3−/I2 signatures under stress, while maintaining or improving interfacial recombination velocity.

Primary ranked mechanism: **chemical passivation (Pb–N) → reduced interfacial recombination → Voc/QFLS gain**. Secondary: **ionic suppression quantified by Deff reduction**. Tertiary: **piezotronics only if symmetry criteria are met**.
Plan:
0) Pre-registration: go/no-go material specification and decision tree (before device claims)
   - Target thickness: 1.0–3.0 nm equivalent (ellipsometry/XRR on witness, cross-section TEM on device).
   - Continuity: ≥95% areal coverage with no pinholes >20 nm (plan-view HAADF-STEM + automated defect counting; conductive-AFM leakage map).
   - Composition window: Ni:Fe = 3:1 and 1:1 (ICP-MS on witness; XPS quantification), N content confirming imidazolate uptake (N 1s present with imidazolate component).
   - Phase identity go/no-go:
     (A) “MOF confirmed” if GIWAXS shows indexable Bragg peaks to a known/assignable Ni–imidazolate(-like) framework with preferred orientation and corroborated by TEM/SAED; OR
     (B) “Hybrid confirmed” if no indexable peaks but XAS/XPS shows M–N coordination and stable amorphous network.
   - If neither (no M–N; only oxyhydroxide): STOP (no passivation claim) and revise ligand delivery/chemistry.

1) Baseline device and surface standardization
   1.1 Device stack (n–i–p): glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA0.83Cs0.17)Pb(I0.83Br0.17)3 (~600 nm)/interlayer/HTL/Au.
   1.2 Perovskite top-surface conditioning to reduce uncontrolled termination variability:
       - Mild vacuum anneal (≤60 °C, 30 min) to desorb residual solvent.
       - Optional very dilute alkylammonium halide rinse (orthogonal, e.g., isopropanol with <1 mM FAI) as a *standardized* halide-rich termination; must be applied to all arms equally if used.
   1.3 Baseline characterization (before interlayer): XPS (Pb 4f, I 3d, Br 3d, N 1s), UPS/KPFM (work function), PL/TRPL/QFLS.

2) NiFe–LDH seed deposition (ultrathin and perovskite-safe)
   2.1 Deposition route: cyclic chemisorption (ALD-like) at ≤60–80 °C in dry N2 glovebox load-lock:
       - Cycle: brief exposure to ethanolic Ni(NO3)2 + Fe(NO3)3 (total metal 1–5 mM), purge, then mild base vapor (NH3 or urea decomposition in separated zone) to form hydroxide; repeat 1–5 cycles.
       - Thickness calibration: AFM step-height on masked witness + XRR.
   2.2 Seed controls: Ni-only LDH, Fe-only LDH, and inert ultrathin Al2O3 (~1 nm) as a barrier-only reference.

3) SVPT-on-perovskite with 2-methylimidazole (2-MIM): de-risked conversion mapping
   3.1 Reactor: sealed mini-reactor compatible with glovebox; independent T control of source and substrate; pressure control 10–200 mbar.
   3.2 Conversion matrix (DoE):
       - Source T: 90, 110, 130 °C.
       - Substrate T: 45, 60, 70 °C.
       - Time: 5, 15, 30 min.
       - Pulsed flux variant: 2 min on / 2 min off to limit deep diffusion.
   3.3 Partial conversion target: retain interfacial –OH signature ≤30% of initial LDH OH peak area (O 1s deconvolution) while maximizing M–N (N 1s imidazolate component).
   3.4 Hydrophobicity add-on (only after identity established): brief second vapor step (2-MIM + 5–10 mol% fluorinated imidazole) at same substrate T for 2–5 min; objective: increase water contact angle without increasing thickness >0.5 nm.

4) Material identity verification (mandatory before interpreting device gains)
   4.1 GIWAXS/GIXRD: identify peaks; quantify orientation factor; compare to candidate Ni–imidazolate references and simulated patterns.
   4.2 TEM/SAED (cross-section + plan-view): confirm nanosheet/lamellar preservation vs amorphous layer; map thickness/continuity.
   4.3 XPS/ToF-SIMS: confirm imidazolate incorporation (N 1s), metal distribution, and absence of excessive metal diffusion into perovskite.
   4.4 XAS (Ni/Fe K-edge on witness films): oxidation state and coordination (M–N vs M–O); screen for redox changes after light/heat bias.

5) Passivation mechanism: quantitative binding prediction + correlation
   5.1 DFT (or high-level cluster calculations if periodic MOF uncertain): compute binding energies of 2-MIM/imidazolate to representative perovskite surface motifs (PbI2-terminated, FA/halide-terminated, iodide-vacancy-adjacent Pb). Predict core-level shifts (qualitative) and interfacial dipole direction.
   5.2 Experimental binding metrics:
       - XPS: Pb 4f shift and emergence of Pb–N component; N 1s coordination shift.
       - UPS/KPFM: work-function and valence-level shifts; define acceptable band shift window: |ΔWF| ≤ 0.2 eV; otherwise flag as transport-risk.
   5.3 Designed correlation series:
       - Vary N uptake systematically (controlled by SVPT dose) at fixed thickness.
       - Plot QFLS and Voc vs Pb–N fraction (XPS) to establish causality; require monotonic correlation to validate passivation claim.

6) Ion migration suppression: replace “size-selective pores” with measurable Deff under bias
   6.1 Primary metric: effective diffusion coefficient Deff for iodide (and optionally A-site) under bias/illumination.
   6.2 Experiments:
       - Bias-stress ToF-SIMS: apply defined bias (e.g., ±1 V, 60 °C, fixed time), then quantify iodide redistribution depth profile; fit to drift–diffusion model to extract Deff.
       - Temperature-dependent transient ion drift (TID) or EIS-based ionic capacitance: extract activation energy (Ea) for ion motion; success criterion: ΔEa ≥ 0.1 eV vs control or Deff reduction ≥10×.
       - Edge/bypass control: fabricate devices with and without intentional edge sealing; compare Deff and hysteresis to verify whether grain-boundary/edge pathways dominate.

7) Piezotronics: treated as a hypothesis test with symmetry and artifact controls
   7.1 Symmetry requirement (go/no-go for piezotronics claim):
       - Second harmonic generation (SHG) microscopy positive from the interlayer region OR polarized-GIWAXS consistent with non-centrosymmetric order.
       - PFM must show switchable phase contrast not attributable to electrostatics (use band-excitation PFM + on/off field protocol).
   7.2 Quantitative estimate and target effect size:
       - Measure effective d33 (PFM calibrated) on witness films; estimate interfacial polarization under ε ≤0.1% strain.
       - Predicted device-relevant signature: strain-modulated Voc and PL intensity changes that track polarization sign and persist when series resistance is held constant.
   7.3 Artifact exclusion controls:
       - Dummy non-piezo interlayer: amorphous Al2O3 (same thickness) and/or centrosymmetric ZIF-8-like Zn–2-MIM layer.
       - Strain-insensitive electrical fixture + in situ 4-probe/contact resistance monitoring to decouple contact changes.
       - If strain effects correlate only with Rs changes, piezotronics claim rejected.

8) Redox/chemical risk controls for Ni/Fe
   8.1 Operando/near-operando screening:
       - Light + bias aging (MPP, 65–85 °C) followed by XPS/ToF-SIMS depth profiles for Ni/Fe migration and iodide oxidation markers.
       - XAS before/after stress to detect Ni/Fe oxidation state shifts.
   8.2 Acceptance criteria:
       - No measurable increase in oxidized iodine species signals relative to control; no Ni/Fe penetration beyond interlayer within SIMS detection limits.
       - Device does not show new deep-trap signature: ideality factor and temperature-dependent Voc should not worsen.

9) Device completion and benchmarking
   9.1 HTL selection based on measured work function: PTAA (anisole) or alternative compatible HTL; only proceed if UPS indicates no extraction barrier.
   9.2 Benchmark controls (thickness-matched): PEAI 2D cap, MeO-2PACz SAM, ~1 nm Al2O3.
   9.3 Performance statistics: ≥30 devices per condition; report Voc distribution, QFLS–Voc offset, hysteresis index, stabilized MPP.

10) Stability qualification (causal readouts linked to mechanisms)
   - ISOS-L2: MPP tracking at 65–85 °C in N2; ISOS-O2 in ambient.
   - Damp heat 85/85 (encapsulated) and humidity cycling (unencapsulated).
   - Post-mortem: XRD (PbI2), SEM/TEM (delamination), XPS/ToF-SIMS (iodide/metal redistribution), and correlate failure mode with Deff and Pb–N metrics.

Go/no-go decision points:
   - D1 (Material): must meet continuity + M–N evidence; otherwise stop.
   - D2 (Passivation): require QFLS increase ≥20 meV and monotonic correlation with Pb–N fraction; otherwise de-emphasize passivation claim.
   - D3 (Ion): require Deff reduction ≥10× or Ea increase ≥0.1 eV; otherwise barrier claim limited.
   - D4 (Piezotronics): require SHG-positive + strain effect independent of Rs; otherwise drop piezotronics from narrative.
Feasibility:
This revision directly de-risks the central uncertainties by (i) **pre-registering material identity outcomes** (crystalline MOF vs amorphous hybrid) and tying each to distinct, testable device physics; (ii) making the dominant benefit **passivation-first**, quantified by DFT-predicted Pb–N binding and experimentally by XPS chemical shifts with a required QFLS/Voc correlation; (iii) replacing ambiguous “size selectivity” with an experimentally extracted **effective diffusion coefficient (Deff)** and activation energy for ion motion under bias, including edge/bypass controls to address grain-boundary leakage; (iv) demoting piezotronics to a **symmetry-gated hypothesis test** requiring SHG (non-centrosymmetry) and resistance-artifact exclusion; and (v) explicitly managing Ni/Fe redox risk with operando/near-operando oxidation-state and diffusion checks plus band-alignment acceptance limits (|ΔWF| ≤ 0.2 eV).

The SVPT concept remains feasible because ligand delivery is solvent-free and temperature-bounded, while the NiFe–LDH seed provides a templated, reactive scaffold that can incorporate N-donor ligands at low substrate temperatures. Crucially, the proposal no longer depends on assuming a canonical NiFe–(2-MIM) ZIF analogue exists at 45–70 °C; instead it formalizes a pivot to a metal–imidazolate hybrid if crystallinity is not achieved, preserving the core concept chain (SVPT-derived interlayer → Pb–N passivation + quantified ionic suppression → stability/Voc gains) while preventing over-claiming.
Critique: This is an unusually rigorous and self-aware proposal that anticipates the most common failure modes in perovskite/MOF-interlayer literature and neutralizes them through pre-registration, pivot logic, and quantitative acceptance criteria. Engineering resolution is very high: the SVPT process window, thickness control, identity verification, and bias-driven ion-transport measurements are all technically credible and appropriately constrained for perovskites. Logical consistency is strong because mutually exclusive material outcomes are defined a priori, each with its own falsifiable mechanism, preventing post hoc narrative drift. The primary deduction arises from the TARGET CONCEPT CHAIN alignment: the proposal explicitly demotes electrocatalysis and piezotronics to conditional or tertiary roles, whereas the chain implies a more direct piezoelectric–electrocatalytic–stability causality. While scientifically correct, this weakens strict adherence to the stated chain. Evidence grounding is otherwise solid, but NiFe electrocatalytic activity is treated mainly as a risk to be suppressed rather than a functional lever, which partially breaks the chain. Rationale quality is high because the work addresses a genuine bottleneck—ambiguous interlayers and overclaimed mechanisms—by structurally redesigning how claims are validated, though it is more corrective and de-risking than radically exploratory.

Hypothesis: Embedding a bicontinuous mesoporous single-atom M–N–C interlayer (Schwarz P-type architecture) directly at the perovskite/transport-layer interface will simultaneously (i) suppress interfacial non-radiative recombination by coordinative passivation of under-coordinated Pb/I (via FeN4 or CoN4 sites acting as Lewis base/electron-density modulators) and (ii) reduce interfacial electrochemical overpotential for parasitic redox processes (I3−/I−, O2/O2•−) by accelerating charge-transfer kinetics away from the perovskite lattice. A methodological adaptation is proposed: translate bmFeSAC-style negative Gaussian curvature bicontinuous mesoporosity—originally optimized for ORR—into a conformal, sub-30-nm-thick ‘electrocatalytic buffer’ that is electrically percolative but ion-blocking, and that can be metal-switched (Fe→Co or Fe/Co dual-SAC) to tune interfacial reaction energetics. Mechanistically, negative-curvature channels increase accessible single-atom site utilization while minimizing local current constriction; this lowers kinetic barriers (effective overpotential) for interfacial redox shuttling and flattens interfacial band bending, thereby increasing quasi-Fermi level splitting (higher Voc) and stabilizing operation under bias/illumination by diverting interfacial radicals from attacking the perovskite.
Plan:
Step 1: Device target selection and baseline controls.
- Build baseline n–i–p and p–i–n PSC stacks (e.g., ITO/SnO2/perovskite/HTL/Au and ITO/NiOx/perovskite/ETL/Ag) using a mixed-cation perovskite (FA0.85Cs0.15Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3) to avoid composition-driven artifacts.
- Prepare controls: (a) no interlayer, (b) planar N-doped carbon interlayer without SAC, (c) conventional passivation (e.g., PEAI 2D layer) for benchmarking.

Step 2: Methodological adaptation—bmFeSAC-derived bicontinuous mesoporous SAC thin interlayer integration.
- Synthesize a cubosome-templated bicontinuous mesoporous N-doped carbon scaffold (Schwarz P-type) with thickness control via dilute precursor loading and short deposition times (target: 10–30 nm, RMS roughness < 5 nm).
- Incorporate single-atom sites: generate FeN4, CoN4, and Fe/Co dual-SAC variants by MOF- or chelate-assisted impregnation followed by confined pyrolysis tuned to preserve single-atom dispersion (verify via HAADF-STEM + XAS).
- Convert powder synthesis into a thin-film process: disperse the mesoporous SAC in orthogonal solvents (e.g., alcohols) and deposit by blade-coating or spray-coating onto the transport layer (or onto the perovskite, depending on polarity), followed by low-temperature anneal (<120 °C) to maintain perovskite integrity.
- Add an ion-blocking functional adaptation without sacrificing percolation: infiltrate the bicontinuous channels with an ultrathin perfluorosulfonate (Nafion-like) or zwitterionic polymer at sub-monolayer equivalent coverage to create steric hindrance to mobile iodide while retaining electronic connectivity; systematically vary infiltration fraction to map the trade-off between ion-blocking and series resistance.

Step 3: Mechanism-resolving validation and quantitative analytics.
- Structural/chemical confirmation: GISAXS (bicontinuous periodicity), BET/ellipsometric porosimetry (effective porosity), XPS/UPS (work function shift, Pb–N interaction signatures), HAADF-STEM + XAS (single-atom coordination), ToF-SIMS depth profiling (interlayer continuity and polymer infiltration).
- Photophysical tests: steady-state PL and TRPL on perovskite/interlayer/CTL stacks; absolute PLQY to quantify non-radiative loss; transient photovoltage/photocurrent to extract recombination and transport times.
- Electrochemical overpotential proxy at PSC interfaces: build symmetric cells (CTL/interlayer/CTL and perovskite/interlayer/perovskite) and measure EIS under illumination and bias; use intensity-modulated photovoltage spectroscopy to separate interfacial charge-transfer resistance from ionic contributions; quantify bias-dependent interfacial reaction kinetics by operando UV–vis/photothermal deflection to monitor iodine species formation.
- Device metrics and stability: J–V (forward/reverse), stabilized MPP tracking; Voc(T) to infer dominant recombination pathway; operational stability at 65–85 °C and 1 sun in N2 and dry air; damp-heat (e.g., 85/85 modified) to test moisture barrier effect.
- Comparative mapping: correlate (i) single-atom type (Fe vs Co vs Fe/Co), (ii) curvature/porosity metrics, and (iii) polymer infiltration fraction with Voc, FF, hysteresis index, ion-migration activation energy, and operational lifetime (T80).
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: bmFeSAC demonstrates that negative Gaussian curvature bicontinuous mesoporosity maximizes utilization of M–N–C single-atom sites and lowers reaction barriers in electrocatalysis; Co-based catalysts are empirically linked to low overpotential through optimized intermediate adsorption and kinetic acceleration, while M–N–C engineering is a proven lever for tuning charge-transfer resistance and catalytic kinetics. Translating these principles to PSC interfaces targets the known failure mode where interfacial redox (iodine chemistry, oxygen reduction) accelerates degradation and increases interfacial recombination.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): PSC bottlenecks are interfacial recombination and bias/illumination-driven interfacial electrochemistry coupled to ion migration. A conformal bicontinuous SAC interlayer is an interface-engineering solution: (i) coordinative defect passivation improves quasi-Fermi level splitting (Voc), (ii) curvature-enabled high site accessibility provides kinetic ‘sinks’ that redirect deleterious redox away from the perovskite lattice, and (iii) controlled channel infiltration introduces an ion-blocking function analogous to steric hindrance effects (as in Nafion-modified catalysts) but repurposed to suppress iodide flux and reactive species penetration.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with conventional 2D perovskite or small-molecule passivation, the proposed interlayer is multifunctional and tunable: it offers (a) scalable thin-film deposition (spray/blade), (b) programmable interfacial energetics via Fe↔Co single-atom substitution (overpotential tuning), (c) decoupled optimization of electronic percolation and ionic blocking via partial channel infiltration, and (d) mechanistic measurability through electrochemical/operando probes linking ‘overpotential-like’ kinetic barriers to PSC stability. This is not a simple material swap; it is a curvature- and site-utilization-driven architectural adaptation tailored to PSC interfacial electrochemistry and recombination physics.
Critique: This is a highly sophisticated and technically ambitious proposal with strong command of both electrocatalysis and perovskite interfacial physics. The engineering plan is unusually detailed, spanning synthesis, thin-film translation, and multi-modal characterization. The central logic—that negative-curvature bicontinuous SAC architectures can act as kinetic redox sinks and coordinative passivation layers at PSC interfaces—is internally consistent and intellectually compelling. However, there are two notable weaknesses that limit a perfect score. First, the causal link between 'lowering electrochemical overpotential' (a well-defined electrocatalysis metric) and measurable improvements in Voc and stability in PSCs is conceptually plausible but not yet rigorously formalized; the proposal relies on analogy rather than a quantitative interfacial energy/kinetics model. Second, the ion-blocking strategy via partial Nafion-like infiltration risks undermining the very charge-transfer kinetics the SAC layer is meant to enhance, and the proposal does not yet specify clear percolation or transport criteria (e.g., target conductivity, ionic transference numbers) that would define success versus failure. These gaps slightly weaken the logical closure between mechanism and device-level outcomes, despite the otherwise excellent design.

Hypothesis: Installing an electronically conductive, redox-capacitive cMOF@nanostructured-carbon interlayer can increase stabilized power density and operational stability in carbon-based perovskite solar cells, but only if the cMOF’s redox is made truly reversible in a dry laminated stack via an internal, non-perovskite-dependent charge-compensation pathway. We hypothesize that an ultrathin, oriented 2D π–d conjugated cMOF film grown conformally on hierarchical nanostructured carbon and subsequently converted into a solid-state ‘single-ion pseudocapacitor’—by immobilizing counter-ions within/through the cMOF using tethered anions (polyanionic dopants) or an interpenetrated single-ion-conducting polymer—will (i) provide fast electron extraction (lower Rct) and (ii) provide a measurable, reversible interfacial redox capacitance (Cint) that buffers transient interfacial charge under illumination/bias without sourcing compensating ions from the perovskite. Mechanistically: (a) fast electronic transport arises from the crystalline π–d conjugated cMOF network plus intimate electrical contact to carbon; (b) the redox buffer is enabled by internal fixed counter-charge (e.g., sulfonated polyanion) that allows ligand-/metal-centered redox switching with only short-range cation motion inside the interlayer (or local ion rearrangement within a polymer electrolyte nanophase), rather than halide/A-site migration. This creates a well-defined interfacial RC element with a time constant τbuffer = Rct·Cbuffer engineered to be far below the dominant ion-relaxation time τion extracted from low-frequency impedance/IMVS, thereby suppressing ion-migration-driven interfacial field fluctuations (reduced hysteresis, improved Voc/FF) while maintaining chemical stability through a conformal, electronically thin but chemically robust diffusion barrier between cMOF metal nodes and halides.
Plan:
Step 1 — Device baseline and materials selection (with explicit constraints)
1.1 Baseline carbon-PSC stack: glass/FTO/SnO2/(FA,Cs)Pb(I,Br)3/perovskite surface passivation (minimal)/laminated hierarchical nanostructured carbon top contact (CNT/graphene ink + mesoporous carbon). Target baseline: PCE and hysteresis quantified via stabilized MPP tracking; record low-frequency impedance signature of ion motion (0.1–10 Hz arc/Warburg-like response) to define τion.
1.2 Conductive 2D cMOF selection (redox window + catalysis constraint): choose a π–d conjugated 2D MOF with demonstrated solid-state conductivity (≥10^-3–10^-1 S cm^-1 as film) and redox activity within ±0.6 V around the expected carbon contact quasi-Fermi level under operation, but with minimized halide-catalysis risk. Screening set:
  (i) Ni/Cu/Co catecholate–semiquinone families (high capacitance potential but higher halide reactivity risk) and
  (ii) metal-bis(dithiolene) frameworks (often more redox-delocalized; evaluate halide affinity).
Downselect criterion before any perovskite contact: no detectable I− oxidation/iodine formation in sealed halide exposure tests (Step 4.2).
1.3 Quantitative capacitance target is redesigned to be falsifiable from site density: define an areal redox-site density Ns (sites cm^-2) from film mass loading and framework stoichiometry and an accessible redox fraction swing Δx under device bias. The expected areal pseudocapacitance is bounded by:
  Qareal = Ns·e·Δx  (for 1e− per site),  Cbuffer ≈ dQ/dV ≈ (Ns·e·Δx)/ΔV.
We set a realistic initial gate: demonstrate Cbuffer,areal ≥ 1–10 μF cm^-2 in dry conditions (not electrolyte) across ΔV = 0.2–0.4 V, with τbuffer at least 10× faster than τion (τbuffer ≤ 0.1·τion). The earlier 10–100 μF cm^-2 remains an aspirational stretch goal contingent on measured Ns and Δx.

Step 2 — Build the solid-state charge-compensation architecture (mandatory reviewer fix)
2.1 On-carbon oriented cMOF growth (conductive scaffold preserved):
  • Carbon functionalization: sparse diazonium grafting to introduce ~0.5–2% surface coverage of –COOH/–OH anchoring sites (quantify by XPS C 1s/O 1s), maintaining sheet resistance increase <10% vs pristine carbon.
  • Interfacial coordination growth: two-phase method (organic ligand phase / aqueous metal-ion phase) to nucleate a 2D cMOF skin on carbon. Control thickness by growth time and precursor concentration to 5–15 nm (verify by cross-sectional TEM and XRR/ellipsometry on flat carbon surrogates). Target preferential in-plane orientation confirmed by GIWAXS (dominant (hk0) reflections aligned with substrate).
2.2 Convert cMOF into a ‘single-ion pseudocapacitor’ to enable dry-state redox reversibility (two implementable options; start with A, pivot to B if needed):
  Option A (polyanion-tethered internal counter-charge, no mobile anions):
  • Infiltrate a nanometer-thin polyanionic dopant into the cMOF/carbon composite: e.g., poly(styrene sulfonate) (PSS−) or perfluorosulfonated ionomer fragments (fixed SO3− groups). Procedure: brief dip-coating or vapor-assisted infiltration from low-surface-tension solvent, followed by mild anneal (<80 °C) to leave a sub-percolation ionomer fraction confined to the cMOF pore network.
  • Mechanism: fixed anions provide charge compensation; only small cations (e.g., residual tetralkylammonium from doping step or deliberately introduced non-reactive cations) redistribute over nanometer scales within the interlayer. No halide/A-site ions are required.
  Option B (interpenetrated single-ion conductor network):
  • Photopolymerize a single-ion-conducting polymer inside cMOF pores (e.g., sulfonated polymer with tethered anion and mobile Li+/Na+ or bulky organic cation chosen for low perovskite reactivity). Keep polymer volume fraction minimal to preserve electronic percolation (verify conductivity drop <2×).
  • Confirm ionic conductivity of the interpenetrated phase in dry state (target σion ≥10^-7–10^-6 S cm^-1 at 25–60 °C) using blocking-electrode EIS on standalone films.
2.3 Electrochemical pre-doping is re-scoped as ‘state initialization’ with retention testing (not assumed):
  • Pre-doping medium: use a non-aqueous electrolyte compatible with the cMOF and polyanion architecture (e.g., acetonitrile with inert salt), apply potentiostatic steps to set redox fraction x0.
  • Remove free electrolyte rigorously (rinse + vacuum dry). The retained state must be demonstrated by spectroscopy and open-circuit potential drift tests (Step 3.2).
  • Important: if pre-charge self-discharges upon contact, the interlayer can still function as a reversible buffer under operation provided that the internal counter-ion mechanism supports cycling; thus, the decisive metric becomes reversible Cbuffer and τbuffer in the dry stack, not the absolute persistence of x0 alone.

Step 3 — Quantitative, falsifiable model + go/no-go gates (mandatory)
3.1 Solid-state redox-capacitance model used to set design targets:
  • Equivalent circuit under illumination near MPP: perovskite recombination resistance Rrec in parallel with chemical capacitance Cμ, series with interfacial charge-transfer resistance Rct, and a buffer capacitance Cbuffer (pseudocapacitive) at the carbon contact.
  • Define τion from low-frequency features (ion-related capacitance dispersion) in control devices; define τbuffer = Rct·Cbuffer for the cMOF interlayer. Design rule: τbuffer ≤ 0.1·τion so that the buffer responds before ion redistribution perturbs band-bending.
  • Predict Cbuffer from Ns and Δx measured independently (Step 3.3); compare predicted vs measured interfacial capacitance under operating bias/light to validate mechanism.
3.2 Self-discharge/equilibration experiment (mandatory):
  • Construct test stack: cMOF@carbon (initialized at x0) contacted to (i) Au, (ii) ITO, and (iii) an inert wide-bandgap semiconductor (e.g., ALD-Al2O3-coated ITO to block charge transfer; and SnO2 as a realistic electron-contact analog) with controlled work functions.
  • Metrics: track (a) work function/CPD via Kelvin probe over 10^2–10^4 s in dry N2, (b) redox signatures by Raman/EPR/XPS over time, and (c) transient current upon contact (integrated charge = effective stored charge).
  • Go/no-go: if >80% of spectroscopic redox signature decays within <10^2 s upon contact to conductive substrates, then the proposal pivots from ‘pre-charged reservoir’ to ‘operando reversible buffer only’ and focuses on maximizing cycling Cbuffer rather than retaining x0.
3.3 Direct measurement of dry-state Cbuffer and redox accessibility (no perovskite yet):
  • Two-terminal solid-state EIS on cMOF@carbon pressed against inert counter-electrode with an ion-blocking spacer vs an ion-permitting but perovskite-free solid (e.g., polymer single-ion conductor layer). Extract areal capacitance vs bias and frequency (target: μF cm^-2 in 1–10^3 Hz band, minimal low-frequency divergence that would indicate slow ionic drift).
  • Galvanostatic intermittent titration-like pulses in solid state (small ΔV) to test reversibility and coulombic efficiency of redox switching.
  • Ns and Δx determination: quantify redox-site density from elemental analysis/XPS + film thickness/density; quantify accessible Δx from integrated charge in controlled potential steps (dry cell). Use this to compute predicted Cbuffer and compare to measured.
3.4 Device-level τbuffer vs τion gating:
  • Build full PSCs and run bias-/light-dependent impedance and IMVS/IMPS.
  • Go/no-go: demonstrate τbuffer ≤ 0.1·τion and a correlated reduction in hysteresis index and Voc transient overshoot. If τbuffer is not sufficiently faster than τion, increase Ns (thicker within 5–15 nm limit, higher surface area carbon), increase Δx (broaden redox window safely), or reduce Rct (improve orientation/contact).

Step 4 — Chemical compatibility and barrier architecture (mandatory stability gates)
4.1 Chemical barrier is upgraded from a <1 nm SAM-only concept to a conformal, electronically permissive diffusion barrier matched to rough topography:
  • Apply an ultrathin (1–3 nm) ALD Al2O3 or alucone (molecular layer deposition) on the cMOF surface facing perovskite OR on perovskite top surface (depending on adhesion), then functionalize with a conductive/semiconductive molecular layer (e.g., ultrathin fullerene derivative or conjugated zwitterion) if needed to maintain tunneling/transport.
  • Design constraint: barrier must block direct coordination of halides to open metal sites while keeping added series resistance ΔRs minimal (verify by TLM/contact resistance mapping).
4.2 Accelerated halide exposure tests prior to device integration (mandatory):
  • Expose cMOF@carbon (with and without barrier) to controlled I2/I−/Br− sources in dry conditions and at 60 °C (e.g., vapor exposure to iodine, and contact with solid halide salts under controlled humidity). Monitor:
    – XPS (metal oxidation state shifts; I 3d uptake),
    – UV–vis-NIR (new charge-transfer bands),
    – Raman/EPR (radical changes),
    – GIWAXS (crystallinity retention).
  • Go/no-go: if halide uptake or metal reduction/oxidation indicates strong irreversible reaction within 24–72 h at 60 °C, switch metal node/ligand family and/or enforce barrier-first architecture.

Step 5 — Full device fabrication and performance validation
5.1 Assemble PSCs by lamination (<80 °C, low pressure) with cMOF@carbon facing perovskite. Ensure conformal contact; quantify real contact area/roughness by cross-sectional SEM/TEM.
5.2 Parametric matrix (kept mechanistically tied):
  • cMOF thickness: 5, 10, 15 nm.
  • Counter-ion architecture: none vs Option A vs Option B.
  • Barrier: none vs 1–3 nm ALD/MLD barrier.
  • Pre-doping level x0: low/medium/high (as defined by integrated charge during initialization).
5.3 Performance metrics:
  • Stabilized MPP power density and J–V hysteresis; Voc/FF changes correlated to Rct, Rrec, and Cbuffer.
  • Operando KP/UPS (work function shifts under light/bias) and operando Raman/EPR (reversible redox signatures) to prove that any observed Cint increase is linked to cMOF redox activity in the dry stack.

Step 6 — Controls and explicit pivot plan
6.1 Controls to isolate mechanism:
  (i) pristine nanostructured carbon;
  (ii) carbon + non-redox crystalline porous layer (thickness-matched);
  (iii) carbon + insulating polymer (thickness-matched);
  (iv) cMOF@carbon without immobilized counter-ion architecture (tests reviewer’s concern directly);
  (v) conventional 2D-perovskite or small-molecule passivation benchmark.
6.2 Pivot if gates fail (mandatory):
  • If dry-state redox reversibility/capacitance is inadequate (Cbuffer < 1 μF cm^-2 or strong irreversibility), pivot to hybrid interlayer: cMOF retained primarily for electronic bridging/passivation, while a separately deposited 5–20 nm solid single-ion conductor (fixed anion polymer) supplies the counter-ion reservoir. The perovskite is protected by a conformal barrier to prevent ion exchange with the absorber; the ion conductor interfaces only with the cMOF/carbon side to enable pseudocapacitance without drawing halides/A-site ions.
Feasibility:
1) Reviewer-critical physics (ion compensation) is explicitly engineered, not assumed. The proposal no longer relies on a ‘dry cMOF redox capacitor’ without ions; instead, it implements internal fixed counter-charge (polyanionic dopant) or an interpenetrated single-ion conductor so that cMOF redox switching can proceed with localized ion rearrangement within the interlayer rather than perovskite ion migration. This directly addresses the contradiction that pseudocapacitance typically requires counter-ion motion.

2) Quantitative, falsifiable capacitance model ties materials to device timescales. We bound Cbuffer by Ns·Δx and require τbuffer = Rct·Cbuffer to be at least 10× faster than τion measured from low-frequency impedance/IMVS. This links the capacitance claim to measurable site density and establishes a concrete success criterion for suppressing ion-driven field fluctuations.

3) Pre-doping persistence is treated as an empirical question with a dedicated self-discharge/equilibration gate. Kelvin probe + Raman/EPR/XPS time-traces on controlled work-function contacts will determine whether an initialized mixed-valence state survives device-relevant times (10^2–10^4 s) or rapidly equilibrates. The project remains viable even if x0 does not persist, because the core mechanism can pivot to operando reversible buffering provided dry-state cycling Cbuffer is demonstrated.

4) Chemical compatibility is moved from ‘minimal SAM if needed’ to a defined, conformal diffusion barrier strategy with accelerated halide exposure go/no-go tests before device integration. This is essential because many conductive 2D cMOFs can coordinate halides or catalyze oxidation; the plan therefore screens chemistry under controlled halide stress and uses ultrathin ALD/MLD barriers that can conform to rough carbon/perovskite interfaces while limiting added series resistance.

5) The approach remains aligned with the original concept chain (cMOF@nanostructured carbon nanoreactor interlayer improving charge transfer + stability), but is now physically self-consistent in a dry PSC stack and includes explicit decision points and a hybrid-interlayer pivot if the solid-state redox-capacitance gates are not met.
Critique:
This is a substantially improved, physically self-consistent revision versus the usual “dry MOF pseudocapacitance” handwave: you explicitly address the core contradiction (counter-ion requirement) by building a single-ion charge-compensation architecture and you add hard gates (Cbuffer in dry state; τbuffer relative to τion; halide reactivity screens; self-discharge tests). Engineering is strong: oriented thin-film cMOF growth on hierarchical carbon, polymer/polyanion infiltration, and ALD/MLD barriers are all plausible with modern toolsets, and the control matrix is well structured.

Key score deductions come from (i) remaining ambiguity in whether the proposed μF·cm−2-scale Cbuffer at 1–10^3 Hz is realistically achievable in a 5–15 nm interlayer without introducing slow ionic polarization that contaminates the extracted capacitance (CPE/Maxwell–Wagner effects), and (ii) incomplete separation of ‘true redox pseudocapacitance’ from interfacial dipolar/ionic accumulation in the polymer/polyanion phase under device bias. Your EIS plan gestures at this, but the discrimination strategy is not yet sufficiently rigorous (e.g., demonstrating Nernstian/broad redox features, oxidation-state tracking under bias with quantitative charge balance, and frequency/temperature scaling consistent with a bounded finite-site redox process rather than dispersive ion drift).

A second logical vulnerability is the assumption that adding fixed anions + mobile cations inside the interlayer will not introduce new long-time-constant field screening that could worsen hysteresis (even if it avoids perovskite ion migration). You propose σion targets, but you do not bound the ionic relaxation time of the interlayer itself in-device nor show that its polarization will stay in the “fast buffer” regime across temperature and illumination.

Finally, chemical compatibility is treated seriously, but the barrier stack risks undermining the very Rct reductions you seek; the plan lacks a quantitative transport budget (maximum allowable tunneling thickness/energy offset) tied to FF loss, and does not specify how you will ensure uniform 1–3 nm coverage on rough carbon/cMOF without pinholes (a dominant failure mode for halide blocking claims).

Hypothesis:
Embedding a perovskite-compatible, electrically percolating “ionic–electronic metainterface” composed of (i) a self-limited ultrathin 2D Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) perovskite skin and (ii) a redox-programmed conjugated MOF (HHTP-like catecholate framework) as a single continuous interphase at the 3D perovskite/charge-transport junction will simultaneously (a) reduce steady-state contact resistivity while preserving carrier selectivity in photovoltaics and (b) provide genuine saturable-absorber (SA) action (intensity-dependent absorption/transfer with a finite recovery time) that can be parameterized and inserted into a standard mode-locking model to predict pulse width and threshold. Mechanistically, the proposal explicitly separates three effects that were previously conflated: 
(1) Coherent third-order nonlinearity χ(3) (Kerr/nonlinear refraction and nonlinear absorption) is treated only as a contributor to intensity-dependent optical response; SA behavior is not assumed from χ(3) alone. Instead, SA arises from population dynamics: under high instantaneous carrier density the interphase exhibits (i) bleaching/state-filling of interfacial delocalized states (MOF band/CT states and/or interfacial charge-transfer states) and (ii) a concurrent increase in interfacial transmission probability (reduced effective injection barrier) due to quasi-Fermi level shifts and occupation of a broad interfacial density-of-states (DOS). These yield a measurable modulation depth ΔT, saturation fluence F_sat (or I_sat), recovery time τ_rec, and nonsaturable loss T_ns.
(2) The “reduced interfacial transfer barrier” is formalized as carrier-density-dependent transport across a thin tunneling/contact region: the RP skin fixes ionic/defect chemistry and provides a controlled dipole and tunneling thickness; the MOF provides a high-DOS, redox-tunable transport manifold. Under a pump pulse, the interfacial quasi-Fermi level splitting (ΔE_F) and DOS filling lower the effective barrier height φ_eff(N) and increase tunneling probability, causing a measurable decrease of specific contact resistivity ρ_c(F) and extraction time constant τ_ext(F) with fluence. This is distinct from photothermal changes (T-dependent mobility) and from field-screening artifacts (transient band flattening without bleaching).
(3) Chemical decoupling is made falsifiable: the RP skin is an ion-blocking and coordination-shielding layer with explicit quantitative acceptance criteria for halide/metal interdiffusion and for MOF node-valence drift under operation. The RP skin prevents direct catecholate–halide coordination and suppresses redox exchange between perovskite surface iodine/defect species and the MOF metal nodes, enabling stable redox programming of the MOF work function/conductivity without triggering perovskite decomposition.
Predicted outcomes: (PV) A reduced ρ_c at the target interface (≥3× improvement) with unchanged or improved surface recombination velocity S and increased implied Voc (iVoc) / PLQY, within a pre-registered go/no-go window. (Ultrafast) Extracted SA parameters (ΔT, F_sat, τ_rec, T_ns) inserted into a Haus master equation (or equivalent lumped cavity model) reproduce measured pulse width and mode-locking threshold. The interphase will not change repetition frequency f_rep except via any deliberate cavity-length change; it can change threshold, pulse width, and stability through ΔT, F_sat, τ_rec, and insertion loss.
Plan:
Step 0 — Device architectures and where the metainterface sits (pre-registered):
0.1 Photovoltaics (n–i–p): Glass/ITO/SnO2/(3D perovskite)/[RP skin + MOF]/HTL (MeO-2PACz or Spiro-OMeTAD) /Au; and a HTL-free carbon-contact variant if MOF is used as an extraction scaffold. The metainterface is implemented only at one junction at a time (perovskite/ETL or perovskite/HTL) to preserve interpretability.
0.2 Ultrafast testbeds (two tiers):
  Tier-1 (stack-level SA metrology without lasing): Substrate/transport/perovskite/[RP+MOF] as an optical stack for pump–probe/Z-scan and ultrafast photocurrent.
  Tier-2 (cavity demonstration): perovskite waveguide or microcavity where the interphase is placed in a region of controlled mode overlap Γ with the optical field (e.g., contact/cladding layer); cavity length L is fixed across interphase variants to isolate effects on pulse width/threshold rather than f_rep.

Step 1 — Self-limited RP skin growth with explicit architectural targets:
1.1 RP thickness and n-value target: n=1–2 RP phase, thickness t_RP = 1.0–2.0 nm (≈ 1–2 inorganic slabs), continuous coverage ≥95% (AFM/ToF-SIMS lateral uniformity).
1.2 Chemistry: vapor-assisted bulky-cation halide treatment using PEA-I, BA-I, or fluorinated-PEA-I to tune dipole; substoichiometric exposure in a sealed chamber at 40–60 °C. Growth is diffusion-limited and stopped in the self-limited regime.
1.3 In-situ growth stop criteria: real-time ellipsometry (ΔΨ/ΔΔ) calibrated to t_RP; stop when Δt <0.1 nm over 10 min. Confirm by angle-resolved XPS (attenuation of Pb 4f / I 3d) and GIWAXS (appearance of RP diffraction at q consistent with n=1–2).
1.4 Dipole/work-function pre-design: target interfacial vacuum level shift ΔWF = 0.15–0.35 eV measured by UPS/Kelvin probe on reference stacks (transport/RP/perovskite). Selection among PEA/BA/F-PEA is made to hit ΔWF without increasing energetic offset that would degrade selectivity.

Step 2 — Surface-confined conjugated MOF growth with thickness/percolation targets and chemical safeguards:
2.1 MOF selection and node strategy: Cu3(HHTP)2 and Ni3(HHTP)2 as endpoints plus mixed-node (Cu/Ni) to tune conductivity and redox stability. Rationale: conjugated π-pathways and redox-tunable carrier density (Asset 2), with proven strong NLO/SA behavior in ultrathin heterostructures (Asset 1) but here implemented without graphene.
2.2 Surface-confined growth (SAG) protocol (explicit):
  (i) Linker-first adsorption: HHTP (or HHTP-derivative) adsorption onto RP surface from anhydrous alcohol at ≤25 °C, 5–10 min, followed by solvent rinse.
  (ii) Metalation cycles: immerse in metal salt solution (Cu(OAc)2 or Ni(OAc)2 in alcohol) at 25–60 °C for 5–10 min, rinse; repeat N cycles to reach t_MOF = 3–7 nm. Thickness is controlled by cycle count; growth is halted before island/grain formation.
  (iii) Anneal: ≤80 °C under inert atmosphere, 10–30 min to improve conjugation without perovskite damage.
2.3 Percolation and optical parasitics targets: sheet resistance R_sh < 10^5 Ω/sq at 5 nm; optical insertion loss at 532–850 nm < 5% for the metainterface stack (integrating sphere measurement). If loss exceeds threshold, reduce t_MOF or adjust redox set point.
2.4 Chemical isolation design rule: MOF is never grown directly on 3D perovskite—only on RP skin. A “no-RP” control is fabricated to prove necessity and to quantify chemical damage risk.

Step 3 — Redox programming with stability windows and monitoring:
3.1 Redox set step: iodine vapor microdose (calibrated partial pressure/time) or mild electrochemical gating on test coupons to achieve partial oxidation that maximizes conductivity while limiting free-carrier absorption. Target: increase conductivity ≥10× from as-grown while keeping insertion loss <5%.
3.2 Redox-state locking: counterion selection via final rinse with bulky, weakly coordinating anions (pre-registered candidates) to stabilize charge density.
3.3 Node valence stability window (acceptance criterion): operando spectroscopies must show node oxidation state drift ≤10% (relative change in characteristic XAS/XPS features) after 100 h 1-sun MPP or after ultrafast pumping dose equivalent.

Step 4 — Quantitative SA model extraction and mode-locking framework (mandatory directive i):
4.1 Measure SA parameters on full stacks (not powders):
  (i) Open-aperture Z-scan to extract nonlinear absorption coefficient and effective saturation: fit transmission T(I) = 1 − (ΔT)/(1 + I/I_sat) − T_ns (or fluence form).
  (ii) Pump–probe transient absorption/reflection to extract τ_rec (fast/slow components) and confirm bleaching dynamics.
  (iii) Separate Kerr vs SA: closed-aperture Z-scan for nonlinear refraction n2; show that mode-locking-relevant behavior is dominated by absorptive saturation (ΔT) and τ_rec rather than purely dispersive n2.
4.2 Insert extracted parameters into a standard cavity model:
  Use Haus master equation (or equivalent lumped model) with saturable absorber term characterized by {ΔT, F_sat, τ_rec, T_ns} plus cavity dispersion (GVD), gain bandwidth, and output coupling. Predict pulse width and mode-locking threshold vs interphase variant.
4.3 Repetition frequency statement (pre-registered): f_rep = c/(n_eff·L). Since L and n_eff are fixed across variants, the interphase is not expected to change f_rep measurably; it can change threshold, pulse duration, pulse stability, and achievable fundamental mode-locking regime. Any observed f_rep shift beyond measurement uncertainty triggers an investigation of unintended cavity-length/index changes.

Step 5 — Carrier-density-dependent interfacial transport model + discriminating tests (mandatory directive ii):
5.1 Transport model (measurable predictions):
  Represent the RP as a tunneling/dipole layer with thickness t_RP and barrier φ0. Represent MOF as a redox-tunable conductor with DOS g(E) and quasi-Fermi shift ΔE_F under photoexcitation. Predict:
  φ_eff(F) = φ0 − α·ΔE_F(F) (DOS filling / quasi-Fermi splitting term)
  and contact resistivity ρ_c(F) ∝ exp[β·t_RP·sqrt(φ_eff(F))] / G_MOF(redox)
  giving a monotonic decrease of ρ_c with fluence until saturation when DOS is filled.
  Extraction time τ_ext(F) from TRPL/TA or ultrafast photocurrent should track ρ_c(F) (pre-registered correlation).
5.2 Measurements that directly map ρ_c(F) and τ_ext(F):
  (i) Ultrafast photocurrent sampling (rise-time vs fluence) under fixed average power using pulse-picker (vary peak intensity independent of heating).
  (ii) Fluence-dependent TRPL quenching rate with selective-side excitation (from transport layer side) to isolate interfacial transfer.
  (iii) Intensity-dependent impedance/photovoltage response under constant average power to separate peak-intensity effects from thermal.
5.3 Discriminating against artifacts:
  (i) Temperature-controlled pump–probe/Z-scan (fixed sample temperature using a stage; monitor with IR sensor). A purely thermal mechanism would scale with average power and temperature, not with peak fluence at fixed average.
  (ii) Field-screening control: replicate absorption but alter DOS filling by using an insulating MOF analog (nonconjugated linker) and a conductivity-matched but low-bleaching layer; if band-flattening alone dominated, these would mimic the effect—pre-registered expectation is they will not.
  (iii) Identical linear absorption control: adjust thickness so variants have matched linear absorption; then any change in τ_ext(F) is not due to different absorbed energy.

Step 6 — Operando chemical acceptance criteria + probes (mandatory directive iii):
6.1 Hard quantitative acceptance criteria:
  (A) Halide ingress into MOF: iodine content in MOF region after stress < 1 at.% (ToF-SIMS calibrated, depth-resolved) OR below a pre-set detection-calibrated threshold corresponding to <10^13 cm−2 areal density.
  (B) Metal-node migration into perovskite: Cu/Ni in perovskite bulk < 10^17 cm−3 equivalent (ToF-SIMS quantification on sister devices).
  (C) RP integrity: RP diffraction signature (GIWAXS) retained with <20% reduction in peak intensity after stress.
  (D) MOF redox drift: ≤10% change in node valence indicator (XAS/XPS/Raman band ratios) under illumination/bias.
6.2 In-operando / quasi-operando probes (added beyond post-mortem):
  (i) Bias/light ToF-SIMS on sister devices (time-staggered set) to obtain diffusion kinetics, not only endpoints.
  (ii) In-situ Kelvin probe / UPS shift under illumination to track work-function drift and quasi-Fermi level effects.
  (iii) Operando Raman/IR (MOF vibrational signatures) and operando GIWAXS for structural stability during bias/light.

Step 7 — Photovoltaic selectivity validation + go/no-go (mandatory directive iv):
7.1 Selectivity metrics (explicit):
  (i) Surface recombination velocity S extracted from TRPL (and/or transient photoconductance on suitable films) with selective excitation.
  (ii) Implied Voc and PLQY of full stacks at 1-sun equivalent to detect nonradiative interface losses.
  (iii) UPS/IPES-derived injection barriers and band alignment; confirm that redox tuning does not create minority-carrier leakage pathways.
  (iv) Dark J–V leakage and ideality factor changes; EIS recombination resistance under illumination.
7.2 Go/no-go criterion:
  If redox tuning reduces Rs (or ρ_c) but causes >10 mV drop in implied Voc or a ≥2× increase in interfacial recombination rate (from PLQY/TRPL/EIS), that redox set point is rejected; proceed by (a) adjusting RP dipole (cation choice), (b) lowering MOF DOS via node selection/mixed node, or (c) relocating metainterface to the opposite junction where selectivity constraints differ.

Step 8 — Controls (pre-registered) to isolate each mechanism:
8.1 RP-only (no MOF): isolates ionic blocking/passivation and dipole.
8.2 MOF-only directly on 3D perovskite (intentional stress control): quantifies chemical incompatibility and validates the necessity of RP.
8.3 Insulating MOF analog (nonconjugated linker): similar chemistry/thickness, no delocalized DOS; tests whether conductivity/DOS is essential.
8.4 Conductivity-matched but low-bleaching interlayer: separates electrical improvement from SA behavior.
8.5 Thickness-matched but different redox states: isolates work-function/conductivity effects from geometry.

Milestones and decision gates:
M1 (Materials): Achieve t_RP 1–2 nm and t_MOF 3–7 nm with percolation and insertion loss <5%.
M2 (Chemistry): Meet halide/metal diffusion and redox drift criteria under 100 h 1-sun MPP.
M3 (Transport): Demonstrate ρ_c improvement ≥3× and τ_ext reduction with fluence dependence consistent with DOS-filling model (and not with average-power heating).
M4 (Ultrafast): Extract {ΔT, F_sat, τ_rec, T_ns} and accurately predict pulse width/threshold in cavity using Haus model; confirm f_rep unchanged for fixed L.
M5 (PV): Demonstrate improved stabilized efficiency or stability without selectivity penalty; otherwise pivot to alternative redox/node/cation set points per go/no-go.
Feasibility:
1) Why the SA claim is now mechanistically rigorous: The revised plan no longer equates χ(3) with saturable absorption. χ(3) is measured separately (n2 via closed-aperture Z-scan), while SA action is quantified by ΔT, F_sat (or I_sat), τ_rec, and T_ns extracted from open-aperture Z-scan and pump–probe on complete device-relevant stacks. These parameters are then used in a Haus master-equation framework to predict pulse width and mode-locking threshold, explicitly acknowledging that repetition frequency is set by cavity length and effective index. This directly satisfies the reviewer’s demand for a quantitative dynamical model.

2) Why intensity-dependent “barrier reduction” is now testable and separable from artifacts: The interfacial transport hypothesis is reformulated as DOS filling + quasi-Fermi level shift reducing φ_eff and enhancing tunneling/contact conductance across a thin RP layer, predicting a specific scaling ρ_c(F) and τ_ext(F) with fluence until saturation. The plan pre-registers discriminating experiments that hold average power constant while varying peak intensity, uses temperature-controlled pump–probe to eliminate photothermal explanations, and includes matched-absorption and mechanism-specific controls (insulating MOF analog; conductivity-matched low-bleaching layer). This converts a qualitative claim into falsifiable scaling laws.

3) Why RP genuinely decouples MOF chemistry from perovskite ion chemistry (now with hard acceptance criteria): Catecholate MOFs can coordinate halides and participate in redox exchange; the revised proposal treats this as a primary risk with explicit quantitative diffusion limits (halide ingress, metal-node migration) and redox-drift thresholds. Crucially, operando and time-staggered sister-device ToF-SIMS, in-situ Kelvin probe/UPS under illumination, and operando GIWAXS/Raman/IR are added to establish causality and kinetics rather than relying on post-mortem snapshots. The RP layer is therefore not an assertion but a measured barrier with go/no-go thresholds.

4) Why PSC selectivity is protected despite redox-tuned conductivity: The plan explicitly measures and constrains minority-carrier leakage and recombination via implied Voc/PLQY, TRPL-derived S, UPS/IPES injection barriers, dark leakage, and illuminated EIS. A pre-registered go/no-go rule prevents optimizing Rs at the expense of interfacial recombination. Energetic tuning is split between RP dipole control (coarse alignment) and MOF redox programming (fine conductivity/work-function tuning), reducing the risk that conductivity improvements inadvertently destroy selectivity.

5) Literature and empirical basis supporting feasibility: Conjugated MOFs exhibit semiconducting transport with redox/annealing-dependent conductivity and π-delocalization (Asset 2), enabling a controllable interfacial conductor. Separately, ultrathin MOF-based heterostructures demonstrate strong nonlinear optical response and SA-enabled ultrafast pulse generation (Asset 1); here, that capability is translated into stack-level SA parameters instead of inferred from χ(3) alone. Ultrathin RP surface layers are an established strategy for perovskite defect/ion management when kept in the tunneling-thin regime; the proposal adds in-situ thickness stopping and operando proof of ionic blocking. Together, these elements make the metainterface concept feasible while addressing the reviewers’ mechanistic and validation demands.
Critique: Methodological execution is unusually well-specified (thickness targets, stop criteria, control matrix, and go/no-go windows) and addresses common reviewer failure modes (χ(3)≠SA; thermal vs peak-fluence artifacts; chemical incompatibility). However, two scientific gaps reduce logical strength. (i) The “carrier-density-dependent barrier reduction” model is presented as an exponential tunneling scaling with an ad hoc φ_eff(F)=φ0−αΔE_F(F), but the proposal does not specify how ΔE_F(F) will be quantitatively obtained/validated at the interface (separate from bulk perovskite photophysics) nor how α relates to a measurable interfacial DOS/charging capacitance; without that, fits risk being phenomenological. (ii) The dual-function interphase (low ρ_c while preserving selectivity, plus SA action) is plausible but not shown to be mutually compatible: the same added DOS/percolation that reduces contact resistance can increase sub-gap absorption, free-carrier absorption, and minority-carrier leakage; the proposal has safeguards (PLQY/iVoc, dark JV), but no explicit design-space mapping (e.g., required ΔT and F_sat vs allowable T_ns and added recombination) that demonstrates simultaneous attainability. Evidence grounding is strong overall, but feasibility hinges on whether 3–7 nm conjugated MOFs can reliably achieve the targeted R_sh and <5% insertion loss on real RP/perovskite stacks (not ideal substrates), and whether operando ToF-SIMS/UPS under illumination can be executed with sufficient depth/energy resolution to cleanly attribute changes to the metainterface rather than ion-migration-induced bulk effects.

Hypothesis: Integrating a Schwarz P–type bicontinuous, negatively curved nitrogen/sulfur co-doped porous carbon (NS-PC) interlayer that hosts immobilized single-atom metal–N4 sites (M–N4 SAC; M = Fe or Co) at the perovskite/charge-transport interface will simultaneously (i) suppress non-radiative interfacial recombination and (ii) inhibit halide/metal-ion interdiffusion, thereby increasing Voc, fill factor, and operational stability. Mechanistically, the negative Gaussian curvature in the bicontinuous network increases the utilization and uniformity of electronically active M–N4 and heteroatom (N/S) Lewis-base sites by enforcing continuous, low-tortuosity percolation pathways and curvature-induced electronic polarization; this enables strong coordination-based defect passivation (Pb–X vacancy and undercoordinated Pb2+), reduced local ion-accumulation (lowering electric-field hot spots), and accelerated interfacial charge extraction. The methodological adaptation is to translate an ORR-optimized curvature/half-wave-potential design principle into PSC interface engineering by (a) templating a nanoscale Schwarz P bicontinuous carbon scaffold directly on the perovskite, (b) anchoring sparse M–N4 single atoms into the curved framework, and (c) tuning the framework’s redox/electronic level alignment using an electrochemical ‘half-wave potential’ descriptor measured on the same film to predict/select interlayers that minimize interfacial energy barriers and hysteresis in PSC operation.
