Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Bicontinuous negative-curvature scaffold formation (methodological adaptation):
- Prepare polymer cubosome templates (e.g., Pluronic-based or block-copolymer cubosomes) that self-assemble into a Schwarz P morphology.
- Spin-coat a thin cubosome layer (5–20 nm effective thickness) atop the perovskite (or atop NiOx/SnO2 depending on architecture) using an orthogonal solvent system to avoid perovskite damage.
- Infiltrate carbon/nitrogen/sulfur precursors (e.g., dopamine/aniline + thiourea or cysteamine) into the template; then perform low-temperature conversion using a two-step route: (i) UV/ozone or plasma-assisted crosslinking to lock morphology, followed by (ii) rapid photothermal/flash-Joule annealing (milliseconds–seconds) under inert atmosphere to carbonize while limiting perovskite thermal exposure. Remove the template by selective solvent extraction.
2.2 Single-atom site installation:
- Introduce metal precursors at ultralow loading (target 0.1–1.5 wt%) via vapor infiltration or solution coordination to N-rich sites, followed by mild activation to form isolated M–N4 motifs (no nanoparticles). Use Fe and Co as primary candidates; include a metal-free NS-PC control.
- Confirm SAC dispersion with aberration-corrected HAADF-STEM, XAS (XANES/EXAFS for M–N coordination), and Mössbauer (for Fe) to exclude metallic clusters.
2.3 Electrochemical descriptor calibration using half-wave potential (transfer of Asset logic):
- Deposit identical interlayer films on glassy carbon and ITO substrates; measure ORR half-wave potential (E1/2) and Tafel slopes in alkaline electrolyte as a proxy for film electronic/charge-transfer competency and local coordination environment.
- Establish a correlation between E1/2 (and derived kinetic current density) and PSC interfacial metrics (contact resistivity, recombination resistance, hysteresis index). Use this to down-select interlayers with optimal electronic coupling while avoiding overly catalytic/chemically aggressive surfaces.
2.4 Interface integration modes:
- Mode A (HTL/perovskite): Place SAC@NS-PC between perovskite and NiOx or spiro-OMeTAD to passivate Pb-related surface traps and create a graded energetic contact.
- Mode B (ETL/perovskite): Place SAC@NS-PC between perovskite and C60/SnO2 to mitigate halide accumulation and suppress interfacial ion-induced degradation.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Optoelectronic validation:
- Measure absolute PLQY and time-resolved PL at the perovskite surface before/after interlayer to quantify non-radiative recombination reduction; extract implied Voc.
- Perform transient photovoltage/photocurrent and impedance spectroscopy (recombination resistance, chemical capacitance) to identify changes in interfacial recombination and ion migration signatures.
- Use UPS/KPFM to map work function and surface potential uniformity; test whether curvature-based scaffolds reduce potential inhomogeneity.
3.2 Defect/ion-migration mechanism tests:
- ToF-SIMS depth profiling after bias-stress to quantify I−/Br− migration and metal electrode diffusion; compare with planar carbon and no-interlayer controls.
- In-situ/operando GIWAXS under humidity/light to track phase segregation (I/Br) and lattice changes.
- Solid-state NMR or XPS core-level shifts to evidence Pb–N/S coordination and halide-vacancy passivation.
3.3 Device metrics and stability:
- Benchmark PCE, Voc, FF, hysteresis; perform statistical analysis over >30 devices per condition.
- Operational stability: maximum power point tracking at 1 sun, 45–65 °C, controlled RH (20–50%) for >1000 h; report T80.
- Thermal and damp-heat tests (ISOS protocols), plus reverse-bias stress to probe ion-driven failure.
3.4 Comparative controls to prove adaptation value:
- Control 1: planar NS-doped carbon without Schwarz P curvature.
- Control 2: Schwarz P carbon without N/S doping.
- Control 3: NS-PC with metal nanoparticles (intentional) vs true SAC to isolate single-atom effect.
- Control 4: conventional passivation (e.g., PEAI/2D RP layer) to compare against state-of-the-art interface engineering.
- Quantitatively attribute gains to curvature (negative Gaussian), doping (N/S), and SAC sites using ablation-style experiments and multivariate regression vs E1/2 descriptor.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Bicontinuous Schwarz P architectures with negative Gaussian curvature have demonstrated unusually high utilization of single-atom M–N4 sites and high half-wave potentials in oxygen electrochemistry, implying strong electronic coupling, accessible active sites, and continuous transport pathways. N/S co-doped porous carbon is known to tune work function, increase conductivity, and provide Lewis-basic sites capable of coordinating undercoordinated metal ions and suppressing trap-assisted recombination.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): PSC losses and instability are dominated by interfacial non-radiative recombination and ion migration. The proposed SAC@NS-PC Schwarz P interlayer is an interface-engineered, electronically percolating, chemically coordinating scaffold: N/S sites passivate Pb-related defects; bicontinuous channels reduce tortuosity for electronic extraction while avoiding dense barriers that can trap ions; isolated M–N4 motifs provide tunable local electronic structure to align energy levels and homogenize interfacial fields. Using half-wave potential as a film-level descriptor is a methodological adaptation to rapidly screen interlayers for charge-transfer quality and coordination environment, then correlate to photovoltaic outcomes.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike conventional molecular passivators or 2D capping layers that can introduce insulating barriers and impede charge transport, the negatively curved bicontinuous carbon provides simultaneous passivation and high lateral conductivity with controlled porosity. Compared to nanoparticle additives, SACs avoid parasitic absorption/scattering and reduce catalytic side reactions by limiting metallic domains. The curvature-driven increase in active-site utilization enables lower loading (minimal optical/electrical penalty) while delivering stronger interfacial field homogenization and ion-blocking, targeting higher Voc/FF and longer T80 under realistic MPP stress.
Critique: The plan is unusually detailed and control-rich, and the concept chain is integrated rather than name-checked. The main technical weakness is feasibility at the perovskite interface: cubosome templating plus precursor infiltration plus plasma/UV and flash-Joule carbonization on a completed perovskite stack is high-risk for chemical/physical damage (solvent ingress, iodide/organic decomposition, surface reduction, interfacial voiding) and may compromise reproducibility over 30+ devices. Mechanistically, the claimed benefits of negative Gaussian curvature (curvature-induced electronic polarization, field homogenization, reduced ion accumulation) are plausible but not yet anchored to a falsifiable, quantitative model; several effects could be confounded with simpler variables (coverage, conductivity, work function, carbon thickness/porosity). The ORR half-wave potential descriptor is an inventive screening handle, but its transferability is under-justified: E1/2 in alkaline electrolyte is strongly influenced by wetting, O2 transport, and electrolyte/film interactions that do not map cleanly onto solid-state energy-level alignment, interfacial recombination velocity, or ion-blocking in PSCs; without a clear causal bridge, correlations may be accidental and architecture-dependent. Finally, introducing Fe/Co–N4 sites at the perovskite interface risks unintended redox/catalysis (iodide oxidation, superoxide formation under illumination, Fenton-like chemistry with trace water) that could worsen stability unless explicitly bounded by operando chemical diagnostics and rigorous “chemical inertness” criteria.

Hypothesis: Embedding Fenton-active single-atom sites (Fe-SA and/or Cu-SA) in a MOF-derived N-doped carbon interlayer at the perovskite/ETL interface, and engineering a humidity-triggered “release profile” of low-dose H2O2 from a neighboring polymer nanoreservoir, will create a self-limited, light-assisted photo-Fenton microenvironment that continuously scavenges superoxide/singlet oxygen while converting trace peroxide into short-lived ·OH confined within the carbon interlayer. Mechanistically, the Fe/Cu single atoms (maximal atomic utilization, suppressed clustering) catalyze ROS interconversion and decomposition of long-lived oxidants (O2·−/H2O2/1O2) that otherwise oxidize iodide/organic cations and accelerate ion migration. Spatial confinement in a thin MOF-carbon layer limits ·OH diffusion to the perovskite lattice, so oxidative cleaning occurs primarily at the interface where oxygen ingress and electron accumulation generate ROS, thereby reducing interfacial trap density, suppressing non-radiative recombination (higher Voc), and slowing operational photo-oxidation and hysteresis (improved stability). The methodological adaptation is the translation of AOP/photo-Fenton catalysis from aqueous pollutant degradation to a solid-state, interface-confined, release-rate-controlled ROS management layer in PSCs, designed to be self-limiting via controlled peroxide flux and active-site isolation (single atoms) to avoid uncontrolled radical attack on the perovskite.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Choose a high-efficiency baseline stack (e.g., glass/ITO/SnO2/perovskite/spiro-OMeTAD/Au) using a mixed-cation perovskite (FA/MA/Cs) with I/Br tuned bandgap; establish baseline PCE, Voc, hysteresis, and operational stability under 1-sun + controlled O2/H2O.
1.2 Prepare MOF-derived N-doped carbon hosting isolated Fe-SA and/or Cu-SA: (i) start from Zn-based MOF scaffold to aid atomic dispersion; (ii) introduce Fe/Cu precursors at low loading; (iii) pyrolyze to yield M–N4 (or M–N2+2) coordination; (iv) confirm single-atom nature via HAADF-STEM, XAS (XANES/EXAFS), and ICP for loading.
1.3 Formulate a humidity-triggered peroxide nanoreservoir: encapsulate urea–hydrogen peroxide (UHP) or sodium percarbonate in a hydrophilic-but-peroxide-stable polymer (e.g., PVA/PVP blend) as 20–100 nm nanodomains; calibrate H2O2 release profile vs RH and temperature by titration/fluorimetry, targeting sub-ppm to low-ppm flux per hour.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Deposit an ultrathin (3–10 nm) Fe-SA/Cu-SA@N–C interlayer on SnO2 (or directly on perovskite, depending on best band alignment) by dispersing the carbon in a benign solvent and using blade/slot-die compatible coating with controlled surface coverage; anneal mildly (<120 °C) to avoid perovskite damage.
2.2 Integrate the peroxide nanoreservoir adjacent to (not mixed into) the perovskite: place the reservoir within the encapsulant edge-seal or as a patterned peripheral layer on top of the ETL region outside the active aperture. This structural adaptation enforces diffusion-limited delivery of H2O2 into the interlayer region, preventing bulk exposure of the perovskite.
2.3 Tune catalytic selectivity by varying: (i) metal identity (Fe-SA vs Cu-SA vs Fe/Cu dual SAs), (ii) coordination environment (N4 vs N2+2 by controlling pyrolysis atmosphere), and (iii) interlayer thickness/porosity to confine radicals. Use operando illumination to activate photo-Fenton-like cycles (Fe3+→Fe2+ photoreduction) while maintaining low peroxide flux.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Quantify ROS near interfaces under operation using operando EPR spin trapping and fluorescent probes embedded in an inert overlayer (calibrated for 1O2, O2·−, and ·OH); compare devices with/without SA layer and with/without peroxide release.
3.2 Track perovskite chemical integrity: operando PL/QFLS mapping, TRPL (surface recombination velocity), XPS depth profiling for I0/I− ratio and Pb–O signals, and ToF-SIMS for oxygen ingress and iodine migration.
3.3 Correlate interfacial energetics and extraction: UPS/KPFM for work function/band alignment, impedance spectroscopy for recombination resistance, and transient photocurrent/photovoltage for charge extraction vs recombination.
3.4 Reliability testing: ISOS-L (continuous 1-sun), ISOS-O (oxygen), and damp-heat-like stressing with controlled RH; report T80, Voc retention, hysteresis index evolution, and failure-mode analysis. Include “overdose” controls (higher H2O2 flux) to demonstrate the necessity of the engineered release profile and confinement.
3.5 Mechanistic falsification tests: (i) replace SA layer with nanoparticle Fe/Cu to show loss of selectivity and/or accelerated degradation; (ii) block peroxide delivery to show reduced benefit; (iii) add radical scavengers in an inert topcoat to verify that interfacial ROS modulation (not bulk passivation) drives performance/stability changes.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Single-atom catalysts in MOF-derived N-doped carbon are established as highly active AOP/photo-Fenton catalysts that generate/convert ROS with high atomic efficiency and minimized aggregation; controlled release profiles of oxidant sources are known to tune ROS production kinetics. In PSCs, oxygen/light-induced ROS at electron-rich interfaces is a recognized degradation pathway; therefore, a selective ROS-management layer is chemically motivated.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The adaptation is not “adding a catalyst,” but engineering a solid-state, interface-confined AOP analogue where (i) single atoms provide selective redox cycling, (ii) a deliberately slow peroxide release profile prevents radical runaway, and (iii) spatial separation keeps oxidant precursors largely outside the absorber while allowing interfacial ROS cleanup where degradation initiates. This directly targets PSC bottlenecks: photo-oxidation, interfacial recombination, and ion migration driven by interfacial chemistry.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to conventional passivating ligands or 2D capping alone, the proposed layer is regenerative (catalytic) rather than consumptive, addressing continuous ROS generation during operation. Compared to nanoparticle catalysts, single-atom sites reduce parasitic absorption/scattering, minimize shunting risk, and avoid uncontrolled radical hotspots. The release-profile control introduces a tunable kinetic “safety valve,” enabling net ROS suppression (short-lived ·OH confined in the carbon) while removing long-lived oxidants that propagate bulk degradation, thus aiming to improve Voc and operational T80 simultaneously.
Critique: The proposal is unusually well engineered (SA synthesis/verification, controlled oxidant release, operando ROS diagnostics, and falsification controls are all specified). The main scientific risk is internal: introducing an H2O2 source into a PSC—even diffusion-limited—can create non-benign failure pathways that the current mechanistic argument does not quantitatively bound. In particular, the assumption that ·OH remains confined to the carbon interlayer is asserted rather than demonstrated with transport/kinetic limits (radical lifetime vs pore network vs proximity to perovskite A-site organics/iodide). The plan also under-specifies interfacial electronic consequences of inserting an N-doped carbon layer (possible Schottky barriers, increased series resistance, altered SnO2 surface states) and does not define acceptance metrics (e.g., maximum tolerable ΔRs/ΔFF, target QFLS gains) that would adjudicate tradeoffs. Finally, the ROS readouts (EPR spin traps/fluorescent probes) are notoriously perturbative in solids and near perovskites; without a clearly defined, non-invasive calibration strategy and probe localization control, the operando ROS claims risk ambiguity. Overall, the concept chain is coherent and the adaptation is creative, but the proposal needs harder quantitative constraints and materials-compatibility guardrails to justify that net chemistry remains protective rather than accelerative under realistic oxygen/water flux and illumination histories.
